title: MAGNIFIED: RL Fine-tuning of Multimodal Large Language Models for Motion Planning
summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in semantic understanding and common sense reasoning, making them promising candidates for solving planning problems in autonomous driving. However, the next-token text prediction objectives traditionally used in pre-training and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of MLLMs may fall short of fulfilling the planning objectives for autonomous vehicles. The next-token prediction objective merely encourages per-token imitation in text, often irrespective of multi-step consequences and the alignment with crucial planning considerations such as giving space to other road actors. To overcome these limitations, we propose a reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RLFT) approach, MAGNIFIED, that aligns the MLLM-based driving agent with planning objectives by learning from token-level rewards. By mapping a sequence of predicted tokens to corresponding vehicle trajectories and learning from planning rewards, MAGNIFIED optimizes for the true planning objectives rather than focusing solely on token prediction accuracy, enabling the model to refine its understanding of the planning task beyond simple imitation. We validate our approach on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset with a novel setup incorporating rasterized birds-eye views and tokenized trajectories as inputs and planning-oriented outputs. An initial SFT phase establishes a strong baseline in outputting plan trajectories as sequences of X-Y coordinates in text, while subsequent RL fine-tuning substantially enhances planning performance relative to the SFT baseline (demonstrating over a 10.5% reduction in overlap rate and a 38.9% reduction in off-road rate), underscoring the potential of RLFT on MLLMs to achieve vehicle planning that is better aligned with compliant, comfortable, and efficient driving.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MAGNIFIED, a reinforcement learning fine-tuning approach for Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) used in autonomous driving planning. It replaces traditional next-token prediction objectives with token-level planning rewards, achieving substantial improvements in overlap rate (10.5% reduction) and off-road rate (38.9% reduction) on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset.
AI.motivation: Traditional next-token text prediction objectives used in pre-training and SFT of MLLMs are insufficient for planning tasks in autonomous driving, as they merely encourage per-token imitation without considering multi-step consequences or alignment with crucial planning considerations like giving space to other road actors.
AI.method: MAGNIFIED uses reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RLFT) with token-level planning rewards to align MLLM-based driving agents with true planning objectives. It maps predicted token sequences to vehicle trajectories and learns from planning rewards rather than token prediction accuracy. The setup uses rasterized birds-eye views and tokenized trajectories as inputs/outputs, with an initial SFT phase followed by RL fine-tuning.
AI.result: Over 10.5% reduction in overlap rate and 38.9% reduction in off-road rate compared to the SFT baseline on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset.
AI.conclusion: RLFT on MLLMs has significant potential to achieve vehicle planning that is better aligned with compliant, comfortable, and efficient driving, outperforming standard SFT approaches that rely solely on next-token prediction.

title: TACT-ful: Multi-Channel Terrain Affordance and Compliance Training for Payload-Robust Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Foothold selection on structured terrain requires explicit reasoning about contact planarity, surface steepness, and kinematic reachability, properties not captured by a single height-based terrain signal. We propose a multi-channel terrain cost combining flatness, steepness, and velocity-aware height feasibility, plus a forward climb reward, that simultaneously drives a GPU-parallel divergent component of motion (DCM) foothold planner and shapes a dense per-step affordance reward for an asymmetric actor-critic policy trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) from depth images. A Bézier swing trajectory with adaptive apex bias extends foothold tracking to joint position-and-orientation, using the arc tangent to guide sole orientation through riser crossings and tread landings. To support payload tasks, we introduce a lower-body compliance training procedure in which a virtual wrench is injected at a sampled load attachment point, generating physically consistent force and moment; wrench-aware compliance targets replace rigid pose penalties, and the policy learns to yield to load-induced perturbations without force sensing. The full system trains end-to-end with standard PPO, no distillation, and no teacher-student staging, and is deployed on a humanoid directly from simulation with configuration changes only. In simulation, the policy reaches $1.0~\mathrm{m/s}$ on stairs with risers up to $0.20~\mathrm{m}$ and improves payload robustness up to ${\sim}15~\mathrm{kg}$ centered load and for moment-dominated wrist loads without fine-tuning. We also provide a qualitative hardware demonstration on structured terrain. Project website: https://fai-rl-tech.github.io/tact-locomotion.github.io/

AI.tldr: A multi-channel terrain cost and asymmetric actor-critic PPO framework for humanoid foothold selection on structured terrain, enabling 1.0 m/s stair climbing, payload robustness up to ~15 kg, and sim-to-real deployment without teacher-student staging.
AI.motivation: Foothold selection on structured terrain requires reasoning about contact planarity, surface steepness, and kinematic reachability, which are not captured by a single height-based terrain signal.
AI.method: Multi-channel terrain cost (flatness, steepness, velocity-aware height feasibility) + forward climb reward drives GPU-parallel DCM foothold planner and shapes per-step affordance reward for asymmetric actor-critic PPO trained from depth images. Bézier swing trajectory with adaptive apex bias and arc tangent sole orientation. Lower-body compliance training via virtual wrench injection at sampled load attachment point.
AI.result: 1.0 m/s on stairs with risers up to 0.20 m; payload robustness up to ~15 kg centered load and moment-dominated wrist loads; qualitative hardware demonstration on structured terrain.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end PPO training, no distillation or teacher-student staging, achieves sim-to-real deployment on a humanoid with configuration changes only, improving structured terrain locomotion and payload robustness.

title: Tessellated Biomes: Distributed Robotic Assemblies for Architectural Resilience
summary: This paper presents Tessellated Biomes, a cyber-physical framework for the adaptive robotic construction and reconfiguration of modular multi-material assemblies. It challenges the linear lifecycle of standard construction by fusing (1) local microfactory fabrication, (2) discrete multi-material optimization, and (3) distributed robotic assembly into a unified circular process of spatial adaptation. The research details methods for the digital fabrication of self-aligning modular primitives in multiple materials (PLA, timber, and concrete) produced in local microfactories; the aggregation and optimization of these primitives into compression-based discrete structures; and the deployment of custom quadrupedal robots that collaboratively relocate material into realized physical aggregations. The framework is validated through the fabrication, optimization, and robotic assembly of discrete structures. Together, these results position Tessellated Biomes as a model for resilient, reconfigurable architecture.

AI.tldr: Tessellated Biomes is a cyber-physical framework for adaptive robotic construction using modular multi-material assemblies, integrating microfactory fabrication, discrete optimization, and distributed robotic assembly into a circular construction process validated with PLA, timber, and concrete primitives assembled by quadrupedal robots.
AI.motivation: To challenge the linear lifecycle of standard construction by enabling adaptive, reconfigurable, and circular spatial construction processes rather than conventional single-use static structures.
AI.method: The framework integrates (1) local microfactory fabrication of self-aligning modular primitives in PLA, timber, and concrete, (2) aggregation and optimization of primitives into compression-based discrete structures, and (3) deployment of custom quadrupedal robots that collaboratively relocate material into physical aggregations.
AI.result: Successful fabrication, optimization, and robotic assembly of discrete multi-material structures, validating the cyber-physical framework.
AI.conclusion: Tessellated Biomes offers a model for resilient, reconfigurable architecture that unifies fabrication, structural optimization, and robotic construction in a circular process.

title: Learning Control as Enabling Layer for Embodied Intelligence Research explored with Soft Robotic Swimming in diverse Flow Speeds
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Data and code availability statements included
summary: Soft robots are valuable robophysical platforms for studying body-caudal undulatory locomotion, but their compliant bodies are difficult to control precisely under changing hydrodynamic loading. Conventional proportional-integral-derivative (PID) feedback stabilizes periodic undulation in static water, but can accumulate flow-dependent tracking delay and increasing inter-trial variability when environmental flow becomes non-trivial. Here, we evaluate whether augmenting PID control with a Linear Repetitive Learning Estimation Scheme (PID-LRLES) recovers tracking accuracy and repeatability under dynamic flow. The LRLES generalizes classical integral action from constant to periodic, non-constant references, while using a stable transfer-function realization whose poles have negative real parts to avoid the long-term instability issues of classical repetitive control. Closed-loop experiments were carried out in a recirculating flow tank at five bulk flow speeds spanning 0 to 32.6 cm s^-1, using an embedded soft capacitive bending sensor at a 1 kHz control-loop rate. With controller gains tuned once in static water and then held fixed across all conditions, PID-LRLES tracked the periodic bending-envelope reference more closely than the PID baseline and significantly reduced the inter-trial spread of the per-trial RMSE (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 1.8 x 10^-4, n = 25). Embedded soft proprioception and cycle-to-cycle learning act as complementary contributors to robustness: the sensor exposes the periodic hydrodynamic bias in body deformation, while the learning term absorbs it over recent oscillation cycles. By reducing flow-dependent control-induced variability, the approach provides an enabling layer for future robophysical studies seeking to isolate the effects of morphology, sensing, and environmental flow on aquatic locomotion.

AI.tldr: PID control augmented with a Linear Repetitive Learning Estimation Scheme (PID-LRLES) improves tracking accuracy and reduces inter-trial variability for soft robot undulatory locomotion under dynamic hydrodynamic flow, outperforming conventional PID across flow speeds from 0 to 32.6 cm s⁻¹.
AI.motivation: Soft robots are useful for studying body-caudal undulatory locomotion, but their compliant bodies are difficult to control precisely under changing hydrodynamic loading. Conventional PID feedback stabilizes periodic undulation in static water but accumulates flow-dependent tracking delay and increasing inter-trial variability when environmental flow becomes non-trivial.
AI.method: The authors augment PID control with a Linear Repetitive Learning Estimation Scheme (PID-LRLES), which generalizes classical integral action from constant to periodic, non-constant references using a stable transfer-function realization. Closed-loop experiments were conducted in a recirculating flow tank at five bulk flow speeds (0–32.6 cm s⁻¹), with an embedded soft capacitive bending sensor at a 1 kHz control-loop rate. Controller gains were tuned once in static water and held fixed across all conditions.
AI.result: PID-LRLES tracked the periodic bending-envelope reference more closely than the PID baseline and significantly reduced inter-trial spread of per-trial RMSE (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, n = 25).
AI.conclusion: Embedded soft proprioception and cycle-to-cycle learning act as complementary contributors to robustness: the sensor exposes periodic hydrodynamic bias in body deformation, while the learning term absorbs it over recent oscillation cycles. This approach reduces flow-dependent control-induced variability, providing an enabling layer for future robophysical studies isolating effects of morphology, sensing, and environmental flow on aquatic locomotion.

title: On the Identifiability of User Adaptation in Co-Adaptive Neural Interfaces
summary: We analyze identifiability in co-adaptive human-machine systems. We show that closed-loop encoder estimates do not uniquely identify user adaptation, but instead reflect properties of the joint system. We discuss implications for interpreting behavioral adaptation and propose conditions for identification.

AI.tldr: The paper examines identifiability issues in co-adaptive human-machine systems, demonstrating that closed-loop encoder estimates fail to uniquely isolate user adaptation and instead reflect joint system properties, with implications for behavioral adaptation interpretation and identification conditions.
AI.motivation: To address the fundamental challenge of distinguishing user adaptation from machine adaptation in co-adaptive systems, where closed-loop measurements confound the contributions of both subsystems.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of identifiability in closed-loop co-adaptive systems, examining encoder estimates and their relationship to joint system dynamics.
AI.result: Closed-loop encoder estimates do not uniquely identify user adaptation but rather reflect properties of the joint human-machine system as a whole.
AI.conclusion: Interpretation of behavioral adaptation in co-adaptive systems must account for the confounding nature of closed-loop estimates; specific conditions are required for proper identification of user adaptation.

title: MemoryVAM: Integrating Memory into Video Action Model for Robot Manipulation
summary: Video-world-model policies learn action-relevant representations by predicting future observations. However, they condition on only a short observation window, which renders long-horizon manipulation non-Markovian when the correct action depends on earlier events that are no longer visible. We present MemoryVAM, an episodic memory mechanism for video-world-model policies. We employ a Recap-Cue (RC) module, in which a Perceiver-based Recap Compressor maps per-frame CLIP embeddings into compact memory tokens, and a lightweight Cue Gate estimates task completion from memory and language. These tokens are injected into both the video backbone and the action decoder, aligning policy imagination with episode progress and conditioning actions on history. Our model trains the memory module with video prediction, a delta-reconstruction auxiliary loss, and episode-boundary supervision, requiring no per-frame progress labels. The same mechanism applies to UNet and Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbones by changing only the cross-attention injection interface. On LIBERO-Mem, our model improves average success from 5% to 42.5%. On real robots, it achieves 78.3% success on counting tasks, 80.0% on spatial recall, and 75.0% on sequential tracking. Project page: https://MemoryVAM.github.io/

AI.tldr: MemoryVAM introduces an episodic memory mechanism (Recap-Cue module) for video-world-model policies, enabling long-horizon manipulation by conditioning actions on historical context, achieving significant improvements on LIBERO-Mem (5%→42.5%) and real robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard video-world-model policies condition on only a short observation window, making long-horizon manipulation non-Markovian when correct actions depend on earlier events no longer visible in the current window.
AI.method: MemoryVAM uses a Recap-Cue (RC) module: a Perceiver-based Recap Compressor maps per-frame CLIP embeddings into compact memory tokens, and a lightweight Cue Gate estimates task completion from memory and language. Memory tokens are injected into both the video backbone and action decoder via cross-attention. The memory module is trained with video prediction, delta-reconstruction auxiliary loss, and episode-boundary supervision, requiring no per-frame progress labels. The mechanism works with both UNet and DiT backbones.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Mem, success improves from 5% to 42.5%. On real robots: 78.3% on counting tasks, 80.0% on spatial recall, and 75.0% on sequential tracking.
AI.conclusion: Episodic memory significantly enhances video-world-model policies for long-horizon non-Markovian manipulation tasks, with a compact and backbone-agnostic design.

title: Beyond Fixed Budgets: Characterizing the Inelasticity and Limitations of Tree-of-Thought Reasoning Strategies
summary: Tree of Thought (ToT) search has become a promising direction for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but deploying these methods in practice raises a question that has received little systematic attention: how do different search strategies behave under varying compute budgets, model sizes, and problem difficulties? In this work, we evaluate two representative ToT methods; DPTS, a Monte Carlo tree search based approach, and SSDP, a semantic deduplication based approach, across two mathematical reasoning benchmarks (Math500 and GSM8K), two model scales (Llama-3B and Llama-8B), and four token budgets (3k--10k). Our analysis reveals that the two methods exhibit limitations that pull in opposite directions. DPTS suffers from a cold-start bottleneck at low budgets: it requires sufficient exploration before its value estimates become reliable, making it a poor fit for resource-constrained settings despite strong scaling behavior at higher budgets. SSDP, on the other hand, reaches candidate solutions efficiently but is prone to frontier depletion; its aggressive node merging permanently discards unexplored paths, leaving it unable to improve regardless of how much budget remains. Together, these findings suggest that neither a fixed exploration strategy nor a fixed pruning strategy is sufficient across compute continuum. We argue that effective search for scientific reasoning agents requires strategies that can adapt their behavior based on search progress and available resources.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates two Tree of Thought methods (DPTS with Monte Carlo tree search and SSDP with semantic deduplication) across different compute budgets, model sizes, and problem difficulties. DPTS struggles at low budgets due to cold-start issues but scales well, while SSDP efficiently finds initial solutions but suffers from frontier depletion, unable to improve with more budget. The authors argue for adaptive search strategies.
AI.motivation: Little systematic attention has been given to how different ToT search strategies behave under varying compute budgets, model sizes, and problem difficulties, which is critical for practical deployment.
AI.method: Evaluation of DPTS (Monte Carlo tree search based) and SSDP (semantic deduplication based) across two math reasoning benchmarks (Math500, GSM8K), two model scales (Llama-3B, Llama-8B), and four token budgets (3k-10k).
AI.result: DPTS suffers from cold-start bottleneck at low budgets but scales well; SSDP efficiently reaches candidates but suffers from frontier depletion, unable to improve with more budget.
AI.conclusion: Neither fixed exploration nor fixed pruning strategy suffices across the compute continuum; effective search requires adaptive strategies based on search progress and available resources.

title: JPPD: Joint Prediction_Planning Diffusion with Differentiable Safety Guidance for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance in Intelligent Transportation Systems
summary: Shared-space transportation operation requires low-speed autonomous platforms to navigate safely and efficiently among pedestrians, service robots, micromobility users, carts, and other road users. Most existing systems decompose this problem into trajectory prediction followed by motion planning, which creates one-way information flow: predicted participant futures influence the robot plan, but the selected robot plan cannot influence the predicted multi-agent evolution. This paper presents a joint prediction-planning diffusion framework that treats participant prediction and robot planning as a single conditional trajectory generation problem, where the model samples the future robot trajectory and all participant trajectories from one coupled distribution using a causal Transformer with cross-trajectory attention. To replace heuristic repulsive post-processing, the framework introduces differentiable safety potential guidance, a time-varying occupancy-probability potential whose gradient directly guides the joint sampler, and conditional flow matching is used to reduce inference steps while preserving multimodal trajectory diversity. The evaluation emphasizes shared-space operational effects, including near misses, blockage time, induced participant deviation, hard-braking events, and embedded latency, rather than treating average displacement error and final displacement error as the main result. Experiments in scenario-grounded simulation, naturalistic pedestrian replay, Isaac Sim validation, and ROS/Orin deployment show that joint sampling improves tail safety and runtime efficiency over a separated prediction-then-planning baseline.

AI.tldr: A joint prediction-planning diffusion framework that treats multi-agent trajectory prediction and robot planning as a single conditional generation problem, using a causal Transformer with cross-trajectory attention and differentiable safety potential guidance, achieving improved tail safety and runtime efficiency in shared-space navigation.
AI.motivation: Existing shared-space navigation systems decompose the problem into trajectory prediction followed by motion planning, creating a one-way information flow where the robot plan cannot influence predicted multi-agent evolution, leading to suboptimal safety and efficiency.
AI.method: A joint prediction-planning diffusion framework that (1) models robot and participant trajectories as a single coupled distribution using a causal Transformer with cross-trajectory attention; (2) introduces differentiable safety potential guidance with time-varying occupancy-probability potential for gradient-based joint sampling; (3) uses conditional flow matching to reduce inference steps while preserving multimodal diversity.
AI.result: Experiments in scenario-grounded simulation, naturalistic pedestrian replay, Isaac Sim validation, and ROS/Orin deployment show joint sampling improves tail safety and runtime efficiency over separated prediction-then-planning baselines.
AI.conclusion: Joint prediction-planning diffusion framework outperforms conventional separated approaches in shared-space operation, particularly on safety-critical tail metrics such as near misses, blockage time, induced participant deviation, hard-braking events, and embedded latency.

title: The New Associationism: Lessons from Deep Learning
summary: What can the success of modern AI tell us about how humans learn? This paper argues that taking AI seriously as a model of human learning supports a modest but genuine associationism. The central finding is that supervised learning -- learning driven by evaluative feedback -- underlies a surprisingly wide range of contemporary AI systems, from large language models to game-playing agents, differing primarily in how much work is required to generate the relevant feedback signal. This vindicates associationist ideals of a uniform, gradual, error-driven learning mechanism operating across domains, and defuses the once-influential argument that associationist mechanisms are too limited to account for human cognitive capacities. At the same time, the successes of deep learning depend on computational architectures that go well beyond anything classical associationists envisaged, and supervised learning operates within these as one component rather than a complete account of learning.

AI.tldr: Modern AI success supports a modest associationism: supervised learning (error-driven, uniform, gradual) underlies diverse AI systems, vindicating associationist ideals, though deep learning's complex architectures go beyond classical associationism.
AI.motivation: To argue that the success of modern AI (especially supervised learning) provides evidence for a modest form of associationism as a model of human learning, and to counter the criticism that associationist mechanisms are too limited to explain human cognition.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis and argumentation: examining supervised learning across diverse AI systems (LLMs, game-playing agents) and showing how they share a uniform, gradual, error-driven learning mechanism, while also noting that deep learning architectures exceed classical associationist frameworks.
AI.result: Supervised learning is a widespread mechanism across AI systems, differing mainly in how feedback signals are generated, which vindicates associationist principles; however, modern architectures go beyond classical associationism and supervised learning is only one component of learning.
AI.conclusion: Modern AI supports a modest associationism: a uniform error-driven learning mechanism is viable across domains, but the computational architectures of deep learning surpass classical associationist views, and supervised learning is one component rather than a complete theory of learning.

title: SafeDojo: Safe Reinforcement Learning for VLA via Interactive World Model
summary: Safe control is a prerequisite for real-world embodied intelligence, for which safe reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising paradigm. However, existing safe reinforcement learning methods either require costly real-world exploration or depend on hand-crafted safety functions. Neither scales to vision-language-action models deployed in open-world physical environments. We propose SafeDojo, the first model-based safe reinforcement learning framework for vision-language-action policies designed to learn safe actions through world model-based imagination. Specifically, SafeDojo performs online reinforcement learning on top of an interactive video world model. The world model generates action-conditioned future predictions, from which a tailored ResNet success classifier estimates per-step task progress from imagined frames and a lightweight safety head predicts per-step safety costs from latent context together with the proposed action chunk, enabling simultaneous assessment of task execution and trajectory safety. The decoupled task-reward and safety-cost signals are balanced through a Lagrangian-based constrained GRPO objective, enabling coordinated improvement of task success and safety under explicit constraints. On SafeLIBERO, SafeDojo achieves the best aggregate task success, safe success, and execution efficiency among inference-time safety, model-free RL, and model-based RL baselines, with the best average safe-success rate on both levels and an 8.25 percentage-point improvement over the strongest baseline on Level I. Real-world Franka deployment further shows the best average task and safe-success rates across five tasks. Our results position world model-based safe reinforcement learning as a scalable and generalizable path toward safe embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: SafeDojo is the first model-based safe RL framework for vision-language-action policies that learns safe actions via world model-based imagination, using a Lagrangian-based constrained GRPO objective to balance task success and safety. It achieves state-of-the-art results on SafeLIBERO and real-world Franka tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing safe RL methods require costly real-world exploration or hand-crafted safety functions, which do not scale to vision-language-action models deployed in open-world physical environments.
AI.method: SafeDojo performs online RL on an interactive video world model. It uses a ResNet success classifier for per-step task progress from imagined frames and a lightweight safety head for per-step safety costs from latent context with action chunks, balanced via a Lagrangian-based constrained GRPO objective.
AI.result: On SafeLIBERO, SafeDojo achieves best aggregate task success, safe success, and execution efficiency, with an 8.25 percentage-point improvement on Level I over the strongest baseline. Real-world Franka deployment shows best average task and safe-success rates across five tasks.
AI.conclusion: World model-based safe reinforcement learning is a scalable and generalizable path toward safe embodied intelligence.

title: Specifying AI-SDLC Processes: A Protocol Language for Human-Agent Boundaries
comment: Position paper with formal specification, failure rate analysis, and feasibility demonstration. Companion empirical paper and open-source implementation forthcoming
summary:
AI agents now participate as first-class team members across the software development lifecycle, yet no specification language exists for expressing the human-agent responsibility boundaries, approval gates, and governance constraints this collaboration requires. Existing approaches encode process in agent prompts (subject to drift), target adjacent domains (workflow management, business processes), or address only fragments (access control, approval gates).
  We propose a domain-specific language for specifying AI-SDLC processes as protocols, with formal syntax, well-formedness conditions, operational semantics, and enforcement invariants. The language distinguishes policy (declared intent) from mechanism (structural enforcement), enabling implementations to bound process non-determinism through primitives such as validation tokens and capability boundaries.
  Three results follow. A failure rate analysis shows that structural enforcement bounds system failure rates at a weighted product of agent and validator rates, while behavioral compliance permits cumulative or near-saturating growth. The 2+N team pattern (two human-in-control roles plus N specialized agent members) formalizes classical Separation of Duties for AI-SDLC. Kleene closure of orchestration loops and reflexive protocol-adherence validation emerge as design properties rather than special-case constructs.
  We position the contribution against multi-agent frameworks (MetaGPT), workflow specification (FlowAgent, BPMN extensions), and capability-based security (SAGA): the novelty lies in the specific integration, not any single primitive. A working implementation demonstrates feasibility; empirical evaluation is future work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a domain-specific language (DSL) for specifying human-agent responsibility boundaries, approval gates, and governance constraints in AI-assisted software development lifecycles (AI-SDLC), distinguishing policy from structural enforcement with formal syntax and semantics.
AI.motivation: AI agents now act as first-class team members in software development, but no specification language exists to formally express human-agent responsibility boundaries, approval gates, and governance constraints. Existing approaches (agent prompts, workflow management, access control) are fragmented or subject to drift.
AI.method: The authors propose a DSL for AI-SDLC processes as protocols, featuring formal syntax, well-formedness conditions, operational semantics, and enforcement invariants. It distinguishes policy (declared intent) from mechanism (structural enforcement), using primitives like validation tokens and capability boundaries to bound process non-determinism.
AI.result: (1) Failure rate analysis: structural enforcement bounds failure at a weighted product of agent and validator rates, while behavioral compliance permits cumulative/saturating growth. (2) The 2+N team pattern formalizes Separation of Duties for AI-SDLC. (3) Kleene closure of orchestration loops and reflexive protocol-adherence validation emerge as design properties.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is positioned against MetaGPT, FlowAgent, BPMN extensions, and SAGA, with novelty in the specific integration of primitives. A working implementation demonstrates feasibility; empirical evaluation is left as future work.

title: Real-World Deployment of Massively Parallel Sampling-Based MPC for Contact-Rich Manipulation
comment: Presented at ICRA Workshop on Frontiers of Optimization for Robotics, 2nd Edition (OpenReview, 2026) OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=0KFJunxC8I&noteId=go6pmKSpzr
summary: Sampling-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) is a promising strategy for contact-rich robotic manipulation, combining gradient-free optimization with massively parallel GPU simulation. Yet, most prior work relies on simplified dynamics or remains confined to simulation. We present an MPC framework that leverages JAX for large-scale parallelization and efficient computation, coupled with the high-fidelity MuJoCo MJX simulator, and deploy it on a Franka Research 3 executing the Push-T manipulation task through a complete real-to-sim-to-real pipeline. The MTP variant with structured global sampling outperforms unimodal baselines such as CEM, MPPI, and PS across tasks that require mode switching, both in simulation and on hardware. Furthermore, we evaluate online domain randomization within the MPC sample budget, showing that contact-initiation parameters yield interpretable adaptation signals, whereas global physics parameters provide feedback that is too weak for reliable exploitation at typical replanning frequencies. These findings highlight key challenges for sampling-based MPC in contact-rich manipulation-contact sensitivity, tight compute budgets, and the difficulty of obtaining informative domain-randomization signals in real time.

AI.tldr: An SMPC framework using JAX and MuJoCo MJX is deployed on a real Franka Research 3 for Push-T task. MTP with structured global sampling outperforms unimodal baselines. Online domain randomization shows contact-initiation parameters provide useful adaptation signals but global physics parameters do not at typical replanning frequencies.
AI.motivation: Prior SMPC work relies on simplified dynamics or remains confined to simulation; there is a need for real-world deployment of sampling-based MPC for contact-rich manipulation.
AI.method: Leverages JAX for large-scale parallelization and MuJoCo MJX for high-fidelity simulation; implements MTP variant with structured global sampling; evaluates online domain randomization within MPC sample budget.
AI.result: MTP outperforms CEM, MPPI, and PS in mode-switching tasks in both simulation and hardware. Contact-initiation domain randomization yields interpretable adaptation; global physics parameters provide too weak feedback for real-time exploitation.
AI.conclusion: Highlights key challenges for sampling-based MPC in contact-rich manipulation: contact sensitivity, tight compute budgets, and difficulty of obtaining informative domain-randomization signals in real time.

title: PEAR: Permutation-Equivariant Adaptive Routing Multi-Agent Debate
summary: Multi-agent debate improves the reliability of large language models (LLMs) through iterative peer critiques. However, fixed topologies often introduce persistent positional biases, amplify unreliable agents, and cause high sensitivity to role assignments. We introduce \textit{Permutation-Equivariant Adaptive Routing Multi-Agent Debate (PEAR)}, an inference-time protocol that dynamically reconfigures communication roles and sparse topologies across consecutive debate rounds. By strategically switching agent-to-role assignments based on evolving agent states, PEAR prevents any agent from permanently occupying a privileged network position or distributes influence more evenly across the debate. We theoretically characterize PEAR as an equivariant sparse router: it preserves accuracy under agent relabeling while reducing routing complexity and improving generalization. Comprehensive empirical evaluations across four reasoning benchmarks and six diverse LLM backbones demonstrate PEAR significantly improves average accuracy over the strongest debate baselines. The code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/PEAR.

AI.tldr: PEAR is an inference-time protocol that dynamically reconfigures communication roles and sparse topologies across debate rounds, using permutation-equivariant adaptive routing to overcome positional biases and role sensitivity in multi-agent LLM debates, achieving superior accuracy across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Fixed topologies in multi-agent debate introduce persistent positional biases, amplify unreliable agents, and cause high sensitivity to role assignments, degrading robustness and fairness.
AI.method: PEAR dynamically reconfigures agent-to-role assignments and sparse topologies across consecutive debate rounds based on evolving agent states, functioning as an equivariant sparse router that preserves accuracy under agent relabeling.
AI.result: PEAR significantly improves average accuracy over the strongest debate baselines across four reasoning benchmarks and six diverse LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Permutation-equivariant adaptive routing effectively mitigates topological biases in multi-agent debate, reducing routing complexity while improving generalization and reliability.

title: Coupled Routing and Configuration Optimization for Multi-Viewpoint Robotic Inspection
summary: We present a unified framework that turns a set of 6-DoF inspection viewpoints into a time-optimal, collision-free route for a 9-DoF robotic system. Unlike modular pipelines that fix a single inverse-kinematics (IK) configuration per viewpoint, build an all-pairs travel-time map, and then route, our method jointly optimizes the visiting order and the per-viewpoint configuration in a single global search. The three-dimensional self-motion manifold of each viewpoint is parameterized in closed form so that the pose constraint holds by construction, the rest-to-rest travel time is approximated by a closed-form admissible double-integrator surrogate, and the tour is encoded by random keys. A derivative-free optimizer (CMA-ES) minimizes a cheap penalized objective over order and configuration, after which direct-collocation trajectory optimization is applied only to the edges of the selected route to certify dynamic feasibility and torque limits, and to return exact timings. This reduces the trajectory solves from quadratic to linear in the number of viewpoints and removes the decoupling that prevents modular pipelines from being globally time-optimal. Simulations and real-robot experiments on a KUKA LBR iiwa with a 2-DoF linear stage validate feasibility, smooth execution, and reduced end-to-end inspection time relative to modular and naive distance-based baselines.

AI.tldr: A unified framework jointly optimizes viewpoint order and IK configurations for a 9-DoF robotic system to achieve time-optimal, collision-free inspection tours, using closed-form parametrization of self-motion manifolds, a double-integrator surrogate for travel time, CMA-ES optimization, and direct-collocation trajectory verification only on selected edges.
AI.motivation: Modular pipelines decouple IK assignment from routing, leading to globally suboptimal inspection tours. The goal is to achieve globally time-optimal, collision-free routes by jointly optimizing visiting order and per-viewpoint robot configurations.
AI.method: (1) Closed-form parametrization of the 3D self-motion manifold per viewpoint to enforce pose constraints; (2) Closed-form admissible double-integrator surrogate for rest-to-rest travel time; (3) Random-key encoding of the tour; (4) CMA-ES derivative-free optimization minimizing a cheap penalized objective over order and configuration; (5) Direct-collocation trajectory optimization only on selected edges to certify feasibility and compute exact timings.
AI.result: Reduced trajectory solves from quadratic to linear in the number of viewpoints. Validated in simulation and on a KUKA LBR iiwa with a 2-DoF linear stage, showing feasibility, smooth execution, and reduced end-to-end inspection time compared to modular and naive distance-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing viewpoint order and IK configurations within a single global search yields time-optimal routes that outperform modular decoupled pipelines, while maintaining dynamic feasibility and torque limit satisfaction via targeted direct-collocation verification.

title: Darwin Mobile Agent: A Roadmap for Self-Evolution
summary: The goal of artificial intelligence is to create agents capable of general, adaptive behaviour in open-ended environments. Guided by the "Bitter Lesson", we argue that the most effective path toward this goal is to systematically remove human priors and allow intelligence to naturally emerge through interaction with a "Big World" that is orders of magnitude more complex than the agent itself. We propose the mobile Graphical User Interface (GUI) as a practical proxy for such a world and introduce Darwin Mobile Agent, an open-source infrastructure designed as a foundation for autonomous reinforcement learning in this domain. This framework addresses the data-collection bottleneck in real-world mobile interactions by using an asynchronous agent-environment loop across parallel cloud-phone instances. We further propose a conceptual roadmap to systematically remove human priors from three fundamental pillars of a self-evolving agent: task curricula, outcome verification, and memory management. We validate that the Darwin infrastructure provides the stability and scalability required for the first stage of this roadmap: policy optimisation in the GUI domain. This work establishes the practical and theoretical foundation necessary to move toward truly autonomous, self-evolving GUI agents.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that the path to general AI is through removing human priors and enabling autonomous learning in a "Big World", proposing mobile GUI as a practical proxy. It introduces Darwin Mobile Agent, an open-source infrastructure using asynchronous parallel cloud-phone instances to overcome data-collection bottlenecks, and outlines a roadmap to remove human priors from task curricula, outcome verification, and memory management for self-evolving GUI agents.
AI.motivation: To create agents capable of general, adaptive behaviour in open-ended environments by following the "Bitter Lesson" — systematically removing human priors and letting intelligence emerge through interaction with a complex world.
AI.method: Proposes mobile GUI as a proxy for a "Big World"; introduces Darwin Mobile Agent, an open-source infrastructure with asynchronous agent-environment loops across parallel cloud-phone instances to address data-collection bottlenecks; outlines a conceptual roadmap to remove human priors from task curricula, outcome verification, and memory management.
AI.result: Validation that the Darwin infrastructure provides the stability and scalability required for the first stage of the roadmap: policy optimisation in the GUI domain.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the practical and theoretical foundation necessary to move toward truly autonomous, self-evolving GUI agents.

title: A Digital Twin Framework for Traffic-Aware UAV Pavement Monitoring without Lane Closure
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 6th Annual IEEE International Conference on Digital Twins and Parallel Intelligence (DTPI 2026)
summary: UAV-based pavement inspection can reduce the cost and risk of road-surface monitoring, but real-world deployment remains difficult when traffic, pedestrians, and temporary occlusions affect the visibility of defects. This paper presents a Unity-based digital twin framework for traffic-aware UAV pavement monitoring without lane closure. The proposed environment integrates procedurally generated road defects, dynamic vehicles and pedestrians, autonomous UAV navigation, and an embedded road-damage perception pipeline. The perception module uses a two-stage approach: a lightweight YOLOv8n detector first localises road defects, pedestrians, and vehicles, while a second classifier distinguishes among potholes, single cracks, and crocodile cracks. On the simulator test set, the full pipeline achieved 99.26% overall accuracy across five classes. The digital twin was then used to evaluate three recovery strategies for occluded road segments: hover-and-recheck, micro-repositioning, and skip-and-revisit. Experiments were conducted across different traffic densities and flight altitudes using coverage, mission time, energy consumption, and revisit ratio as operational metrics. Results show that flight altitude has a strong influence on inspection coverage and that adaptive recovery improves performance under occlusion. In particular, hover-and-recheck achieved the most consistent coverage under medium and high traffic conditions, reaching up to 97.03% coverage, while skip-and-revisit was most effective in low-traffic scenarios, reaching 97.95\% coverage at medium altitude. These results demonstrate that digital twins can support the development and evaluation of traffic-aware UAV inspection strategies before real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Unity-based digital twin framework for traffic-aware UAV pavement inspection without lane closure, integrating procedurally generated road defects, dynamic traffic agents, autonomous UAV navigation, and a two-stage detection pipeline (YOLOv8n + classifier) that achieved 99.26% accuracy. Three occlusion recovery strategies (hover-and-recheck, micro-repositioning, skip-and-revisit) were evaluated across traffic densities and altitudes, with hover-and-recheck reaching up to 97.03% coverage under high traffic.
AI.motivation: UAV-based pavement inspection reduces cost and risk but real-world deployment is challenged by traffic, pedestrians, and occlusions affecting defect visibility. The authors aim to develop and evaluate traffic-aware UAV inspection strategies without requiring lane closure.
AI.method: A Unity-based digital twin framework with procedurally generated road defects, dynamic vehicles/pedestrians, autonomous UAV navigation, and a two-stage perception pipeline (YOLOv8n detector + secondary classifier). Three recovery strategies (hover-and-recheck, micro-repositioning, skip-and-revisit) were evaluated across traffic densities and flight altitudes using coverage, mission time, energy, and revisit ratio metrics.
AI.result: The two-stage pipeline achieved 99.26% overall accuracy across five classes. Hover-and-recheck achieved most consistent coverage under medium/high traffic (up to 97.03%), while skip-and-revisit was most effective in low-traffic scenarios (97.95% at medium altitude). Flight altitude strongly influenced inspection coverage.
AI.conclusion: Digital twins can support the development and evaluation of traffic-aware UAV inspection strategies before real-world deployment, with adaptive recovery strategies improving performance under occlusion.

title: Path-dependent program induction under resource constraints explains human sequence learning
summary: How do people build abstract, reusable knowledge from sequential experience under bounded cognitive resources? To answer this question, we integrate rate-distortion theory with recent advances in program induction to describe how prior knowledge shapes which future structures are cheap to encode and easy to discover. We formalize this in a hierarchical Adaptor Grammar (HAG) with distinct local (within-task) and global (across-task) libraries, governed jointly by constraints on memory and computation. In simulations, HAG achieves better rate-distortion trade-offs and stronger generalization than fixed grammars or shallow chunking methods. In an online melodic sequence-learning experiment, participants' recall errors reflected systematic simplifications and reaction times increased at inferred program boundaries. Trial-by-trial fits further showed that hierarchical libraries best explained individual differences in both recall and out-of-sample continuation choices, outperforming all alternative models. These findings cast structured learning as bounded program induction in which the order of experience shapes future abstractions a learner builds.

AI.tldr: The paper integrates rate-distortion theory with program induction to model how people build hierarchical, reusable knowledge from sequential experience under cognitive constraints. The proposed Hierarchical Adaptor Grammar (HAG) outperforms alternative models in both computational benchmarks and human experiments on melodic sequence learning, with participants' recall errors, reaction times, and continuation choices best explained by hierarchical library learning.
AI.motivation: To understand how people construct abstract, reusable knowledge from sequential experience despite bounded cognitive resources (limited memory and computation).
AI.method: Integrates rate-distortion theory with program induction in a Hierarchical Adaptor Grammar (HAG) featuring distinct local (within-task) and global (across-task) libraries, constrained by memory and computation limits. Tested in simulations and an online melodic sequence-learning experiment with model comparison.
AI.result: HAG achieved better rate-distortion trade-offs and stronger generalization than fixed grammars or shallow chunking. In human experiments, recall errors showed systematic simplifications, reaction times increased at inferred program boundaries, and hierarchical libraries best explained individual differences in recall and continuation choices.
AI.conclusion: Structured learning can be understood as bounded program induction where the order of experience shapes the abstractions a learner builds.

title: Toward Machine Risk Perception: Integrating Trust Calibration and Precursor-Based Risk Estimation for Humanoid
summary: Humanoid robots are emerging as co-workers in smart manufacturing, yet their dynamic, human-like movements introduce safety risks that differ fundamentally from those of fixed or wheeled robots. Conventional safety paradigms based on reactive force or distance limits fail to capture the sequential, uncertain nature of humanoid failures. This study proposes a precursor-driven, trust-calibrated framework to enable proactive humanoid risk perception. Accident evolution is modeled through sequential precursor cues using a Logistic-Exponential (LE) formulation that couples logistic escalation from diverse precursors with exponential decay for temporal dissipation. Trust is defined as the inverse of the estimated accident probability, allowing humanoids to adapt behavior in real time, reducing aggressiveness when risk intensifies, and restoring confidence as stability returns. A multi-source dataset of 126 documented events and 241 precursors revealed twelve dominant accident modes, most evolving through overlapping cues within one second. A simulated case study ("fall-onto-human") demonstrated how the LE-Trust coupling can trigger early intervention and prevent collapse. The results advance humanoid safety from static thresholds toward dynamic, evidence-based inference, establishing a foundation for risk-aware and trustworthy human-robot collaboration in Industry 5.0 environments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a precursor-driven, trust-calibrated framework (LE-Trust) for proactive humanoid robot risk perception in smart manufacturing, modeling accident evolution via Logistic-Exponential formulation and defining trust as inverse accident probability, validated on 126 events/241 precursors and a "fall-onto-human" case study.
AI.motivation: Conventional safety paradigms (reactive force/distance limits) fail to address the sequential, uncertain failure modes of humanoid robots in human-robot collaboration; a proactive risk perception framework is needed.
AI.method: Logistic-Exponential (LE) formulation coupling logistic escalation from diverse precursors with exponential temporal decay; trust defined as inverse of estimated accident probability enabling real-time behavior adaptation.
AI.result: 12 dominant accident modes identified from 126 events/241 precursors, most evolving through overlapping cues within 1 second; LE-Trust coupling enabled early intervention and collapse prevention in "fall-onto-human" simulation.
AI.conclusion: Advances humanoid safety from static thresholds to dynamic, evidence-based inference, establishing a foundation for risk-aware human-robot collaboration in Industry 5.0.

title: In LLM Reasoning, there is Irrationality on top of Value Misalignment
summary: Significant progress has been made in aligning LLMs with target value functions. We argue that, even when an LLM has been well aligned in (post-)training, it may still fail to maximise the aligned value in reasoning. We mathematically formalise this gap as rational value risk: the utility discrepancy between a model's deployed reasoning strategy and its rational counterpart, which is defined to be the responses that maximise expected utility in the steepest direction. The estimation error of rational value risk is further decomposed into three components from finite candidates, finite prompts, and imperfect verifiers. Extensive experiments are conducted, covering models Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5, T{\"}ulu-3 families (7B-72B), GPT-5.2, GPT-5.5, and DeepSeek-V4, and benchmarks UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MathArena. The results validate that (1) rational value risk is widespread; (2) value alignment can reduce, but cannot eliminate, it; (3) the risk is highly sensitive to inference-time reasoning strategy; and (4) longer reasoning improves rationality with diminishing returns. The code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/LLM-Rationality.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "rational value risk" to formalize the gap between an LLM's actual reasoning and its optimal rational reasoning even after alignment training, decomposes the estimation error, and empirically demonstrates this risk is widespread, persistent post-alignment, sensitive to inference strategies, and reduced by longer reasoning with diminishing returns.
AI.motivation: Even well-aligned LLMs may fail to maximize aligned values during reasoning (inference time), creating a gap that current alignment methods (post-training) do not fully address. The authors aim to formalize and measure this gap.
AI.method: Mathematically formalizes "rational value risk" as the utility discrepancy between a model's deployed reasoning strategy and its rational counterpart (responses maximizing expected utility in the steepest direction). Decomposes estimation error into three components: finite candidates, finite prompts, and imperfect verifiers. Empirically evaluates across Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5, Tülu-3 (7B-72B), GPT-5.2, GPT-5.5, and DeepSeek-V4 on UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MathArena.
AI.result: (1) Rational value risk is widespread across models; (2) value alignment reduces but cannot eliminate it; (3) the risk is highly sensitive to inference-time reasoning strategy; (4) longer reasoning improves rationality but with diminishing returns.
AI.conclusion: A formal gap exists between alignment training and rational inference-time behavior. Mitigating this requires attention to inference strategies beyond post-training alignment. Longer reasoning helps but yields diminishing improvements.

title: Perturbation-Based Uncertainty for Failure Detection in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong performance in robotic manipulation, but reliable uncertainty quantification remains challenging, particularly under distribution shift. Unlike autoregressive policies, many modern VLA models generate continuous actions through regression or flow-based generation, where explicit predictive probabilities are unavailable. Moreover, existing approaches often rely on stochastic action sampling or supervised failure labels, limiting their applicability across diverse pretrained VLA models. In this work, we propose a label-free and model-agnostic framework for inference-time uncertainty estimation through hidden activation perturbations, motivated by Bayesian perspectives on local model variations. Specifically, we inject Gaussian perturbations into transformer hidden activations and estimate epistemic signals from disagreement across perturbed action predictions. Experiments on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO show that perturbation-based uncertainty consistently improves failure detection under distribution shift compared to sampling-based uncertainty, providing a practical uncertainty signal for VLA models.

AI.tldr: A label-free, model-agnostic framework using hidden activation perturbations (Gaussian noise injected into transformer activations) to estimate epistemic uncertainty for VLA models, improving failure detection under distribution shift on LIBERO/LIBERO-PRO benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models lack reliable uncertainty quantification, especially under distribution shift. Autoregressive policies provide predictive probabilities, but many modern VLA models use regression/flow-based generation without explicit probabilities. Current methods rely on stochastic action sampling or supervised failure labels, limiting applicability across diverse pretrained models.
AI.method: Inject Gaussian perturbations into transformer hidden activations, then estimate epistemic uncertainty from disagreement (variance) across perturbed action predictions at inference time. This is motivated by Bayesian perspectives on local model variations.
AI.result: Perturbation-based uncertainty consistently outperforms sampling-based uncertainty for failure detection under distribution shift on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical, label-free, and model-agnostic uncertainty signal for VLA models, improving reliability in robotic manipulation without requiring model modifications or failure supervision.

title: AlphaMemo: Structured Search-Process Memory for Self-Evolving Alpha Mining Agents
summary: LLM agents are promising for alpha mining via combining financial priors, symbolic reasoning, executable factor generation, and feedback-driven refinement. Yet, they face a combinatorial search space, noisy non-stationary feedback, redundant discoveries, and overfitting risks from naively reusing past successes. To address these challenges, we propose AlphaMemo, a self-evolving alpha mining agent with Structured Search-Process Memory. Rather than memorizing only final factors or full trajectories, AlphaMemo records reusable evidence about which edit motifs work or fail under specific parent-factor contexts. It extracts motifs from Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) differences, applies confidence-gated residual memory on top of a search-ledger prior, and uses asymmetric veto control to suppress high-confidence failure patterns. Experiments on CSI 500 and S\&P 500 show improved out-of-sample performance and fixed-budget discovery efficiency, with ablations validating the roles of residual learning, confidence gating, AST-diff motifs, and veto memory. Code is at https://github.com/jarrettyu/AlphaMemo.

AI.tldr: AlphaMemo introduces a self-evolving alpha mining agent with structured search-process memory that records reusable edit motifs from AST diffs, using confidence-gated residual memory and asymmetric veto control, achieving improved out-of-sample performance and discovery efficiency on CSI 500 and S&P 500.
AI.motivation: LLM agents for alpha mining face challenges including combinatorial search space, noisy non-stationary feedback, redundant discoveries, and overfitting risks from naively reusing past successes.
AI.method: AlphaMemo records reusable evidence about which edit motifs work/fail under specific parent-factor contexts by extracting motifs from AST differences, applying confidence-gated residual memory on a search-ledger prior, and using asymmetric veto control to suppress high-confidence failure patterns.
AI.result: Experiments on CSI 500 and S&P 500 show improved out-of-sample performance and fixed-budget discovery efficiency; ablations validate residual learning, confidence gating, AST-diff motifs, and veto memory.
AI.conclusion: Structured search-process memory with motif-level abstraction and confidence-gated mechanisms effectively mitigates overfitting and redundancy in LLM-based alpha mining.

title: UNSEEN: Uncertainty-aware Navigation via Sparse Estimation in Unknown Environments
summary: Visual navigation in unknown environments remains a core challenge in mobile robotics, especially for resource-constrained platforms. Most existing approaches rely on loosely coupled modular pipelines and strong assumptions on perception quality or environmental structure, often resorting to multi-modal sensor suites that increase system complexity and deployment cost. Vision-only navigation offers a lightweight alternative, but its performance degrades severely under motion blur, low texture, and illumination changes, largely because they neglect the tight coupling between commanded motion and perception. While perception-aware methods partially address this issue, they typically optimize individual modules and fail to propagate uncertainty consistently across the navigation stack. In this paper, we present UNSEEN, a unified uncertainty- and perception-aware navigation framework that explicitly couples localization, mapping, and planning using only a front-mounted camera. UNSEEN estimates sparse maps and robot poses with associated uncertainties at 6Hz, and leverages them to plan trajectories that jointly optimize task progress and estimation accuracy in receding-horizon. Simulations and extensive real-world experiments in unknown environments demonstrate the robustness of the proposed approach, with UNSEEN-SLAM reducing absolute translational error by 9.8% and UNSEEN-Plan improving estimation accuracy by up to 45% compared to state-of-the-art methods, while achieving a 100% task success rate.

AI.tldr: UNSEEN is a unified uncertainty- and perception-aware navigation framework using only a front-mounted camera that couples localization, mapping, and planning, achieving robust visual navigation in unknown environments with up to 45% better estimation accuracy and 100% task success rate.
AI.motivation: Visual navigation in unknown environments remains challenging for resource-constrained platforms, as existing approaches rely on loosely coupled modular pipelines with strong perception assumptions or multi-modal sensors, while vision-only methods degrade under motion blur, low texture, and illumination changes due to neglecting the tight coupling between motion and perception.
AI.method: UNSEEN is a unified uncertainty- and perception-aware navigation framework that explicitly couples localization, mapping, and planning using only a front-mounted camera. It estimates sparse maps and robot poses with associated uncertainties at 6Hz, then leverages them to plan trajectories that jointly optimize task progress and estimation accuracy in receding-horizon.
AI.result: UNSEEN-SLAM reduces absolute translational error by 9.8% and UNSEEN-Plan improves estimation accuracy by up to 45% compared to state-of-the-art methods, while achieving a 100% task success rate in simulations and real-world experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed UNSEEN framework demonstrates robust vision-only navigation in unknown environments by tightly coupling perception and planning with consistent uncertainty propagation, outperforming existing methods in accuracy and task success.

title: Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning
summary: Planning with world models is bottlenecked by compounding prediction errors and the difficulty of defining optimizable goals. Visual targets provide precise local gradients but poor distant guidance, while language is flexible yet limited by noisy cross-modal alignment or dependence on large generative models unsuited for the high-sampling nature of model-based planning. To address these challenges, we introduce Latent Goal Prediction from Language (LAGO), a framework that predicts both sequences of intermediate goal states from language instructions and action-conditioned rollouts, all within the same latent space. Rather than optimizing toward a single global objective, LAGO dynamically decomposes instructions into explicitly predicted, locally tractable latent subgoals. By updating these subgoals online and using a soft minimum trajectory cost during planning, LAGO enables an agent to follow coherent latent trajectories over long horizons. Evaluation across multiple environments planning horizons shows that LAGO avoids the sharp degradation of prior methods. By achieving robust and precise long-horizon planning purely from language, LAGO bridges the precision of visual goals with the flexibility of text-guided control.

AI.tldr: LAGO predicts sequences of latent subgoals from language instructions and uses them with action-conditioned rollouts to enable robust long-horizon planning, avoiding the compound errors and alignment issues that plague prior methods.
AI.motivation: Planning with world models suffers from compounding prediction errors, and existing goal specification approaches (visual vs. language) each have limitations: visual goals offer precise gradients but poor long-range guidance, while language is flexible but suffers from noisy cross-modal alignment or depends on large generative models unsuitable for the high-sampling demands of model-based planning.
AI.method: LAGO predicts both sequences of intermediate subgoal states from language instructions and action-conditioned rollouts within the same latent space. It dynamically decomposes instructions into locally tractable latent subgoals, updates them online, and uses a soft minimum trajectory cost during planning to guide the agent over long horizons.
AI.result: Across multiple environments and planning horizons, LAGO avoids the sharp degradation seen in prior methods, achieving robust and precise long-horizon planning from language alone.
AI.conclusion: LAGO bridges the precision of visual goals with the flexibility of text-guided control, enabling effective long-horizon planning purely from language instructions.

title: Mind the Privileged-to-Camera Gap: Actor-Centric Sidecar Supervision for Camera-First Open-Loop Waypoint Prediction
summary: Camera-first autonomous-driving models predict future ego waypoints from images, ego-state features, and route commands, but waypoint supervision alone does not explicitly supervise actor-level representations of nearby road users. We study this as supervised representation learning for open-loop waypoint prediction. The deployable model uses multi-view RGB, ego state, and route command at inference. During training, simulator-derived sidecar labels supervise actor grounding, privileged hindsight actor relevance relative to the logged ego trajectory, and selected-actor short-horizon motion; these labels are never inference inputs. We evaluate route-disjoint splits with matched architecture, optimizer, validation criterion, checkpoint selection, and three seeds. A plain waypoint-only RGB baseline obtains 1.815$\pm$0.02 m final displacement error (FDE), and the matched no-teacher non-sidecar RGB control obtains 1.716$\pm$0.02 m. Road-user sidecar supervision (RU-sidecar) reduces FDE to 1.223$\pm$0.01 m, a 32.6% reduction over the plain baseline and 28.7% over the matched no-teacher non-sidecar RGB control. It improves over the plain baseline on 1445/1494 routes and over the matched no-teacher non-sidecar RGB control on 1417/1494 routes. Actor-conditioned slices show gains in all nonempty subsets, including 29.1% reduction for samples with at least four valid sidecar actors and 30.0% when a vulnerable road user is present. Optional simulator-state teacher alignment reaches 1.186$\pm$0.15 m FDE, but higher seed variability makes it secondary. Non-deployable simulator-state diagnostics remain stronger, indicating a privileged-to-camera gap. The evidence is limited to open-loop simulation diagnostics.

AI.tldr: Camera-first autonomous-driving models improve open-loop waypoint prediction by adding privileged sidecar supervision (actor grounding, relevance, short-horizon motion) from simulator labels during training, reducing final displacement error by 32.6% over a plain RGB baseline.
AI.motivation: Waypoint supervision alone does not explicitly supervise actor-level representations of nearby road users in camera-first autonomous-driving models, motivating the use of simulator-derived sidecar labels to provide privileged supervisory signals during training.
AI.method: A deployable model uses multi-view RGB, ego state, and route command at inference, while during training, simulator-derived sidecar labels (actor grounding, privileged actor relevance, selected-actor short-horizon motion) are used to supervise actor-level representations without being inference inputs. Route-disjoint splits with matched architecture, optimizer, validation criterion, checkpoint selection, and three seeds are used for evaluation.
AI.result: Road-user sidecar supervision achieves 1.223±0.01 m FDE, a 32.6% reduction over the plain baseline (1.815±0.02 m) and 28.7% over the matched no-teacher non-sidecar RGB control (1.716±0.02 m). Improvements are seen on 1445/1494 routes over the plain baseline and 1417/1494 over the no-teacher control. Actor-conditioned slices show gains in all nonempty subsets.
AI.conclusion: Sidecar supervision significantly improves open-loop waypoint prediction, but a privileged-to-camera gap remains as non-deployable simulator-state diagnostics are still stronger. The evidence is limited to open-loop simulation diagnostics.

title: Human Decision-Making with AI Assistance under Correlated Features
summary: Humans increasingly make decisions with AI assistance; for example, doctors may follow AI-recommended diagnostic tests and base their diagnoses on the results. A natural question is which tests should AI recommend to balance short-term decision quality and long-term human learning when different features (e.g., test results) are correlated. While prior work establishes that stationary policies that recommend the same tests repeatedly are optimal when features are independent, we prove that feature correlations lead such policies to perform arbitrarily poorly. Instead, we prove that any optimal policy must follow an explore-then-commit structure; initially, the AI should offer diverse tests so humans can learn accurate feature coefficients, then the AI should commit to a single set of tests, with exploration length that depends on the degree of feature correlation. We prove that computing the optimal policy is NP-hard and derive a dynamic programming-based algorithm that finds the optimal policy for finite horizons. We additionally develop an approximation that plans for shorter horizons and appends a stationary suffix, achieving near-optimal performance. Our empirical results complement our theory by showing that stronger feature correlation leads to longer exploration phases.

AI.tldr: This paper studies AI-assisted human decision-making under feature correlations, proving that stationary policies fail and optimal policies follow an explore-then-commit structure. Computing the optimal policy is NP-hard, but the authors provide a DP-based exact algorithm and a near-optimal approximation.
AI.motivation: To understand how AI should recommend tests (features) to humans when features are correlated, balancing short-term decision accuracy with long-term human learning, a problem motivated by real-world settings like medical diagnosis.
AI.method: The authors prove the explore-then-commit structure theoretically, establish NP-hardness of optimal policy computation, and develop a dynamic programming algorithm for exact finite-horizon solutions and a shorter-horizon approximation with stationary suffix.
AI.result: Stationary policies perform arbitrarily poorly under feature correlations; optimal policies require exploration then commitment, with exploration length increasing with correlation strength; the DP algorithm yields optimal policies and the approximation achieves near-optimal performance.
AI.conclusion: Feature correlations fundamentally change the optimal AI recommendation policy, necessitating an explore-then-commit approach, and stronger correlations demand longer exploration before committing to a fixed test set.

title: World Action Models: A Survey
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) are embodied predictive-action models that make a forecast of the future available to action. Recent WAMs repurpose large video generation models, and a parallel line relies on language or vision-language backbones without a video-generation core. This rapid expansion has blurred the boundary among broad world models, video generation models, action-grounded video world models, Vision-Language-Action policies, and WAMs. This survey gives the field a common account. It first clarifies these boundaries, then organizes existing works through two complementary views. The first view asks what each method is required to generate, spanning rendered futures, latent futures, and video-generation-free action reasoning. The second view decomposes each method by predictive substrate, backbone, action coupling, and deployment regime. This anatomy supports a unified discussion of interactability, causality, persistence, physical plausibility, and generalization, followed by data, evaluation, and open challenges. Across these axes, a consistent design pattern emerges: WAMs are not simply video generators with action heads, but predictive-action methods whose design choices trade representational richness against compute, memory, latency, and action-label cost. The field is moving toward methods that generate less of the future while preserving what control requires. The survey homepage is available at https://world-action-models.github.io/.

AI.tldr: This survey clarifies the boundaries of World Action Models (WAMs) vs. video generation models, world models, and VLA policies, organizing methods by what they generate (rendered/latent futures or generation-free action reasoning) and by their architectural components. It identifies a trend: WAMs are moving toward generating less of the future while preserving what control requires.
AI.motivation: The rapid expansion of WAMs, video generation models, world models, and VLA policies has blurred the boundaries among these concepts, creating confusion in the field. This survey aims to provide a common account by clarifying definitions and systematically organizing existing work.
AI.method: The survey uses two complementary views to organize methods: (1) what each method is required to generate (rendered futures, latent futures, video-generation-free action reasoning); (2) decomposition by predictive substrate, backbone, action coupling, and deployment regime. It then discusses interactability, causality, persistence, physical plausibility, and generalization.
AI.result: A consistent design pattern emerges: WAMs are predictive-action methods (not simply video generators with action heads) whose design choices trade representational richness against compute, memory, latency, and action-label cost. The field is trending toward methods that generate less of the future while preserving what control requires.
AI.conclusion: The field is moving away from full video generation toward more efficient predictive representations, and the survey provides a structured taxonomy for understanding this evolution along with open challenges in data, evaluation, and future work.

title: Harnessing Agent Skills: Architectural Patterns and a Reference Architecture for Skill-Mediated LLM Agents
summary: Agent skills externalise reusable agent-facing behavioural knowledge and guidance as persistent artefacts that can be discovered, activated, and interpreted by LLM agents. Although a skill artefact is static at rest, its architectural responsibilities arise in use, when the artefact is selected for a run, bound to context and authority constraints, interpreted by a stochastic agent, and recorded as run evidence. We call this run-specific relation skill-in-use. This paper studies agent skill harnessing: the architectural responsibilities that govern the transition from skill artefacts to skill-in-use, bound the executable consequences associated with skill-in-use, and capture evidence for attribution, verification, repair, and evolution. This paper provides a catalogue of ten empirically grounded architectural patterns (five core, five supporting) for skill harnessing and synthesises them into a reference architecture with four responsibility layers: Supply Chain, Mediation, Execution Control, and Evidence & Feedback. We evaluate the architecture through cross-instantiation across 8 selected systems. The resulting patterns and reference architecture provide a vocabulary and diagnostic frame for analysing skill-harnessing responsibilities across agent systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reference architecture with four responsibility layers (Supply Chain, Mediation, Execution Control, Evidence & Feedback) and ten empirically grounded architectural patterns (five core, five supporting) for agent skill harnessing—the transition from static skill artefacts to run-specific skill-in-use, including binding, execution, and evidence capture. Evaluated across 8 systems.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand and formalize the architectural responsibilities that govern how LLM agents transition from static skill artefacts to run-time skill-in-use, addressing the lack of a unified vocabulary and diagnostic frame for analyzing skill-harnessing mechanisms across agent systems.
AI.method: Empirical grounding of ten architectural patterns (five core, five supporting) synthesized into a reference architecture with four responsibility layers, evaluated through cross-instantiation across 8 selected agent systems.
AI.result: A catalogue of ten architectural patterns and a four-layer reference architecture (Supply Chain, Mediation, Execution Control, Evidence & Feedback) validated across 8 systems.
AI.conclusion: The patterns and reference architecture provide a vocabulary and diagnostic frame for analyzing and comparing skill-harnessing responsibilities across different LLM agent systems.

title: Geometric Entropy: When Trajectory Diversity Helps and Hurts in Imitation Learning
comment: Accepted to IROS 2026. Project page: https://geometric-entropy.github.io/
summary: We study how trajectory-shape diversity in demonstrations affects imitation learning (IL) performance across models, tasks, and data scales.
