We introduce Geometric Entropy (H_G), a task-agnostic metric that quantifies the intrinsic diversity of transit trajectories after normalizing away extrinsic variation, such as goal pose and workspace scale, via target-frame alignment. Across multiple IL architectures and both simulated and real-robot contact-rich manipulation tasks, we observe a consistent inverted-U relationship between success and H_G: increasing geometric diversity improves robustness in low-diversity regimes but degrades performance once diversity induces strategy ambiguity. Moreover, the optimal entropy shifts toward lower values as task mastery increases through more data, easier tasks, or stronger priors, and for a pretrained vision-language-action model the trend becomes effectively monotonic decreasing. Practically, H_G enables fast pre-training auditing of demonstration datasets and offers a simple guideline for calibrating demonstrations toward the learnable regime.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Geometric Entropy (H_G), a task-agnostic metric for quantifying trajectory-shape diversity in demonstration datasets. It reveals an inverted-U relationship between H_G and imitation learning performance across models, tasks, and scales: moderate diversity helps robustness, but too much causes strategy ambiguity. Optimal entropy decreases with more data, easier tasks, stronger priors, or pretrained models.
AI.motivation: To understand how trajectory-shape diversity in demonstrations affects imitation learning performance, and to develop a metric that can characterize this diversity independent of task-specific factors like goal pose or workspace scale.
AI.method: Proposes Geometric Entropy (H_G), a task-agnostic metric that normalizes away extrinsic variation (goal pose, workspace scale) via target-frame alignment, then quantifies intrinsic diversity of transit trajectories. Validated across multiple IL architectures, simulated and real-robot contact-rich manipulation tasks, and various data scales.
AI.result: Consistent inverted-U relationship between success rate and H_G across settings. Optimal entropy shifts lower with more data, easier tasks, or stronger priors. For pretrained vision-language-action models, the trend becomes effectively monotonic decreasing.
AI.conclusion: H_G enables fast pre-training auditing of demonstration datasets and provides a simple guideline for calibrating demonstrations toward the learnable regime, avoiding the pitfalls of both insufficient and excessive geometric diversity.

title: DEMM-Bench: A Cross-Regime Benchmark for Agent-Runtime Governance-Evidence Sufficiency
comment: 41 pages, 8 tables, no figures. Benchmark and dataset paper. Dataset (CC-BY-4.0) and code (Apache-2.0): Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.20426092 and Hugging Face https://huggingface.co/datasets/dev404ai/DEMM-Bench; code at https://github.com/agent-runtime-evidence/decision-evidence-benchmark
summary: Agent-runtime systems emit traces, ledgers, provenance graphs, policy logs, delegation tokens, cache events, and tool-firewall records, but those containers do not necessarily answer governance questions about a specific decision. DEMM-Bench is a cross-regime benchmark for agent-runtime governance-evidence sufficiency, grounded in the Decision Evidence Maturity Model (DEMM): it measures whether records across eight evidence regimes are sufficient to reconstruct decision-level properties rather than merely present. The benchmark normalizes the regimes through adapters, asks property questions over actor, authority, action, policy, decision basis, resource touch, lifecycle context, and verification strength, and applies eight deterministic degradation conditions. Across 64 manuscript cases, trace-present and schema-present baselines overclaim on 75% of cases, ledger-present overclaims on 50%, and the redacted property-level candidate scorer has zero overclaim with 56.25% mean Property Sufficiency Accuracy. The deposited package provides the 64-case dataset, construction-oracle labels, baselines, and adapters, supporting reproducible evaluation of decision-evidence maturity across heterogeneous agent-runtime evidence substrates.

AI.tldr: DEMM-Bench is a cross-regime benchmark that evaluates whether agent-runtime system records (traces, ledgers, provenance graphs, etc.) can sufficiently reconstruct decision-level governance properties, using 64 manuscript cases and eight evidence regimes. It finds that current trace-present and schema-present baselines overclaim on 75% of cases, while the proposed redacted property-level scorer achieves zero overclaim with 56.25% mean Property Sufficiency Accuracy.
AI.motivation: Agent-runtime systems produce various records (traces, ledgers, logs), but these do not necessarily provide sufficient evidence to answer governance questions about specific decisions. There is a need to evaluate whether existing evidence regimes can support decision-level provenance reconstruction.
AI.method: The benchmark normalizes eight evidence regimes through adapters, poses property questions across actor, authority, action, policy, decision basis, resource touch, lifecycle context, and verification strength, and applies eight deterministic degradation conditions. It evaluates 64 manuscript cases against baselines (trace-present, schema-present, ledger-present) and a redacted property-level candidate scorer.
AI.result: Trace-present and schema-present baselines overclaim on 75% of cases; ledger-present overclaims on 50%. The redacted property-level candidate scorer achieves zero overclaim with 56.25% mean Property Sufficiency Accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Current evidence regimes in agent-runtime systems are insufficient for decision-level governance queries. DEMM-Bench provides a reproducible evaluation framework for measuring decision-evidence maturity across heterogeneous evidence substrates, with deposited dataset, labels, baselines, and adapters.

title: Vesta: A Generalist Embodied Reasoning Model
summary: Robots operating in open-world environments must seamlessly integrate localization, spatial reasoning, navigation, and long-horizon planning. While specialist models excel at individual tasks, deploying a multi-model stack is computationally expensive and prone to cascading errors. We present Vesta, a unified embodied generalist that consolidates these capabilities into a single foundation model. Our approach combines a diverse and massive curated corpus designed to induce spatial grounding and a simple multimodal memory harness that enables reasoning over extended time horizons. Across diverse benchmarks, Vesta on average beats individual SOTA baselines by >$20\%$ and beats an ensemble of per-category-best baselines by $>10\%$ -- thus demonstrating that a generalist model can match or exceed specialists. On real-world robotic tasks requiring memory and reasoning, Vesta improves task success by >35\%. Our work thus demonstrates that a single generalist is a feasible, scalable, and arguably preferable alternative to combining specialists.

AI.tldr: Vesta is a unified embodied generalist foundation model that combines localization, spatial reasoning, navigation, and long-horizon planning into a single model, outperforming both individual SOTA baselines (>20%) and ensemble baselines (>10%) across diverse benchmarks, with >35% improvement on real-world robotic memory and reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Robots in open-world environments need multiple capabilities (localization, spatial reasoning, navigation, long-horizon planning), but deploying separate specialist models is computationally expensive and prone to cascading errors. The authors aim to consolidate these into a single generalist model.
AI.method: Vesta combines (1) a diverse and massive curated corpus designed to induce spatial grounding, and (2) a simple multimodal memory harness that enables reasoning over extended time horizons.
AI.result: Vesta beats individual SOTA baselines by >20% on average, beats an ensemble of per-category-best baselines by >10%, and improves real-world robotic task success requiring memory and reasoning by >35%.
AI.conclusion: A single generalist model is a feasible, scalable, and arguably preferable alternative to combining specialists for embodied AI tasks.

title: SkillHarness: Harnessing Safe Skills for Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) are increasingly deployed in dynamic interactive environments, creating a growing need for continual skill learning during interaction. Recent approaches address this challenge by learning reusable skills from successful trajectories. However, these skill learning methods largely assume static and safe environments, overlooking risks from adversarial interactions (e.g., prompt injections) and environmental dynamics (e.g., pop-ups). In dynamic settings, such assumptions can lead to risky skill learning and brittle execution, undermining the reliability of CUAs. This raises the question: how can CUAs learn and use skills safely in dynamic environments? To address this problem, we propose SkillHarness, a framework for safe skill harnessing in dynamic environments. SkillHarness moves beyond static skill abstractions by modeling skill learning and utilization as a safety-constrained interaction process. Specifically, we introduce the skill boundary that leverages multi-source supervision signals to identify safe skills from interaction trajectories, and construct self-improving safety constraints throughout the skill lifecycle. In addition, SkillHarness introduces selective skill reuse, where tasks are guided to decompose according to context and completed through the selective activation of skill subsets. Our experiments demonstrate that SkillHarness significantly reduces the unsafe rate of learned skills by 57.1% and consistently improves execution stability under dynamic environmental changes, outperforming existing baselines.

AI.tldr: SkillHarness is a framework for safe skill learning and reuse in dynamic interactive environments, reducing unsafe skill rates by 57.1% through skill boundaries and selective reuse.
AI.motivation: Existing CUA skill learning methods assume static, safe environments, ignoring risks from adversarial interactions (e.g., prompt injections) and environmental dynamics (e.g., pop-ups), which leads to risky skill learning and brittle execution.
AI.method: SkillHarness introduces (1) skill boundaries using multi-source supervision to identify safe skills from interaction trajectories, (2) self-improving safety constraints throughout the skill lifecycle, and (3) selective skill reuse where tasks are decomposed contextually and completed via selective activation of skill subsets.
AI.result: SkillHarness reduces the unsafe rate of learned skills by 57.1% and consistently improves execution stability under dynamic environmental changes, outperforming existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Modeling skill learning as a safety-constrained interaction process with selective reuse is essential for reliable CUA deployment in dynamic environments.

title: Learning-Based Modeling of Soft Robots via Cosserat Rod Theory
summary: Modeling soft robot dynamics is challenging due to their continuum structure and typically nonlinear dynamics. Creating models based on first-order principles is typically time-demanding, and their expressiveness is limited, whereas data-driven models lack interpretability and physical consistency. This work aims to overcome these challenges by introducing a port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Process Regression framework for learning and simulating the dynamics of planar, rod-like soft robots. In detail, the proposed model integrates Cosserat rod theory and Hamiltonian physics with data-driven inference to preserve the system's energy structure while accurately learning the rod dynamics. Numerical simulations show that we can achieve accurate and energy-consistent representations of a rod-like soft robot, showing the potential for a robust and interpretable pathway for modeling complex continuum mechanics.

AI.tldr: Introduces a port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Process Regression framework that integrates Cosserat rod theory with data-driven inference to learn and simulate soft robot dynamics while preserving energy structure and physical consistency.
AI.motivation: First-principles models for soft robots are time-consuming to create and have limited expressiveness, while purely data-driven models lack interpretability and physical consistency. The work aims to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: Port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Process Regression framework combining Cosserat rod theory (continuum mechanics) with Hamiltonian physics and data-driven inference to preserve energy structure while learning rod dynamics.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate accurate and energy-consistent representations of a rod-like soft robot.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method shows potential for a robust and interpretable pathway for modeling complex continuum mechanics in soft robotics.

title: Constituency Optimisation Through Hamiltonian Representation Of Mandates (COTHROM): Algorithmic Redistricting of Irish Election Boundaries
summary: Electoral redistricting in Ireland's Proportional Representation Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV) system faces the challenge of selecting an optimally representative set of electoral boundaries from an enormous set of possible configurations, and where ``representative'' is a delicate balance of constitutional objectives that are often in tension with one another. We present the first computational framework for Irish electoral redistricting that systematically optimises across multiple constitutional requirements while making trade-offs explicit and quantifiable. The electoral redistricting problem is parsed using statistical physics, where constitutional objectives are considered as terms in a Potts Hamiltonian. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and simulated annealing are employed to minimise this objective function, systematically exploring this configuration space, with coupling constants as proxies for objective weightings. Multi Criterion Decision Analysis (MCDA) and Pareto Optimality is then utilised to remedy the ambiguity in choosing a certain objective weighting combination over others. With respect to proportional representation and compactness objectives evaluated in County Cork, COTHROM consistently improves on the existing legal constituency boundaries for a range of objective weightings.

AI.tldr: A computational framework (COTTHROM) using statistical physics and MCMC to optimise Irish electoral redistricting under PR-STV, demonstrating improved proportional representation and compactness over existing boundaries in County Cork.
AI.motivation: Electoral redistricting in Ireland's PR-STV system involves selecting optimal boundaries from a huge configuration space while balancing multiple conflicting constitutional objectives, which lacks a systematic computational approach.
AI.method: Constitutional objectives are encoded as terms in a Potts Hamiltonian; Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and simulated annealing minimize the objective function; Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis (MCDA) and Pareto Optimality resolve ambiguity in objective weightings.
AI.result: COTTHROM consistently improves on existing legal constituency boundaries in County Cork across proportional representation and compactness metrics for a range of objective weightings.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully provides a systematic, quantifiable approach to balancing trade-offs in Irish electoral redistricting, with demonstrable improvements over current boundaries.

title: Heterogeneous Policy Networks for Composite Robot Team Communication and Coordination
summary: High-performing human-human teams learn intelligent and efficient communication and coordination strategies to maximize their joint utility. These teams implicitly understand the different roles of heterogeneous team members and adapt their communication protocols accordingly. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has attempted to develop computational methods for synthesizing such joint coordination-communication strategies, but emulating heterogeneous communication patterns across agents with different state, action, and observation spaces has remained a challenge. Without properly modeling agent heterogeneity, as in prior MARL work that leverages homogeneous graph networks, communication becomes less helpful and can even deteriorate the team's performance. In the past, we proposed Heterogeneous Policy Networks (HetNet) to learn efficient and diverse communication models for coordinating cooperative heterogeneous teams. In this extended work, we extend Heterogeneous Policy Networks (HetNet) to support scaling heterogeneous robot teams. Building on heterogeneous graph-attention networks, we show that HetNet not only facilitates learning heterogeneous collaborative policies but also enables end-to-end training for learning highly efficient binarized messaging. Our empirical evaluation shows that HetNet sets a new state of the art in learning coordination and communication strategies for heterogeneous multi-agent teams by achieving an 5.84% to 707.65% performance improvement over the next-best baseline across multiple domains while simultaneously achieving a 200x reduction in the required communication bandwidth.

AI.tldr: HetNet extends heterogeneous policy networks with graph-attention mechanisms to enable efficient coordination and binarized communication for heterogeneous robot teams, achieving 5.84%-707.65% performance improvement over baselines and 200x communication bandwidth reduction.
AI.motivation: Prior MARL methods using homogeneous graph networks fail to model heterogeneous team members with different state, action, and observation spaces, leading to unhelpful or even detrimental communication. This work aims to learn efficient, diverse communication protocols for heterogeneous cooperative teams.
AI.method: Extends Heterogeneous Policy Networks (HetNet) using heterogeneous graph-attention networks to support scaling of heterogeneous robot teams, enabling end-to-end training for binarized messaging while learning heterogeneous collaborative policies.
AI.result: HetNet achieves 5.84% to 707.65% performance improvement over the next-best baseline across multiple domains, while simultaneously reducing required communication bandwidth by 200x.
AI.conclusion: HetNet sets a new state of the art for learning coordination and communication strategies in heterogeneous multi-agent teams, demonstrating both superior performance and drastically improved communication efficiency.

title: RIZZ: Routing Interactions to Near Zero-Interference Zones for Continual Adaptation of Black-Box Agents
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as long-lived agents that must adapt across users, tasks, domains, modalities, and feedback regimes without access to model weights. Existing black-box adaptation methods typically optimize a single prompt, maintain an undifferentiated memory, or rely on repeated rollout-heavy search. However, these designs struggle when streams of input are nonstationary, feedback is sparse, and failures from one task family can contaminate behavior on another. We introduce RIZZ (Routing Interactions to Near Zero-interference Zones), a continual adaptation framework for compound language-model systems that learns entirely through verifier-gated memory, routing, and prompt compilation. RIZZ organizes input streams into dynamically spawned memory branches. At inference time, either while online or offline, a context-aware router selects or creates a branch that retrieves branch-local, global, graph-structured, and working-memory context, which is compiled into a bounded prompt together with retrieved task evidence. After the model acts, task verifiers score the output, and only verified interactions can update memory, promote reusable rules, demote harmful rules, or create anti-patterns. This yields a black-box agent that improves through persistent natural-language feedback while explicitly controlling interference. RIZZ targets the regime where adaptation must occur online under context budgets. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework against state-of-the-art baselines on competitive benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RIZZ is a continual black-box adaptation framework for compound LLM systems that uses verifier-gated memory, dynamic routing to interference-free memory branches, and prompt compilation to enable online adaptation under nonstationary streams and sparse feedback, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing black-box adaptation methods (single-prompt optimization, undifferentiated memory, rollout-heavy search) fail under nonstationary input streams, sparse feedback, and cross-task contamination. A framework is needed that enables continual online adaptation for LLM agents without access to model weights, while explicitly controlling interference between different task families.
AI.method: RIZZ organizes input streams into dynamically spawned memory branches. At inference, a context-aware router selects or creates a branch, retrieving branch-local, global, graph-structured, and working-memory context compiled into a bounded prompt with task evidence. After model action, task verifiers score output; only verified interactions update memory (promote/demote rules, create anti-patterns). Entirely black-box — no weight access, no rollout-heavy search.
AI.result: Effectiveness demonstrated against state-of-the-art baselines on competitive benchmarks. RIZZ improves through persistent natural-language feedback while explicitly controlling interference under constrained context budgets.
AI.conclusion: RIZZ provides a viable black-box continual adaptation paradigm for compound LLM systems operating in nonstationary, sparse-feedback environments, with dynamic memory branching and verifier-gated updates as key mechanisms for interference control.

title: Duet: Dual-Robot Understanding via Efficient Teaching
summary: Dual-robot collaboration enables tasks that exceed the reach and payload of a single robot, such as collaboratively transporting objects across environments and executing coordinated handovers. Data acquisition is the primary bottleneck for training these systems. To this end, we introduce DUET, a dual-robot learning framework for mobile manipulation. For efficient data collection, we create a unified dual-embodiment synchronized VR-based teleoperation system for in-domain heterogeneous robot data collection. We further develop a complementary tracking pipeline that records human-human coordination and collaborative mobile manipulation priors. To allow efficient learning, we introduce an Action Chunking Transformer based architecture that first pretrains collaborative policies on efficient human-human demonstrations, before finetuning them on a minimal set of real-robot teleoperation trajectories. We develop a benchmark of four collaborative tasks to evaluate our framework using a Unitree G1 humanoid and a Dexmate Vega1 mobile manipulator. The results demonstrate that harnessing human priors not only yields superior task performance compared to baselines trained only on robot data, but also reduces the total human effort required for data collection. Our human data collection pipeline achieves 5.4x acceleration on average from teleoperation, but we perform equally or better than robot-only data trained policies across all tasks. Our project page is available at https://zhaoy37.github.io/Duet/.

AI.tldr: DUET is a dual-robot learning framework for mobile manipulation that uses a VR-based teleoperation system and human-human demonstration priors with Action Chunking Transformer to achieve efficient collaborative task learning, achieving 5.4x faster data collection with equal or better performance than robot-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Data acquisition is the primary bottleneck for training dual-robot collaboration systems, and existing methods require extensive robot teleoperation data which is inefficient and labor-intensive.
AI.method: DUET introduces a unified dual-embodiment synchronized VR-based teleoperation system for in-domain robot data collection, a complementary tracking pipeline for recording human-human coordination priors, and an Action Chunking Transformer architecture that pretrains on human-human demonstrations then finetunes on minimal robot teleoperation trajectories.
AI.result: The framework achieves 5.4x acceleration in data collection compared to teleoperation, and policies trained with human priors achieve equal or superior performance across all four collaborative tasks compared to policies trained exclusively on robot data.
AI.conclusion: Harnessing human-human coordination priors reduces total human effort for data collection while yielding better task performance, demonstrating that human priors are an effective and efficient alternative to extensive robot-only data collection.

title: An LLM-Explainable DRL Framework for Passenger-Directed Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous vehicles offer the potential for safer and more efficient mobility, yet public trust remains limited due to the lack of transparency in their decision-making. This work addresses this issue by combining deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for adaptive driving control with large language model (LLM)-based explainability modules designed to communicate agent behavior to passengers. DRL agents were trained in simulation using a Dueling Double Deep Q-Network to follow distinct driving requests: \textit{fast}, \textit{comfort}, and \textit{stop}. They demonstrated stable learning, safe compliance with traffic rules, and reliable switching between modes within a single trip. In parallel, LLM modules were introduced to interpret passenger requests, determine when explanations were needed, and generate concise, safety-oriented justifications. Results show that this framework, serving as a proof of concept for integrating RL decision-making and LLMs, balances safety, adaptability, and explainability, and is most effective when requests are delayed or overridden due to safety constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework combining deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for adaptive autonomous driving control with large language model (LLM)-based explainability modules. DRL agents using Dueling Double Deep Q-Network learn three driving modes (fast, comfort, stop) and can switch between them during a trip. LLM modules interpret passenger requests and generate safety-oriented explanations. The system balances safety, adaptability, and explainability, being most effective when passenger requests are delayed or overridden for safety.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles lack transparency in decision-making, which limits public trust despite their potential for safer and more efficient mobility.
AI.method: Combines DRL (Dueling Double Deep Q-Network) for adaptive driving control with LLM-based modules for explainability. DRL agents learn three driving modes (fast, comfort, stop). LLM modules interpret passenger requests, determine when explanations are needed, and generate concise safety-oriented justifications.
AI.result: DRL agents demonstrated stable learning, safe compliance with traffic rules, and reliable mode switching within a single trip. The framework effectively balances safety, adaptability, and explainability, performing best when requests are delayed or overridden due to safety constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework serves as a proof of concept for integrating RL decision-making and LLMs in autonomous driving, demonstrating that combining adaptive control with explainable AI can enhance trust without compromising safety.

title: Inductive Generalization for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Understanding the generalization capabilities of visuomotor policies is essential in the development of capable robotic agents. Generalizable models learn structures that transfer across domains. However, in practice, visuomotor policies test performance by interpolation on known distributions using unstructured domain shifts (e.g. lighting, clutter, diverse objects). We argue that to measure generalization capabilities we must instead test the inductive capacity of policies on progressively harder, out-of-distribution task variants. We call this inductive generalization, drawing directly on how axis-based evaluation has revealed inherent generalization limitations in language models (e.g. sequence length, counting) arXiv:2502.00197 . We provide a reusable and formal evaluation protocol for measuring inductive generalization in any manipulation policy, and establish baselines showing that existing paradigms fail this test; e.g. SoTA Vision-Language-Action models and find that policies that appear to generalize to prior domain shifts (distractors, etc) fail inductive generalization tests. These results expose a class of learning challenges orthogonal to those addressed by data and model scaling in robot learning, yet are imperative to solve in order to realize general purpose robots.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "inductive generalization" as a new evaluation paradigm for visuomotor policies, testing out-of-distribution task variants rather than interpolation on known distributions. The authors show that current SoTA models (including VLA models) fail these tests, revealing a fundamental limitation orthogonal to data and model scaling.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of visuomotor policies measures generalization via interpolation on known distributions with unstructured domain shifts (lighting, clutter, objects). The authors argue this fails to assess true generalization, which requires testing on progressively harder, out-of-distribution task variants.
AI.method: The authors propose a formal evaluation protocol for measuring "inductive generalization" in manipulation policies, drawing inspiration from axis-based evaluation in language models. They establish baselines testing existing paradigms including SoTA Vision-Language-Action models on this protocol.
AI.result: Existing policies that appear to generalize under prior domain shifts (distractors, etc.) fail inductive generalization tests. Current paradigms, including VLA models, do not pass these tests.
AI.conclusion: Inductive generalization exposes a class of learning challenges orthogonal to those addressed by data and model scaling, yet solving them is imperative for realizing general-purpose robots.

title: Hypothesis-Disciplined Multi-Agent Automated Formalization of Asymptotic Statistical Theory
summary: Asymptotic statistical theory is a challenging domain for AI-assisted formalization: its central results mix convergence statements, asymptotic expansions, functional analysis, and regularity conditions that have a large gap from existing infrastructure in Lean 4 formalization. To address these challenges, we propose a hypothesis-disciplined Lean 4 formalization pipeline built from multiple agents: a manager that coordinates seven specialist roles for proof planning, skeleton scaffolding, Mathlib reconnaissance, proof construction, integration, independent review, and audit. The main methodological discipline is the hypothesis-disciplined audit, implemented by the Auditor agent: every main-theorem hypothesis and concept-layer field must be anchored in the source mathematical prose, justified as a Lean encoding adapter, marked as source-implied, or rejected as an unsupported strengthening. Using this workflow, we build a systematic formalization of asymptotic statistical theory, especially the parametric and semi-parametric models' asymptotic distribution and efficiency results. The resulting Lean development is axiom-clean and source-faithful, with Lean-checked and human-audited proofs of core parametric and semi-parametric theorems organized so that theorem-agnostic infrastructure and statistical concept definitions are separated from theorem-specific assembly. The formalization results are available at https://github.com/junwei-lu/Lean-Asymptotic-Statistical-Theory.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-agent Lean 4 formalization pipeline for asymptotic statistical theory, using a hypothesis-disciplined audit approach to ensure source faithfulness. The workflow produces axiom-clean, Lean-checked, and human-audited proofs of parametric and semi-parametric asymptotic distribution and efficiency theorems.
AI.motivation: Asymptotic statistical theory is difficult to formalize in Lean 4 due to the complexity of convergence statements, asymptotic expansions, functional analysis, and the large gap between regularity conditions and existing Mathlib infrastructure.
AI.method: A hypothesis-disciplined multi-agent pipeline with seven specialist roles (manager, proof planner, skeleton scaffolder, Mathlib recon, proof constructor, integrator, reviewer, auditor). The Auditor enforces that every hypothesis and concept-layer field is anchored in source prose, justified as a Lean encoding adapter, marked source-implied, or rejected.
AI.result: Lean-checked and human-audited formalization of core parametric and semi-parametric asymptotic distribution and efficiency theorems, with clean separation between theorem-agnostic infrastructure and theorem-specific assembly.
AI.conclusion: The hypothesis-disciplined audit methodology enables source-faithful, axiom-clean formalization of challenging asymptotic statistics, and the resulting development is publicly available.

title: R2HandoverSim: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-to-Human Object Handovers
comment: Accepted by the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: We present R2HandoverSim, a simulation benchmark for robot-to-human (R2H) object handovers. Although R2H handover methods have advanced rapidly, the lack of standardized evaluation protocols impedes objective comparison. Our benchmark enables reproducible evaluation by systematically comparing four baselines on their predicted shared grasp poses. We conduct a user study with 30 participants, analyze baseline performance, and show that simulation results correlate with real-world evaluation outcomes. Crucially, five complementary metrics (planning feasibility, reachability, grasp stability, grasp affordance, and safety) better reflect user-perceived handover quality than overall success rate alone. Website and code: https://robot-future.github.io/r2handoversim/.

AI.tldr: R2HandoverSim is a simulation benchmark for robot-to-human object handovers, enabling standardized evaluation via four baselines, a 30-participant user study, and five complementary metrics that better capture user-perceived handover quality than success rate alone.
AI.motivation: The lack of standardized evaluation protocols for robot-to-human handover methods prevents objective comparison and reproducible assessment across different approaches.
AI.method: The benchmark systematically compares four baselines on predicted shared grasp poses, conducts a user study with 30 participants, and evaluates using five complementary metrics: planning feasibility, reachability, grasp stability, grasp affordance, and safety.
AI.result: Simulation results correlate with real-world evaluation outcomes, and the five proposed metrics better reflect user-perceived handover quality than overall success rate alone.
AI.conclusion: R2HandoverSim provides a standardized, reproducible evaluation framework for R2H handovers, with multi-metric assessment that aligns with human perception of quality.

title: SPARC: A Multi-Agent System for Electrical Circuit Question Answering
summary: Electrical circuit diagram QA tasks require complex mathematical reasoning, which remains challenging for multimodal LLMs. We present SPARC, a multi-agent system that answers questions over circuit diagrams by grounding reasoning in executable physics-based simulations. SPARC uses LLM agents to synthesize, execute, and analyze simulation programs, improving accuracy and reliability by design. It achieves 83% accuracy, with up to a 58% absolute improvement over baselines, while enabling systematic error diagnosis.

AI.tldr: SPARC is a multi-agent system that answers questions about electrical circuit diagrams by grounding reasoning in executable physics-based simulations, achieving 83% accuracy with up to 58% absolute improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Electrical circuit diagram QA tasks require complex mathematical reasoning, which remains challenging for multimodal LLMs.
AI.method: SPARC uses LLM agents to synthesize, execute, and analyze simulation programs, improving accuracy and reliability by design.
AI.result: It achieves 83% accuracy, with up to a 58% absolute improvement over baselines, while enabling systematic error diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: SPARC improves accuracy and reliability for circuit diagram QA by grounding reasoning in executable physics-based simulations using LLM agents.

title: BayesFP: Posterior Estimation for Flow-Based Policies via Feynman-Kac Sampling
summary: Robots must generate trajectories that remain faithful to learned expert behavior while satisfying safety constraints and task-specific objectives specified only at inference time. We formulate constrained trajectory generation for pretrained diffusion and flow-matching policies as Bayesian posterior sampling, with the learned demonstration distribution as a prior and an inference-time, cost-derived likelihood tilting it toward feasible, optimal trajectories. To sample from this posterior without any retraining of the base policy, we leverage the Feynman--Kac corrector framework, originally formulated for diffusion models, and extend it to deterministic flow-matching policies. The result is a unified, inference-time, retraining-free sampler for diffusion and flow policies. We validate the approach on pretrained Diffusion Policy, GR00T-N1.6, and $π_{0.5}$ checkpoints across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, including planning around non-convex obstacles introduced at inference time, and show improvements over the base $π_{0.5}$ on zero-shot tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an inference-time, retraining-free method for constrained trajectory generation in pretrained diffusion and flow-matching policies, formulated as Bayesian posterior sampling with Feynman-Kac corrector framework, validated on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Robots need to generate trajectories that remain faithful to learned expert behavior while satisfying safety constraints and task-specific objectives that are only specified at inference time, without requiring retraining of the base policy.
AI.method: Formulates constrained trajectory generation as Bayesian posterior sampling with learned demonstration distribution as prior and cost-derived likelihood as tilting factor. Leverages Feynman-Kac corrector framework originally for diffusion models and extends it to deterministic flow-matching policies for unified inference-time sampling.
AI.result: Validated on pretrained Diffusion Policy, GR00T-N1.6, and π₀.₅ checkpoints across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, including non-convex obstacle avoidance, showing improvements over base π₀.₅ on zero-shot tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables retraining-free, inference-time constrained trajectory generation for both diffusion and flow-matching policies, improving performance on zero-shot tasks while satisfying safety constraints.

title: Bridging Multi-Valued Heuristics and Dimensionality Reduction in Multi-Objective Search
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. To appear in Proceedings of SoCS 2026
summary: Multi-objective shortest-path (MOSP) algorithms traditionally rely on single-valued heuristics (SVHs), which associate each state with a single admissible cost vector. While SVHs provide safe lower bounds, they fail to capture the trade-off structure of the Pareto frontier and often yield weak search guidance. Multi-valued heuristics (MVHs) address this limitation by mapping states to sets of cost estimates, enabling a richer approximation of possible trade-offs. Modern MOSP algorithms are highly dependent on dimensionality reduction (DR) techniques to efficiently perform dominance checks. However, integrating MVHs with DR introduces subtle correctness challenges. We show that naively combining DR with MVHs destroys the ordering invariants required for DR, leading to unsound and incomplete search. To address this issue, we develop the first theoretical frameworks for safely integrating MVHs with DR. First, we introduce $\text{NAMOA}^*{\text{dr}\text{-}\text{mvh}}$, a theoretical baseline that restores search correctness by enforcing heuristic consistency. Recognizing the practical limitations of this approach, we then introduce our primary contribution, $\text{L}\text{-}\text{NAMOA}^*{\text{dr}\text{-}\text{mvh}}$. This algorithm employs a "lazy," optimistic approach to DR, preserving exact correctness with only an admissible MVH by dynamically detecting and repairing local ordering violations. Across a range of benchmarks, $\text{L}\text{-}\text{NAMOA}^*{\text{dr}\text{-}\text{mvh}}$ matches or improves over state-of-the-art MOSP algorithms, and achieves speedups of over 10x in instances where the additional guidance provided by the MVH translates into stronger pruning.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies correctness issues when naively combining multi-valued heuristics (MVHs) with dimensionality reduction (DR) in multi-objective shortest-path (MOSP) algorithms, and proposes two theoretical frameworks — NAMOA*dr-mvh (a baseline with strong consistency requirements) and L-NAMOA*dr-mvh (a practical lazy approach) — that safely integrate MVHs with DR, achieving over 10x speedups on some benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional single-valued heuristics (SVHs) fail to capture Pareto frontier trade-offs, limiting search guidance in MOSP. Multi-valued heuristics (MVHs) offer richer cost estimates but integrating them with dimensionality reduction (DR) — which modern MOSP algorithms depend on — breaks correctness, causing unsound and incomplete search.
AI.method: The paper develops two algorithmic frameworks: (1) NAMOA*dr-mvh, a theoretical baseline that enforces heuristic consistency to restore correctness; (2) L-NAMOA*dr-mvh, a practical "lazy" optimistic approach that dynamically detects and repairs local ordering violations, requiring only an admissible MVH.
AI.result: Across benchmarks, L-NAMOA*dr-mvh matches or improves over state-of-the-art MOSP algorithms, achieving speedups of over 10x in instances where MVH guidance yields stronger pruning.
AI.conclusion: Safe integration of MVHs with DR is feasible and yields significant performance gains; the lazy approach (L-NAMOA*dr-mvh) provides exact correctness with only admissible MVHs, avoiding the practical limitations of enforcing full heuristic consistency.

title: Membrane-based Acoustic Microrobots
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). For supplementary video contact fkocabas@wisc.edu
summary: Acoustic microrobots have emerged as a promising frontier for targeted drug delivery and minimally invasive medicine due to their high-power density and biocompatibility. Despite wide-ranging designs, conventional acoustic microrobots mostly rely on air microbubbles trapped within confined microcavities within the robot body, which suffer from limited operational longevity due to rapid gas dissolution and resultant shifts in resonance frequency. In this paper, we propose a robust, membrane-based acoustic microrobot that overcomes these limitations by employing a thin flexible Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) membrane bonded over confined microcavities for microstreaming. The introduced design physically prevents gas diffusion, ensuring stable performance over extended periods at high actuation voltages. We systematically characterized the membrane-based acoustic actuator longevity, demonstrating consistent streaming and propulsion for over 24 hours of continuous operation. In addition, by embedding magnetic microparticles into the structural body, these actuators were successfully employed as microswimmers with directional control using low-intensity (2 mT) external magnetic fields. Finally, we demonstrate the scalability of the proposed design architecture down to ~100 um. This membrane-based approach establishes a reliable framework for the development of high-endurance acoustic microactuators and microrobots capable of performing long-term tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a membrane-based acoustic microrobot using a PDMS membrane over microcavities to prevent gas dissolution, achieving stable microstreaming for over 24 hours, magnetic steering, and scalability down to ~100 µm.
AI.motivation: Conventional acoustic microrobots rely on air microbubbles in microcavities that suffer from rapid gas dissolution and resonance frequency shifts, limiting operational longevity.
AI.method: A thin flexible PDMS membrane is bonded over confined microcavities to physically prevent gas diffusion; magnetic microparticles are embedded for directional control under low-intensity (2 mT) external magnetic fields.
AI.result: The membrane-based actuator demonstrates consistent streaming and propulsion for over 24 hours of continuous operation; directional control is achieved via magnetic steering; the design is scalable down to ~100 µm.
AI.conclusion: This membrane-based approach provides a reliable framework for developing high-endurance acoustic microactuators and microrobots capable of performing long-term tasks in targeted drug delivery and minimally invasive medicine.

title: Learning Splitting Heuristics for Parallel String Solvers
summary: String constraint solvers are crucial for reasoning about string-manipulating programs. However, many practical string constraints are undecidable, and real-world applications often present complex constraints that challenge current solvers. The rise of multi-core architectures offers an opportunity for parallel solving. A key parallel solving method is \emph{cube-and-conquer}, in which the quality of splitting heuristics is critical to effectively dividing the search space. Unfortunately, manually designing the heuristics is labor-intensive, and handcrafted heuristics are often sub-optimal. This paper introduces a data-driven approach to automatically generating splitting heuristics. We frame the problem of selecting a splitting atom as a learning task, using features from input formulas and dynamic data from solver execution. We implement this approach in two popular string solvers, Z3seq and Z3str4, demonstrating that the learned heuristics outperform manually designed ones in the number of solved formulas and the average solving time.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a data-driven approach to automatically generate splitting heuristics for cube-and-conquer parallel string constraint solving, outperforming manually designed heuristics in Z3seq and Z3str4.
AI.motivation: Many practical string constraints are undecidable, real-world applications present complex constraints challenging current solvers, and manually designing splitting heuristics for cube-and-conquer parallel solving is labor-intensive and often sub-optimal.
AI.method: The authors frame splitting atom selection as a learning task using features from input formulas and dynamic solver execution data, then implement the learned heuristics in two popular string solvers: Z3seq and Z3str4.
AI.result: The learned heuristics outperform manually designed heuristics in both the number of solved formulas and the average solving time.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven automatic generation of splitting heuristics is a viable and effective approach for improving parallel string constraint solving on multi-core architectures.

title: ReFPO: Reflow Regularization for Flow Matching Policy Gradients
summary: We present Reflow-regularized Flow Matching Policy Gradients (ReFPO), a simple online RL method that adds explicit Reflow regularization to FPO for efficient flow-based control. We uncover a key structural property: the gradient updates in Flow Matching Policy Gradients (FPO) can be interpreted as an implicit advantage-weighted Reflow process, providing a new geometric perspective on flow-based policy gradients. Building on this insight, ReFPO introduces an explicit geometric regularizer that can be implemented with a single line of code change without incurring additional computational overhead or auxiliary distillation stages. By synergizing advantage-guided updates with path rectification, our method reduces CFM proxy-ratio spikes, stabilizes PPO-style training, and enables high-fidelity one-step inference that often matches or exceeds multi-step performance. We experimentally demonstrate that ReFPO improves average performance and discretization robustness across GridWorld, MuJoCo Playground, and high-dimensional Humanoid Control tasks, providing a scalable and stable approach for generative policies in complex physical simulations.

AI.tldr: ReFPO adds a simple one-line Reflow regularization to Flow Matching Policy Gradients, improving stability and one-step inference performance in flow-based control tasks.
AI.motivation: FPO gradient updates have an implicit advantage-weighted Reflow structure, but lack explicit geometric regularization, leading to proxy-ratio spikes and training instability.
AI.method: ReFPO introduces an explicit geometric regularizer via a one-line code change, combining advantage-guided updates with path rectification without extra computational overhead.
AI.result: Reduces CFM proxy-ratio spikes, stabilizes PPO-style training, enables high-fidelity one-step inference matching multi-step performance, and improves average performance across GridWorld, MuJoCo Playground, and Humanoid Control.
AI.conclusion: ReFPO is a scalable, stable, and efficient approach for flow-based generative policies in complex physical simulations.

title: A-Evolve-Training: Autonomous Post-Training of a 30B Model
summary: Post-training a frontier model is normally weeks of human work: proposing data and recipe changes, launching runs, reading evals, deciding what to keep. We report an autonomous system that runs this loop with no human in the loop, post-training a 30B Nemotron across four rounds over multiple weeks. The autonomously produced model reaches a held-out score of 0.86 against the top human submission's 0.87 on the public NVIDIA Nemotron-Reasoning Challenge leaderboard, placing 8th of ~4000 at the time of writing. More striking than the number: the loop detected that its own dev metric had stopped tracking external performance on the weakest domain -- candidates drove dev to record highs without moving the external target -- and revised its own search policy, no longer maximizing dev but seeking interventions that lowered the now-misleading proxy while improving the external target. We treat this as direct, auditable evidence that a scaled autonomous loop can produce discovery, not only optimization: it detected that its measurement frame had become misleading and changed what counted as evidence. We take the operational view that any system worth the "recursive self-improvement" label must eventually perform end-to-end post-training of a frontier-class model; this is one datapoint of that bar being cleared. We do not claim a "first autonomous match" of human researchers. The claim we make is narrower and auditable: to our knowledge, this is the first publicly reported autonomous post-training run at this scale, where prior public autonomous-ML-research demonstrations sit at GPT-2-class (~124M) budgets. The same system also post-trains the 120B and 550B Nemotron; with no public human baseline there, this shows only that the loop closes at that scale, not that its output is competitive -- infrastructure evidence, with the effectiveness claim deferred until a comparable human anchor exists.

AI.tldr: An autonomous system post-trained a 30B Nemotron model across four rounds without human intervention, achieving a score of 0.86 (vs. 0.87 human baseline) on the NVIDIA Nemotron-Reasoning Challenge, ranking 8th out of ~4000. The system autonomously detected when its dev metric stopped tracking external performance and revised its search policy accordingly — demonstrating discovery, not mere optimization.
AI.motivation: Frontier model post-training currently requires weeks of human labor involving iterative data/recipe changes, evaluation runs, and decision-making. The authors aim to automate this entire loop to enable scalable, autonomous recursive improvement of large models.
AI.method: An autonomous post-training loop running without human intervention across four rounds on a 30B Nemotron model. The system iteratively proposes changes, runs evaluations, and decides what to keep. It also autonomously detected that its dev metric had decoupled from external performance on the weakest domain, and revised its search policy to stop maximizing the misleading proxy and instead seek interventions that lowered the proxy while improving external targets.
AI.result: The autonomously produced 30B model achieved a held-out score of 0.86 vs. the top human submission's 0.87 on the public NVIDIA Nemotron-Reasoning Challenge leaderboard, ranking 8th of ~4000 entries. The system also post-trained 120B and 550B Nemotron models at scale, though no human baseline exists for comparison at those sizes.
AI.conclusion: This is the first publicly reported autonomous post-training run at this scale (prior public demonstrations were at GPT-2-class ~124M budgets). The system's behavior — detecting and correcting a misleading proxy metric — constitutes direct evidence that scaled autonomous loops can produce genuine discovery, not just optimization. The authors position this as clearing the bar for "recursive self-improvement" applied to frontier-class model post-training.

title: MV-WAM: Manifold-Aware World Action Model with Value Augmentation
summary: Achieving robust and generalizable manipulation across diverse environments remains a fundamental challenge in embodied robotics. Recent world action models achieve strong in-domain performance, yet their gains do not extend proportionally to out-of-distribution scenarios. We attribute this to a structural mismatch between visual and action modalities, whose intrinsically heterogeneous manifolds cause joint optimization to disproportionately degrade action robustness under distribution shift. To address this, we propose MV-WAM, a novel end-to-end framework that jointly models visual prediction, action generation, and value estimation designed to effectively leverage video priors during both training and inference for enhanced action generalization. Key to this unification is a cross-modality causal mask that hierarchically grounds actions in predicted video frames and value function tokens in both modalities. To further narrow the generalization gap, MV-WAM adopts a manifold-aware optimization scheme that explicitly accounts for the structural heterogeneity across modalities. Finally, MV-WAM introduces a progress-value regulation mechanism that estimates task completion and detects misalignment between predicted frames and generated actions, enabling the policy to autonomously identify execution deviations and recover through value-guided rollback. On the RoboTwin simulation, MV-WAM achieves a 55.7% mean success rate on random scenarios without any randomized action supervision, outperforming the strongest baseline by 29.3%. MV-WAM achieves a 77.5% mean success rate across four real-world tasks of varying difficulty on a dual-arm robot. Our results demonstrate that manifold-aware cross-modal alignment is essential for robust policy generalization, offering a path toward deployable robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: MV-WAM is an end-to-end framework for robotic manipulation that addresses the generalization gap caused by structural mismatch between visual and action modalities. It uses a cross-modality causal mask, manifold-aware optimization, and progress-value regulation to achieve robust out-of-distribution performance, attaining 55.7% success in simulation (29.3% above baseline) and 77.5% across real-world dual-arm tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing world action models achieve strong in-domain performance but fail to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios due to a structural mismatch between visual and action modalities, whose heterogeneous manifolds cause joint optimization to disproportionately degrade action robustness under distribution shift.
AI.method: (1) Cross-modality causal mask that hierarchically grounds actions in predicted video frames and value function tokens. (2) Manifold-aware optimization scheme that explicitly accounts for structural heterogeneity across modalities. (3) Progress-value regulation mechanism for estimating task completion, detecting misalignment, and enabling value-guided rollback for error recovery.
AI.result: 55.7% mean success rate on RoboTwin simulation random scenarios (29.3% improvement over strongest baseline) without randomized action supervision; 77.5% mean success rate across four real-world dual-arm robot tasks of varying difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Manifold-aware cross-modal alignment is essential for robust policy generalization, offering a path toward deployable robotic manipulation.

title: Expected Free Energy-based Planning as Variational Inference
summary: Planning under uncertainty requires agents to balance goal achievement with information gathering. Active inference addresses this through the Expected Free Energy (EFE), a cost function that unifies instrumental and epistemic objectives. However, existing EFE-based methods typically employ specialized optimization procedures that are difficult to extend or analyze. In this paper, we show that EFE-based planning can be formulated as Variational Free Energy minimization on a generative model augmented with epistemic priors. Our main result demonstrates that minimizing a Variational Free Energy functional with appropriately chosen priors yields a decomposition into expected plan costs (the EFE) plus a complexity term. This formulation reinforces theoretical consistency with the Free Energy Principle by casting planning as the same inferential process that governs perception and learning. We validate our approach on three environments of increasing complexity: a deterministic T-maze, a stochastic Reactivity Maze, and a partially observable MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8 environment. The experiments demonstrate that the epistemic priors induce information-seeking behavior, that the variational formulation yields policy-based inference outperforming plan-based methods under stochastic transitions, and that temporal factorization enables scalability to environments where existing tabular active inference methods cannot operate.

AI.tldr: EFE-based planning can be reformulated as Variational Free Energy minimization with epistemic priors, unifying planning with perception/learning under the Free Energy Principle and enabling scalable information-seeking behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing EFE-based planning methods rely on specialized optimization procedures that are difficult to extend or analyze; a unified variational formulation is needed to establish theoretical consistency with the Free Energy Principle and improve scalability.
AI.method: Formulates EFE-based planning as Variational Free Energy minimization on a generative model augmented with epistemic priors; minimizing the VFE functional with chosen priors yields decomposition into EFE plus a complexity term.
AI.result: Validated on deterministic T-maze, stochastic Reactivity Maze, and partially observable MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8; epistemic priors induce information-seeking behavior; variational policy-based inference outperforms plan-based methods under stochastic transitions; temporal factorization enables scalability beyond tabular methods.
AI.conclusion: Planning can be cast as the same inferential process governing perception and learning under the Free Energy Principle, with practical scalability improvements from variational formulation.

title: How Should a Robot Configure Its Laser Scanner for Inspection?
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Robotic inspection relies on accurate sensing to acquire high-fidelity geometric measurements for defect detection and metrology. While prior work has focused on robot motion and viewpoint planning, how to configure sensing parameters remains largely underexplored, despite their decisive impact on measurement quality. We propose SenseHD, a robotic sensing system that formulates scanner configuration as an instruction-conditioned sensing decision. Instead of predicting precise parameter values, SenseHD treats sensing parameters as discrete sensing actions and selects stable sensing regimes through hyperdimensional associative memory. Experiments on a real robotic inspection platform demonstrate that SenseHD robustly selects appropriate sensing configurations and significantly improves inspection reliability, while remaining lightweight and efficient compared to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: SenseHD is a robotic sensing system that treats scanner configuration as instruction-conditioned sensing decisions, using hyperdimensional associative memory to select stable sensing regimes rather than predicting precise parameter values, improving inspection reliability on real robotic platforms.
AI.motivation: Prior robotic inspection work has focused on robot motion and viewpoint planning, but configuring sensing parameters—which decisively impact measurement quality—remains largely underexplored.
AI.method: SenseHD formulates scanner configuration as an instruction-conditioned sensing decision, treating sensing parameters as discrete sensing actions and selecting stable sensing regimes via hyperdimensional associative memory.
AI.result: On a real robotic inspection platform, SenseHD robustly selects appropriate sensing configurations, significantly improves inspection reliability, and remains lightweight and efficient compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: SenseHD demonstrates that treating sensing parameter selection as discrete action selection through hyperdimensional computing is an effective, lightweight approach for improving robotic inspection reliability.

title: Skill Coverage: A Test Adequacy Metric for Agent Skills
summary: Agent skills encode reusable procedural knowledge that guides large language model agents across tasks and execution contexts. Existing evaluations primarily assess skills through task level outcomes, yet task success alone does not reveal which parts of a skill have been exercised or which remain untested. We introduce skill coverage, a test adequacy metric that treats the skill artifact as the object under test. Our approach extracts observable skill behavior constraints from skill documents and measures whether an agent trajectory provides sufficient evidence to exercise and evaluate each constraint. Skill coverage uses a binary cover or not cover judgment, which reports whether a documented behavior has been exercised with sufficient observable evidence, without assigning an additional outcome label to the behavior. Applying skill coverage to SkillsBench reveals that existing benchmark executions cover only 39.90 to 43.98% of skill behavior constraints, suggesting that current benchmark tasks leave large portions of documented skill guidance untested. These findings show that successful task completion does not imply adequate testing of the skill artifact, highlighting skill coverage as a measure of how thoroughly agent skills are tested.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces skill coverage, a test adequacy metric that measures how thoroughly an agent's execution tests the documented behaviors of a skill. Applying it to SkillsBench shows that only ~40-44% of skill behavior constraints are covered, indicating task success does not guarantee thorough skill testing.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations assess skills only through task-level outcomes, but task success alone does not reveal which parts of a skill have been exercised or remain untested.
AI.method: The authors extract observable skill behavior constraints from skill documents and define a binary "cover/not cover" judgment based on whether an agent trajectory provides sufficient evidence to exercise and evaluate each constraint.
AI.result: Applying skill coverage to SkillsBench shows that existing benchmark executions cover only 39.90% to 43.98% of skill behavior constraints, meaning large portions of documented skill guidance remain untested.
AI.conclusion: Successful task completion does not imply adequate testing of the skill artifact; skill coverage is a useful complementary measure for evaluating how thoroughly agent skills are tested.

title: Factor-Aware Mixture-of-Experts with Pretrained Encoder for Combinatorial Generalization
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures, accepted by the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: The integration of pretrained encoders with diffusion policies has become a dominant paradigm for visual robotic manipulation. However, it still struggles to generalize across complex environments with varying factors such as lighting and surface textures. To address this, we propose FAME, a framework that integrates a factor-aware mixture-of-experts (MoE) with a pretrained encoder to enhance generalization to environmental variations. FAME follows a three-stage training process: (1) policy warmup, where a diffusion policy is trained on standard-environment data with a frozen encoder; (2) factor-specific adapter training, where lightweight adapters inserted between the frozen encoder and the temporarily frozen policy are trained on customized datasets, each targeting a distinct environmental variation; and (3) joint fine-tuning, where a central router and the warmed policy are trained on mixed data to handle multiple factors jointly. FAME is ``factor-aware'' because the central router softly weights frozen factor-specific adapters as a dense MoE, enabling combinatorial generalization across multiple factors. Evaluations on the Meta-World benchmark show that FAME outperforms diffusion policy baselines by 34%. We further validate FAME in a real-world pick-and-place task using a compact model trained on newly collected data, where FAME achieves a 35% improvement in generalization under real-world variations.

AI.tldr: FAME integrates factor-aware mixture-of-experts with pretrained encoders through a three-stage training process to enhance diffusion policy generalization across varying environmental factors (lighting, textures, etc.), achieving 34% improvement on Meta-World and 35% on real-world pick-and-place tasks.
AI.motivation: Pretrained encoders with diffusion policies struggle to generalize across complex environments with varying factors such as lighting and surface textures.
AI.method: FAME uses a three-stage training: (1) policy warmup with frozen encoder on standard data; (2) factor-specific adapter training with frozen encoder and policy on customized datasets; (3) joint fine-tuning with a central router and warmed policy on mixed data. The router softly weights frozen adapters as a dense MoE for combinatorial generalization.
AI.result: FAME outperforms diffusion policy baselines by 34% on Meta-World and achieves 35% improvement in generalization on a real-world pick-and-place task.
AI.conclusion: The factor-aware MoE framework effectively enables generalization across multiple environmental variations, validated both in simulation and real-world settings.

title: From Knowing to Acting: Benchmarking Self-Awareness Capability of LLM Agents
summary: The integration of external tools has transitioned LLM agents from passive responders to autonomous systems. However, current benchmarks prioritize execution success, neglecting self-awareness capability, the ability to discern whether a problem requires necessary external resources or can be solved via internal parametric knowledge. To address this, we introduce KAPRO (Knowing-Acting Quadrant PRObe), a framework that evaluates cognitive-behavioral alignment by decoupling an agent's metacognitive judgment (Knowing) from its spontaneous execution (Acting). We further construct KAware, a dataset rigorously partitioning tasks into external, internal, and hybrid subspaces to systematically probe these epistemic boundaries. Extensive experiments across diverse agent architectures show that self-awareness capability is strongly correlated with task success but degrades sharply in internal-capability settings. Moreover, open-source and instruction-following models exhibit stronger tool overuse due to shallow pattern matching, while proprietary and reasoning-oriented models demonstrate more reliable cognitive gating. Benchmark and codes are available at https://github.com/AI-Santiago/KAware.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces KAPRO, a framework to evaluate LLM agents' self-awareness capability (knowing when to use external tools vs. relying on internal knowledge), along with the KAware dataset that partitions tasks into external, internal, and hybrid subspaces. Experiments show self-awareness strongly correlates with task success, and open-source models overuse tools due to shallow pattern matching while proprietary/reasoning models exhibit better cognitive gating.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for LLM agents prioritize execution success but neglect self-awareness capability—the ability to discern whether a problem requires external resources or can be solved via internal parametric knowledge.
AI.method: The authors propose KAPRO (Knowing-Acting Quadrant PRObe), a framework that decouples metacognitive judgment (Knowing) from spontaneous execution (Acting) to evaluate cognitive-behavioral alignment. They also construct KAware, a dataset that partitions tasks into external, internal, and hybrid subspaces to probe epistemic boundaries.
AI.result: Self-awareness capability is strongly correlated with task success but degrades sharply in internal-capability settings. Open-source and instruction-following models exhibit stronger tool overuse due to shallow pattern matching, while proprietary and reasoning-oriented models demonstrate more reliable cognitive gating.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating and improving self-awareness in LLM agents is critical for reliable tool use, and different model families exhibit distinct patterns in cognitive gating versus tool overuse.

title: PoLAR: Factorizing Extent and Mode in Latent Actions for Robot Policy Learning
summary: Latent action pretraining learns representations of visual change from pairs of observations, but existing methods typically encode each transition as a single unstructured representation that entangles transition extent and transition mode. We introduce Polar Latent Actions with Radial structure (PoLAR), which imposes a radial-direction structure on latent actions, encouraging radius to encode transition extent and direction to retain transition mode. PoLAR uses temporal offset between two observations as a weak proxy for transition extent, encouraging latent action from observation pairs separated by larger temporal gaps to occupy larger radii. We instantiate this structure in hyperbolic space, whose expanding volume with radius offers a natural fit for more diverse transition modes at larger extents. Across in-task and large-scale pretraining settings, PoLAR improves downstream policy performance in simulation and real-world robot experiments, outperforming latent action baselines and strong pretrained VLAs. These results suggest that the geometry of the latent action space is an important design choice for transferring visual pretraining to downstream robot policy learning.

AI.tldr: PoLAR introduces a radial-direction structure on latent actions, where radius encodes transition extent and direction encodes transition mode, using hyperbolic space and temporal offsets as weak supervision. This improves downstream robot policy learning across simulation and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing latent action pretraining methods encode each visual transition as a single unstructured representation that entangles transition extent and transition mode, limiting downstream policy learning.
AI.method: PoLAR imposes a radial-direction structure on latent actions: radius encodes transition extent (using temporal offset as weak proxy), direction retains transition mode. This structure is instantiated in hyperbolic space, whose expanding volume naturally accommodates more diverse transition modes at larger extents.
AI.result: PoLAR improves downstream policy performance in both simulated and real-world robot experiments, outperforming latent action baselines and strong pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models.
AI.conclusion: The geometry of the latent action space is an important design choice for transferring visual pretraining to downstream robot policy learning.

title: Confidence Laundering in Agent Systems: Why Uncertainty Needs a Latent Carrier
summary: Modern agent systems can turn uncertainty into overconfidence. Fragile upstream decisions are often exposed to downstream components as clean intermediate artifacts, while the uncertainty behind those decisions is lost at the interface. As a result, local ambiguity can become system-level error amplification. We argue that this reveals an interface bottleneck in agent uncertainty propagation: uncertainty does not propagate simply because a trajectory contains uncertain steps; it propagates only when it survives the handoff between components. We define uncertain decision handoff as the transfer of an intermediate decision made under uncertainty, and identify confidence laundering as a failure mode in which fragile upstream states are repackaged as procedurally valid artifacts that downstream agents over-trust. To address this bottleneck, we propose latent uncertainty as an uncertainty-bearing carrier attached to decision handoffs. Rather than replacing text with hidden states, latent uncertainty aims to preserve pre-commitment fragility in a form that downstream components can use. This position shifts agent uncertainty propagation from step-wise uncertainty estimation toward uncertainty-preserving interface design for more recoverable agent systems.

AI.tldr: Agent systems suffer from an interface bottleneck where uncertainty is lost during decision handoffs between components, leading to confidence laundering and error amplification. The paper proposes latent uncertainty as a carrier to preserve and propagate uncertainty across agent interfaces.
AI.motivation: Current agent systems propagate fragile upstream decisions as clean intermediate artifacts, causing uncertainty to be lost at component interfaces. This leads to overconfidence and error amplification, motivating the need for uncertainty-preserving interface design.
AI.method: The paper identifies confidence laundering as a key failure mode and proposes latent uncertainty—an uncertainty-bearing carrier attached to decision handoffs that preserves pre-commitment fragility for downstream consumption, without replacing text with hidden states.
AI.result: Conceptual identification of the interface bottleneck, uncertain decision handoff, and confidence laundering as failure modes. Proposes latent uncertainty as a design solution.
AI.conclusion: Agent uncertainty propagation should shift from step-wise uncertainty estimation toward uncertainty-preserving interface design for more recoverable agent systems.

title: Pose-Agnostic Robotic Functional Grasping via Observation-Action Canonicalization
summary: Functional robotic grasping requires a policy that generalizes across diverse object geometries and poses while maintaining task-specific contact precision. We study this challenge through mug-handle grasping, where thin handles, instance variation, and upright or inverted placements make both perception and control sensitive to object configuration. Grasp pose detection methods operate open-loop and are sensitive to estimation errors on thin handle structures. Learned visuomotor policies must implicitly learn to handle the coupled variation in visual appearance and action direction induced by different object placements, limiting generalization. We propose AnyMug, a canonicalized visuomotor reinforcement learning framework for functional grasping that trains a single closed-loop policy entirely in simulation and deploys it zero-shot on a real robot. AnyMug introduces observation-action canonicalization, which transforms both the depth observation and the predicted end-effector action into a shared object-centric frame. The policy therefore sees a consistent mug-centered view and emits actions in a canonical direction regardless of mug placement, allowing the same grasping behavior to be reused across configurations. A handle-aware reward further encourages precise approach, gripper alignment, and opposing-finger placement, while a pose curriculum and domain randomization improve training stability and sim-to-real transfer. In simulation, AnyMug achieves over 93% success rate on both unseen upright and inverted mugs and transfers zero-shot to a real Franka Panda, reaching 80% success rate on 5 held-out physical mugs across both pose categories.

AI.tldr: AnyMug is a canonicalized visuomotor RL framework that trains a single closed-loop policy in simulation for functional mug-handle grasping, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer through observation-action canonicalization, handle-aware reward, and domain randomization.
AI.motivation: Functional robotic grasping (e.g., mug-handle grasping) requires generalization across diverse object geometries, poses (upright/inverted), and thin handle structures. Existing grasp pose detection methods are open-loop and error-sensitive, while learned visuomotor policies struggle with coupled visual-appearance and action-direction variation, limiting generalization.
AI.method: A canonicalized visuomotor RL framework: (1) Observation-action canonicalization transforms depth observations and predicted actions into a shared object-centric frame for consistent perception and action direction; (2) Handle-aware reward encourages precise approach, gripper alignment, and opposing-finger placement; (3) Pose curriculum and domain randomization improve training stability and sim-to-real transfer; trained entirely in simulation, deployed zero-shot on real robot.
AI.result: In simulation: over 93% success rate on unseen upright and inverted mugs. On a real Franka Panda: 80% success rate on 5 held-out physical mugs across both pose categories, zero-shot transfer.
AI.conclusion: AnyMug demonstrates that canonicalization of both observations and actions into a shared object-centric frame enables a single visuomotor policy to generalize across diverse object poses and geometries for functional grasping, achieving effective zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without requiring real-world fine-tuning.

title: DrugBench: Evaluating AI Control Protocols for Medication Harm Mitigation
