summary: Large Language Models have the potential to expand and improve the access to clinical information by enabling new ways of interacting with medical knowledge in natural language. However, their deployment in medical question-answering settings is safety-critical, since misaligned outputs can lead to severe patient harm. AI control is an emerging approach that introduces external safeguards to mitigate unsafe behaviours in misaligned systems and has been shown to be effective in domains such as code generation. However, its applicability and effectiveness in medical settings have not been systematically studied. In this work, we present a pipeline for evaluating AI control protocols to mitigate medication-related harm. To this end, we introduce DrugBench, an AI control evaluation benchmark which combines 3,671 multi-turn medical conversations from HealthBench with drug information from official FDA labels, covering four categories of medication-related harm: drug interactions, contraindications, dosing constraints, and patient action restrictions. Furthermore, inspired by the medical domain, we argue that safety should account for the severity of unsafe outputs, not just their probability. Under this revised definition, we show that existing control protocols can be subverted and propose severity-based monitoring to address this limitation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a pipeline for evaluating AI control protocols in medical settings, introduces DrugBench (a benchmark with 3,671 multi-turn conversations and FDA drug labels covering four medication-related harm categories), proposes severity-based monitoring to address the limitation that existing control protocols can be subverted when safety accounts for severity of unsafe outputs rather than just their probability.
AI.motivation: LLMs in medical question-answering are safety-critical since misaligned outputs can cause patient harm. AI control has been effective in code generation but its applicability in medical settings has not been systematically studied, motivating the need for a dedicated evaluation pipeline and benchmark.
AI.method: The authors present a pipeline for evaluating AI control protocols to mitigate medication-related harm. They introduce DrugBench, combining 3,671 multi-turn medical conversations from HealthBench with official FDA drug labels covering four harm categories. They also propose severity-based monitoring to address the subversion of existing control protocols under a severity-aware safety definition.
AI.result: Existing control protocols can be subverted when safety is defined to account for severity of unsafe outputs rather than just their probability. The severity-based monitoring approach is introduced to address this limitation.
AI.conclusion: AI control protocols need to account for severity of harm in medical settings, not just probability. The DrugBench benchmark and severity-based monitoring provide a foundation for safer medical LLM deployment.

title: OmniV2X: A Generative Foundation Planner for Efficient End-to-End Cooperative Driving
summary: We present OmniV2X, a generative foundation model for vehicle-to-everything (V2X) cooperative driving. The model directly interprets independent context sequences comprising multi-modal and multi-agent observations. The new design mitigates the computational cost of dense 3D perception, the vulnerability to data scarcity in cooperative scenarios, and the poor compliance with standardized messaging in existing methods that fuse multi-modal inputs into a shared representation. For training, we present an end-to-end supervised pipeline using a downstream trajectory generation loss, in which a high-capacity generative sequence planner implicitly learns to steer the model and leverage multi-modal inputs via cross-attention injection. As a foundation model, we demonstrate that OmniV2X pre-trained on large-scale single-agent planning datasets can efficiently adapt to cooperative environments by integrating the conditioning context with lightweight, standard-compliant V2X tokens. Evaluated on the DAIR-V2X-Seq dataset, OmniV2X outperforms existing end-to-end cooperative driving baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance with less than 10% of the fine-tune V2X dataset and less than 1% of the communication bandwidth. We conduct comprehensive evaluations to demonstrate its computational efficiency and robustness under real-world constraints.

AI.tldr: OmniV2X is a generative foundation model for V2X cooperative driving that processes multi-modal, multi-agent context sequences using a generative sequence planner with trajectory supervision, achieving SOTA performance with minimal data and bandwidth fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing V2X methods suffer from high computational cost of dense 3D perception, vulnerability to data scarcity in cooperative scenarios, and poor compliance with standardized messaging due to fusing multi-modal inputs into a shared representation.
AI.method: OmniV2X uses an end-to-end supervised pipeline with downstream trajectory generation loss, where a high-capacity generative sequence planner leverages multi-modal inputs via cross-attention injection. It interprets independent context sequences of multi-modal, multi-agent observations and uses lightweight, standard-compliant V2X tokens for conditioning.
AI.result: Outperforms existing end-to-end cooperative driving baselines on DAIR-V2X-Seq, achieving SOTA performance with less than 10% of fine-tune V2X dataset and less than 1% of the communication bandwidth.
AI.conclusion: OmniV2X demonstrates computational efficiency and robustness under real-world constraints, positioning itself as an effective foundation model that can be pre-trained on single-agent data and efficiently adapted to cooperative driving.

title: A Quantum-Assisted Agentic Distributed Artificial Intelligence Framework for Deadline-Bounded Orchestration of Hybrid Renewable Microgrids
summary: The real-time orchestration of microgrids that combine fluctuating renewable sources, dispatchable units, storage and curtailable consumers requires the repeated solution of combinatorial dispatch and coalition formation problems under hard control deadlines. In this paper, a quantum-assisted agentic distributed artificial intelligence (DAI) framework is proposed in which the dispatch problem of each control slot is formulated as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem by Belief-Desire-Intention extended (BDIx) agents and is solved by a portfolio of quantum, quantum-inspired and classical solvers. Solver selection is elevated to a first-class agentic deliberation action of the coordinator agent. Learned beliefs about solver latencies are maintained and the solver intention that is expected to satisfy the prevailing deliberation deadline is committed in each slot. In addition, a belief-shaped storage valuation mechanism is introduced through which the storage agent prices its energy at a discounted future-peak value, injecting intertemporal information into the otherwise myopic per-slot optimization. The framework is evaluated on a 24-hour simulation of a grid-connected microgrid with photovoltaic, wind, battery, genset and demand-response assets, with the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) executed by statevector simulation and benchmarked per slot against tabu search, simulated annealing, binary particle swarm optimization, greedy descent and exhaustive enumeration. Zero deliberation deadlines are missed, the committed dispatch attains the exact optimum on every slot and the realized daily cost of 146.24 EUR equals the exact lower bound, with 97.83 percent renewable utilization and zero unserved energy. When the storage valuation mechanism is deactivated, the daily cost is increased to 152.75 EUR, a 4.5 percent increase.

AI.tldr: A quantum-assisted agentic distributed AI framework is proposed for real-time microgrid orchestration, using BDIx agents to formulate dispatch as QUBO problems solved by a portfolio of solvers. The framework achieves zero deadline misses, exact optimal dispatch per slot, and a daily cost of 146.24 EUR (the exact lower bound) with 97.83% renewable utilization.
AI.motivation: Real-time microgrid orchestration combining renewables, dispatchable units, storage, and curtailable consumers requires solving combinatorial dispatch and coalition formation problems under hard control deadlines, which is challenging for conventional methods.
AI.method: A quantum-assisted agentic DAI framework where BDIx agents formulate per-slot dispatch as QUBO problems, solved by a portfolio of quantum (QAOA), quantum-inspired, and classical solvers. Solver selection is an agentic deliberation action with learned latency beliefs. A belief-shaped storage valuation mechanism prices storage at discounted future-peak value to inject intertemporal information.
AI.result: Zero deliberation deadlines missed; exact optimal dispatch per slot; daily cost of 146.24 EUR (exact lower bound); 97.83% renewable utilization; zero unserved energy. Without storage valuation, cost increases 4.5% to 152.75 EUR.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum-assisted agentic DAI framework successfully meets hard real-time deadlines while achieving optimal dispatch, demonstrating the viability of quantum-assisted methods for practical microgrid control.

title: Remember what you did?: Learning Behavioral Memories for Partially Observable Object Manipulation
summary: Long horizon, contact-rich manipulation is inherently partially observable. This is as a single visual observation rarely captures a robot's full action context, including prior attempts, interactions, or progress. Consequently, standard visuomotor policies or vision-language-action models are prone to struggle in such tasks due to a lack of memory. To address this, we introduce Compressed Action Memory Policy (CAMP) based on the insight that a robot's own action history serves as a highly informative, self-supervised signal, enabling the policy to learn a robust, compact history representation. In our approach, we train a memory module to maintain a compressed representation of past actions, forcing it to encode a latent behavioral memory of all the robot's past interactions that can then be used to better contextualize future actions. This allows our approach to implicitly track generalized task progress and learn from failed attempts without any additional supervision, or external oversight. We evaluate CAMP across four real-robot setups and two novel simulation benchmarks: Memory-T-Bench and Memory-Manip-Bench. By demonstrating substantial gains over state-of-the-art baselines, CAMP is, to our knowledge, the first policy to demonstrate substantial success on contact-rich partially observable manipulation tasks purely through learned memory.

AI.tldr: CAMP introduces a compressed action memory policy that uses past action history as a self-supervised signal to improve performance in long-horizon, contact-rich partially observable manipulation tasks, demonstrating substantial gains over baselines across real-robot and simulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon contact-rich manipulation is inherently partially observable due to single visual observations lacking full action context (prior attempts, interactions, progress), causing standard visuomotor policies or vision-language-action models to struggle due to memory deficiency.
AI.method: CAMP trains a memory module to maintain a compressed representation of past actions, encoding latent behavioral memory of all past robot interactions to contextualize future actions, without additional supervision or external oversight.
AI.result: Evaluated across four real-robot setups and two novel simulation benchmarks (Memory-T-Bench and Memory-Manip-Bench), CAMP demonstrates substantial gains over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: CAMP is the first policy to demonstrate substantial success on contact-rich partially observable manipulation tasks purely through learned memory.

title: Agent Behavior Mining: Generative AI Agent Governance in Business Processes
comment: Accepted at BPM conference 2026 management main track
summary: As organizations increasingly deploy generative AI agents to automate business processes, they face a governance dilemma: although these agents can increase operational flexibility, their non-deterministic nature challenges the control and standardization that Business Process Management seeks to enforce. This paper addresses this \emph{invisible autonomy risk} by introducing \emph{Agent Behavior Mining}, a governance capability that enables the application of process mining techniques to render generative AI agent decision-making observable and traceable. We (1) improve the understanding of generative AI agent behavior through an event data model that translates granular agent activities -- including reasoning traces, tool usage, and token costs -- into standardized process logs; (2) instantiate the data model in a multi-agent order-to-cash implementation, demonstrating how process managers can leverage agent logs to detect policy deviations and quantify operational variability; and (3) evaluate the perceived practical utility of the approach in an exploratory study with 18 industry practitioners. The results indicate that practitioners view behavioral transparency as a prerequisite for trust and consider the ability to examine agent reasoning as an important governance requirement for the next generation of AI-driven business processes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Agent Behavior Mining, a governance capability that applies process mining to generative AI agents, making their decision-making observable and traceable through standardized event logs. It demonstrates the approach in a multi-agent order-to-cash system and evaluates its perceived utility with 18 practitioners, finding that behavioral transparency is seen as essential for trust in AI-driven business processes.
AI.motivation: Organizations face a governance dilemma: generative AI agents increase operational flexibility but their non-deterministic nature undermines the control and standardization required by Business Process Management (BPM), creating an "invisible autonomy risk."
AI.method: (1) An event data model that translates granular agent activities (reasoning traces, tool usage, token costs) into standardized process logs; (2) instantiation of the model in a multi-agent order-to-cash implementation; (3) an exploratory study with 18 industry practitioners to evaluate perceived practical utility.
AI.result: Practitioners view behavioral transparency as a prerequisite for trust and consider the ability to examine agent reasoning as an important governance requirement for the next generation of AI-driven business processes.
AI.conclusion: Agent Behavior Mining enables process managers to detect policy deviations and quantify operational variability, addressing the governance gap posed by autonomous generative AI agents in business processes.

title: A scalar per patch from pre-trained ViTs enables fast moving navigation in the real world
comment: European Conference on Computer Vision -- ECCV 2026
summary: Trained policies for real-world robotics rely on computer vision components, typically in the form of pre-trained visual encoders. These encoders are an essential component and it has been shown that their power does not emerge from training on robotics downstream losses alone. Pre-training with auxiliary losses in the form of computer-vision pre-text tasks is a defining factor and heavily conditions agent performance in robotics tasks. In this unprecedented large-scale study, we ran 966 navigation episodes of static point goal navigation in a real-world building for 24km and asked which components really matter for the computer vision aspects of robotics: we evaluate state-of-the art visual encoders in realistic conditions. We explore the usefulness of heterogeneous multi-teacher distillation leading to encoders with multiple different and complementary skills. We investigate how much information from these encoders is necessary for robotics by bottlenecking them in a principled and spatially useful way and we show that this leads to the emergence of interpretable features linked to affordances. We also argue that training policies on RGB data alone does not lead to an optimal usage of visual features and show this by finetuning policies pre-trained on privileged information. All in all, we paint a more complete picture of what aspects of computer vision are relevant for real-world navigation.

AI.tldr: This large-scale real-world study (966 navigation episodes, 24km) investigates which computer vision components truly matter for robotic point-goal navigation, finding that pre-trained visual encoders with auxiliary pre-text tasks are crucial, heterogeneous multi-teacher distillation improves performance, principled bottlenecking of encoders yields interpretable affordance features, and finetuning policies pre-trained on privileged information outperforms RGB-only training.
AI.motivation: To systematically disentangle which computer vision components (visual encoders, pre-training strategies, distillation, bottlenecking, privileged information) are truly impactful for real-world robotic navigation, moving beyond simulated or small-scale studies.
AI.method: 966 real-world navigation episodes totaling 24km for static point-goal navigation; evaluated state-of-the-art visual encoders; employed heterogeneous multi-teacher distillation; applied principled spatial bottlenecking to analyze information necessity; finetuned policies pre-trained on privileged information.
AI.result: Pre-training with auxiliary computer-vision pre-text tasks is a defining factor for agent performance; heterogeneous multi-teacher distillation produces encoders with complementary skills; bottlenecking encoders yields interpretable affordance-linked features; RGB-only training is suboptimal compared to finetuning from privileged information.
AI.conclusion: A more complete picture of relevant computer vision aspects for real-world navigation is presented, highlighting the importance of pre-training strategies, multi-teacher distillation, bottleneck analysis, and privileged information over naive RGB-only approaches.

title: Democratizing and accelerating AI-driven pathology research through agentic intelligence
summary: Computational pathology has advanced rapidly with the emergence of foundation models, yet widespread adoption remains limited by substantial technical complexity and programming requirements. Here we present PathLab, an autonomous agentic framework that translates natural-language research objectives into executable and validated computational pathology workflows through the structured composition of domain-specific skills and tools. By organizing workflow generation around reusable methodological modules, including data preprocessing, model development, evaluation and interpretation, PathLab enables studies to be specified at the level of scientific intent rather than implementation details. We evaluated PathLab across 12 public datasets spanning four representative task families: region-of-interest classification, whole-slide image classification, segmentation and survival prediction. Across all task categories, PathLab achieved non-inferior performance relative to expert implementations, while consistently enforcing semantic validity of user prompts and proactively rejecting incompatible workflow specifications prior to execution. In controlled user studies, PathLab substantially reduced the time required to generate executable analytical pipelines and enabled domain experts without programming experience to independently design, execute and evaluate computational pathology studies. Together, these results establish PathLab as a reliable interface between biomedical intent and computational execution, enabling computational pathology studies to be designed at the level of scientific questions rather than programming expertise. By lowering technical barriers to advanced AI methodologies, PathLab provides a foundation for the broader democratization of computational pathology.

AI.tldr: PathLab is an autonomous agentic framework that translates natural-language research objectives into executable computational pathology workflows by composing domain-specific skills and tools, achieving non-inferior performance to expert implementations across 12 datasets while drastically reducing the need for programming expertise.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in computational pathology foundation models, widespread adoption is limited by substantial technical complexity and programming requirements. The authors aim to lower these barriers by enabling studies to be specified at the level of scientific intent rather than implementation details.
AI.method: PathLab is an autonomous agentic framework that organizes workflow generation around reusable methodological modules (data preprocessing, model development, evaluation and interpretation). It translates natural-language prompts into executable pipelines by composing domain-specific skills and tools, with built-in semantic validation to reject incompatible workflows.
AI.result: Across 12 public datasets and four task families (ROI classification, WSI classification, segmentation, survival prediction), PathLab achieved non-inferior performance to expert implementations, enforced semantic validity of prompts, and proactively rejected incompatible specifications. User studies showed substantial reduction in pipeline generation time and enabled domain experts without programming experience to independently conduct studies.
AI.conclusion: PathLab establishes a reliable interface between biomedical intent and computational execution, democratizing computational pathology by allowing studies to be designed at the level of scientific questions rather than programming expertise, thus lowering technical barriers to advanced AI methodologies.

title: A UAV-Mounted Sensor Network for Close-Range Inspection of Wind Turbine Rotor Blades
comment: The Aerial Inspection for Marine Infrastructures (AIMI) workshop
summary:
Inspection of offshore wind turbine rotor blades is critical for predictive maintenance to maximise efficiency and extend operational lifetime. However, it remains a challenging task due to remote locations, large structural dimensions, and the limitations of current UAV-compatible sensor systems. While existing approaches can detect certain types of surface anomalies, reliable classification of defect types often remains a manual and error-prone process.
  This paper presents the design of a UAV-mounted multimodal sensor network combining an industrial RGB camera, a passive thermal infrared camera, and an in-house developed 3D scanner. All sensors are co-calibrated into a common coordinate frame, enabling spatial superimposition of geometric, colour, and thermal data. The system is designed to operate at close range, addressing three fundamental sensing challenges: platform motion, large field of view, and millimetre-level measurement accuracy. Preliminary laboratory results demonstrate synchronised multi-sensor acquisition and initial point cloud reconstructions, forming the basis for future airborne inspection trials.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a UAV-mounted multimodal sensor network (RGB + thermal + 3D scanner) co-calibrated for close-range offshore wind turbine blade inspection, demonstrating synchronized acquisition and point cloud reconstruction in lab tests.
AI.motivation: Offshore wind turbine rotor blade inspection is critical for predictive maintenance but remains challenging due to remote locations, large structural dimensions, limitations of current UAV-compatible sensors, and error-prone manual defect classification.
AI.method: Design of a UAV-mounted multimodal sensor network combining an industrial RGB camera, passive thermal infrared camera, and an in-house developed 3D scanner, all co-calibrated into a common coordinate frame for spatial superimposition of geometric, colour, and thermal data, operating at close range.
AI.result: Preliminary laboratory results demonstrate synchronized multi-sensor acquisition and initial point cloud reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: The system forms the basis for future airborne inspection trials, addressing platform motion, large field of view, and millimetre-level measurement accuracy challenges.

title: From Question Answering to Task Completion: A Survey on Agent System and Harness Design
summary: LLM-based agents mark a shift from passive question answering to active task completion: they perceive environments, invoke tools, maintain state, and act over extended horizons. As agent systems have evolved from prompt engineering to workflows and context engineering, harness engineering, and agent-native training with co-evolution, a central question has become increasingly important: where does the bottleneck in agent performance reside, in the foundation model, in the execution harness, or in the coupling between them? This survey examines LLM-based agents through a model-harness lens. We first clarify the functional definition of agents and the implementation view of an LLM-based agent as a foundation model coupled with an execution harness. We then analyze the limits of model-centric scaling, trace four paradigms of agent engineering, and decompose the execution harness into six coupled runtime responsibilities: observation, context, control, action, state, and verification. Using this decomposition, we map task properties and domain pressures to harness configurations, review benchmark and evaluation practices, and synthesize model-harness evidence on how runtime design affects long-horizon task completion, efficiency, and reliability. Finally, we identify open challenges in value-aware evaluation, safety, harness generalization, and model-harness co-evolution. Rather than treating agents as models with auxiliary tools, this survey argues that agent quality -- including success, efficiency, safety, and generalization -- emerges from the interaction between model capability, runtime infrastructure, task structure, and evaluation design. A collection of papers discussed in this survey is provided in https://github.com/ggjy/Awesome-Agent-Engineering.

AI.tldr: This survey analyzes LLM-based agents through a model-harness lens, decomposing agent systems into foundation models and execution harnesses, tracing four paradigms of agent engineering, and arguing that agent quality emerges from the interaction between model capability, runtime infrastructure, task structure, and evaluation design.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents shift from passive QA to active task completion, the central question is where the bottleneck in agent performance resides: the foundation model, the execution harness, or their coupling. The paper aims to systematically examine agents through this model-harness lens.
AI.method: The survey clarifies the functional definition of agents and implementation view of LLM-based agents as foundation model + execution harness. It analyzes limits of model-centric scaling, traces four paradigms of agent engineering (prompt engineering, workflows, context engineering, harness engineering, and agent-native training with co-evolution), and decomposes the execution harness into six runtime responsibilities: observation, context, control, action, state, and verification.
AI.result: The decomposition maps task properties and domain pressures to harness configurations. The survey reviews benchmark and evaluation practices, and synthesizes evidence on how runtime design affects long-horizon task completion, efficiency, and reliability.
AI.conclusion: Agent quality (success, efficiency, safety, generalization) emerges from the interaction between model capability, runtime infrastructure, task structure, and evaluation design, rather than treating agents as models with auxiliary tools. Open challenges include value-aware evaluation, safety, harness generalization, and model-harness co-evolution.

title: FleetAgent: Teleoperation Assistant for Autonomous Fleets via Vectorized V2N Messages
summary: Large-scale autonomous fleets rely on teleoperation to resolve rare failures, yet streaming raw sensor data from many vehicles is costly, and remote operators can only monitor a limited number of vehicles at a time. We introduce FleetAgent, a cloud-hosted multimodal large language model (MLLM) assistant that consumes compact vectorized vehicle-to-network (V2N) messages, such as map elements, detected objects, and the ego planned path. It provides a structured natural-language response (including narration, explanation, and evaluation of the plan and scene), along with an intervention urgency score for operator prioritization. To make structured messages compatible with token-based MLLMs, we propose VecFormer, a vector-to-embedding interface with differentiable top-K context selection that bounds context length and GPU KV-cache growth, enabling more efficient batch processing, which is important under the context of cloud-hosted large-scale fleet management. We also construct VecEval, a nuScenes-derived dataset with paired human and synthetic imperfect plans and human-verified language labels, to facilitate the training and evaluation of our proposed system. Our proposed system can reduce uplink payload by up to 625 times compared with raw images and reduce KV-cache memory by 16.54 times compared with original text descriptions. On VecEval, FleetAgent improves Lingo-Judge score by 16.8% and reduces intervention failure rate by 19.9%, compared with Qwen2.5-VL-7B using language descriptions. These results demonstrate that FleetAgent can utilize compact structured V2N messaging to enable efficient, explainable teleoperation monitoring for autonomous fleets.

AI.tldr: FleetAgent is a cloud-hosted MLLM assistant for autonomous fleet teleoperation that uses compact vectorized V2N messages (via VecFormer) instead of raw sensor data, achieving 625x payload reduction, 16.54x KV-cache savings, 16.8% better Lingo-Judge score, and 19.9% lower intervention failure rate on the VecEval dataset.
AI.motivation: Large-scale autonomous fleets rely on teleoperation for rare failures, but streaming raw sensor data from many vehicles is expensive and operators can only monitor a limited number of vehicles simultaneously.
AI.method: FleetAgent uses a cloud-hosted MLLM consuming compact vectorized V2N messages (map, objects, ego path). VecFormer is a vector-to-embedding interface with differentiable top-K context selection to bound token length and GPU KV-cache growth. VecEval is a nuScenes-derived dataset with imperfect plans and human-verified labels for training/evaluation.
AI.result: Reduces uplink payload by 625x vs. raw images, reduces KV-cache memory by 16.54x vs. text descriptions. On VecEval, improves Lingo-Judge score by 16.8% and reduces intervention failure rate by 19.9% compared to Qwen2.5-VL-7B with language descriptions.
AI.conclusion: FleetAgent demonstrates that compact structured V2N messaging enables efficient, explainable teleoperation monitoring for large-scale autonomous fleets.

title: Artificial Intelligence as Monism: Ontological, Organisational, and Methodological Implications
summary:
This paper argues that Artificial Intelligence should be understood as a form of monism:
  a unified substance that cannot be decomposed into separate elements such as data,
  algorithms, or technical architectures. Drawing from philosophical traditions of monism,
  dualism, and holism, the paper contends that AI is not merely a collection of components
  but a single, indivisible essence reflecting the phenomena it replicates. Treating AI as
  monism has deep implications across multiple dimensions. Epistemologically, it positions
  AI as the central interpretive force across technological, organisational, and societal
  domains, while raising ethical and existential concerns regarding singularity, the
  homogenisation of innovation, and the concentration of decision-making power. At the
  organisational level, a monistic approach challenges traditional siloed structures,
  advocating instead for transversal, problem-centric teams whose mandate derives from
  the integrity of the problem rather than from departmental hierarchy. In project
  management, it implies a unified vision and an integrated evaluation of complexity in
  which no single stakeholder perspective dominates the assessment of outcomes. In data
  and information management, it calls for architectures that reflect the irreducible unity
  of the phenomena being modelled. Ultimately, this paper calls for a paradigm shift in
  how AI is conceptualised, governed, and integrated, suggesting that only by embracing AI
  as monism can organisations achieve genuine agility and avoid the structural
  inefficiencies inherent to reductionist approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes viewing Artificial Intelligence as monism—a unified, indivisible essence—rather than a collection of separate components (data, algorithms, architectures). It explores the implications of this perspective across epistemology, ethics, organisational design, project management, and data management, arguing that embracing AI as monism enables genuine organisational agility and avoids reductionist inefficiencies.
AI.motivation: The paper argues that reductionist views of AI (treating it as decomposable into separate elements) lead to structural inefficiencies, siloed thinking, and concentration of power. It seeks to offer a unified philosophical framework—monism—to reconceptualise AI's nature and integration.
AI.method: The paper uses philosophical analysis drawing from traditions of monism, dualism, and holism, and applies this framework deductively across multiple domains: epistemology, ethics, organisational theory, project management, and data/information management.
AI.result: The analysis identifies that a monistic view of AI has profound implications: AI becomes the central interpretive force (epistemology); raises ethical concerns about singularity and power concentration; challenges siloed organisational structures in favour of transversal, problem-centric teams; demands unified vision in project management; and requires irreducible data architectures that mirror the unity of modelled phenomena.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a paradigm shift toward understanding AI as monism is necessary for genuine organisational agility and for avoiding the inefficiencies of reductionist approaches to AI governance and integration.

title: Ultra-Fusion: A Resilient Tightly-Coupled Multi-Sensor Fusion SLAM Framework under Sensor Degradation and Spatiotemporal Perturbation for Intelligent Transportation Systems
summary: Reliable localization is essential for intelligent transportation systems (ITS), including autonomous vehicles, quadruped last-mile carriers, and infrastructure-inspection unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Although tightly-coupled multi-sensor fusion improves accuracy in favorable conditions, deployed systems remain vulnerable to sensor degradation -- poor illumination, LiDAR degeneracy, wheel slippage, and GNSS outage -- and to spatiotemporal calibration errors. These failures are common in urban canyons, tunnels, and high-speed corridors, where localization drift can degrade route tracking, tunnel passage continuity, and local map alignment. This paper presents Ultra-Fusion, a tightly-coupled multi-sensor localization framework based on a unified sliding-window estimator. Asynchronous measurements are timestamp-ordered and converted into optional factors within one optimization window, supporting WIO, VIO, LIO, and LVIO with optional wheel and GNSS augmentation. Observability-aware initialization selects the bootstrap mode, factor-wise reliability scheduling gates degraded measurements, and online LiDAR--IMU spatiotemporal calibration refines temporal offsets and rotational extrinsics during operation. We extend the M3DGR benchmark with simulation trajectories and evaluate more than 60 open-source SLAM systems on M3DGR, M2DGR-Plus, KAIST, GrandTour, and MARS-LVIG. The results show competitive accuracy across wheeled, legged, and aerial platforms under long-duration and high-speed operation, degradation, and calibration perturbation, improving localization availability for road-level autonomy, campus and warehouse mobility, and low-altitude aerial inspection. To benefit the industrial and academic community, we will release source code and datasets upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: Ultra-Fusion is a tightly-coupled multi-sensor localization framework using a unified sliding-window estimator that supports various sensor configurations (WIO, VIO, LIO, LVIO) with observability-aware initialization, factor-wise reliability scheduling for handling sensor degradation, and online LiDAR-IMU spatiotemporal calibration. It achieves competitive accuracy across wheeled, legged, and aerial platforms under challenging conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-sensor fusion systems remain vulnerable to sensor degradation (poor illumination, LiDAR degeneracy, wheel slippage, GNSS outage) and spatiotemporal calibration errors, which are common in urban canyons, tunnels, and high-speed corridors, causing localization drift that degrades route tracking and map alignment.
AI.method: Proposes Ultra-Fusion, a tightly-coupled multi-sensor localization framework with: (1) a unified sliding-window estimator processing asynchronous timestamp-ordered measurements as optional factors, (2) observability-aware initialization for bootstrap mode selection, (3) factor-wise reliability scheduling to gate degraded measurements, and (4) online LiDAR-IMU spatiotemporal calibration. Supports WIO, VIO, LIO, and LVIO configurations with optional wheel and GNSS augmentation.
AI.result: Evaluated on M3DGR (extended with simulation trajectories), M2DGR-Plus, KAIST, GrandTour, and MARS-LVIG benchmarks against over 60 open-source SLAM systems. Shows competitive accuracy across wheeled, legged, and aerial platforms under long-duration/high-speed operation, degradation scenarios, and calibration perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Ultra-Fusion improves localization availability for road-level autonomy, campus/warehouse mobility, and low-altitude aerial inspection by maintaining accuracy under sensor degradation and calibration errors. Source code and datasets will be released upon acceptance.

title: Simulated Customers Never Walk Away: Decision Fidelity of LLM User Simulators Measured Against Real Purchase Outcomes
summary: LLM-as-user-simulation has become core infrastructure for conversational AI: agent benchmarks (tau-bench), training pipelines, and a growing body of fidelity studies all rely on LLMs role-playing the human side of dialogue. Existing frameworks measure communicative fidelity -- whether simulators talk like humans -- against ground truth from paid participants role-playing assigned goals. We argue this has a structural blind spot: when the goal is assigned, the user's willingness is exogenous, so no framework can test whether simulators make decisions like real users whose motivation is endogenous, latent, and decaying. We introduce decision fidelity -- whether a simulated population reproduces the decision-state dynamics of real users facing real, consequential choices -- and measure it on a unique testbed: 2,790 production conversations between an LLM sales agent and real customers, including 793 with verified payment outcomes. Using a teacher-forced probe protocol that holds context and instrument fixed, we find a systematic, outcome-correlated failure we call the disengagement deficit: simulators reproduce eventual buyers almost exactly (depth bias +0.09) but inflate eventual non-buyers toward the purchase frame (depth bias +0.40; d=0.38, p<0.001), halving expressed resistance (25.1% to 13.5%) and nearly doubling deliberation (21.9% to 40.1%) while fabricating no purchases. The deficit replicates across model families (DeepSeek: d=0.41, p=0.002) and resists the obvious fix: instructing the simulator that it may disengage cuts marginal bias five-fold but barely moves the outcome-conditioned contrast (d=0.34, p=0.008). Real non-buyers say "not now" and stop; simulated non-buyers ask about price. Evaluating or training sales and persuasion agents against such simulators overstates funnel progress exactly where it matters most -- the customers who walk away.

AI.tldr: Current LLM user simulators fail to reproduce real user disengagement: they accurately simulate buyers but systematically inflate non-buyers' engagement, making them unreliable for evaluating sales/persuasion agents.
AI.motivation: Existing fidelity frameworks only test whether simulators "talk like humans" when given assigned goals, but cannot assess whether simulators make decisions like real users whose motivation is endogenous, latent, and decaying.
AI.method: Using 2,790 production conversations (793 with payment outcomes) between an LLM sales agent and real customers, the authors introduce a teacher-forced probe protocol to measure decision fidelity—whether simulated populations reproduce real users' decision-state dynamics.
AI.result: Simulators reproduce buyers almost exactly (depth bias +0.09) but inflate non-buyers toward purchase frames (depth bias +0.40; d=0.38, p<0.001), halving expressed resistance (25.1%→13.5%) and nearly doubling deliberation (21.9%→40.1%). The deficit replicates across model families (DeepSeek: d=0.41, p=0.002) and resists instructing simulators they may disengage (d=0.34, p=0.008).
AI.conclusion: Evaluating or training agents against such simulators overstates funnel progress for the most critical customers—those who walk away—because simulators fail to capture genuine disengagement.

title: A Human-Inspired Thumb-Index Robotic Hand with Strain Gauges Embedded in Soft Joints
summary: Human hand grasp adaptation depends mainly on the synergy between physical structure and biological feedback. Inspired by this biomechanical principle, the Safe Thumb-Index Robotic (STIR) Hand was developed as a minimal, lightweight, and low-cost two-digit prototype featuring an asymmetric thumb-index configuration. By pairing an underactuated, tendon-driven mechanical design with flexible strain gauges embedded into silicone-encapsulated soft joints, the system achieves passive grasp adaptation while establishing both internal proprioception and external perception. Unsupervised analysis was carried out on a dataset of the STIR hand grasping 20 different objects, along with an object classification task and an ablation study to highlight the contribution of the soft joint sensors. The object classification task discriminated object size, shape, and material stiffness with a high classification accuracy. In contrast to traditional industrial grippers and robotic hands, the STIR Hand demonstrates that sensorized compliant joints significantly improve overall sensitivity and ensure safe grasping, while remaining independent of additional fingertip tactile elements or external vision systems. Finally, a comparison to similar devices grasping identical objects validates the utility of the STIR Hand.

AI.tldr: The STIR Hand is a minimal, low-cost two-digit robotic hand with underactuated tendon-driven design and silicone-encapsulated soft joints embedded with strain gauges. It achieves passive grasp adaptation, internal proprioception, and external perception. Experiments show high-accuracy object classification (size, shape, stiffness) and validate that sensorized compliant joints improve sensitivity and safety without requiring tactile fingertips or external vision.
AI.motivation: Inspired by the biomechanical synergy between physical structure and biological feedback in human hand grasp adaptation, the authors aimed to develop a minimal, lightweight, low-cost robotic hand that achieves safe and sensitive grasping without relying on external vision systems or additional tactile fingertip sensors.
AI.method: The STIR Hand features an asymmetric thumb-index configuration with an underactuated, tendon-driven mechanism. Flexible strain gauges are embedded into silicone-encapsulated soft joints to provide proprioception and exteroception. Unsupervised analysis, object classification, and an ablation study were conducted on a dataset of 20 objects grasped by the hand.
AI.result: The object classification task achieved high accuracy in discriminating object size, shape, and material stiffness. The ablation study highlighted the contribution of the soft joint sensors. Sensorized compliant joints were shown to significantly improve overall sensitivity and ensure safe grasping without additional fingertip tactile elements or external vision.
AI.conclusion: The STIR Hand validates that a minimal, sensorized compliant-joint design can achieve effective passive grasp adaptation and perception, outperforming traditional industrial grippers in sensitivity and safety. Comparison to similar devices grasping identical objects confirms its utility.

title: FairTutor: Equity-Aware Pedagogical LLM Routing for Budget-Constrained AI Tutoring
comment: AI for Education Day at SIGKDD 2026, 14 pages, 2 figures
summary: Generative AI tutors provide real-time, personalized learning support, but also create a new education inequity: students with access to premium AI services may receive clearer explanations, more personalized guidance, and better scaffolding than students limited to free or low-cost services. To address this challenge, we propose FairTutor, an equity-aware model-routing framework that achieves cost-effective AI tutoring via pedagogically motivated multi-agent orchestration. FairTutor combines query analysis, pedagogical planning, low-cost model generation, evaluator-guided critique and revision, and selective escalation to premium AI models. We introduce access-tier AI Education (AIED) Advantage Gap to measure the quality difference between premium-access and budget-constrained tutoring, and TutorAccessEval, a benchmark spanning math, reading, writing, science, and language learning. Empirical evaluations show that FairTutor achieves 97.1% of premium pedagogical quality (in floor-adjusted Likert scale) while reducing serving cost by 71.6%. Sensitivity analysis reveals a tunable cost--quality Pareto frontier, enabling FairTutor to be tailored to the needs of diverse student populations.

AI.tldr: FairTutor is an equity-aware model-routing framework that achieves 97.1% of premium AI tutoring quality while reducing serving cost by 71.6% through multi-agent orchestration, addressing the education inequity between premium and free AI tutoring services.
AI.motivation: Generative AI tutors create a new education inequity where students with access to premium AI services receive higher quality explanations, guidance, and scaffolding compared to those limited to free or low-cost services.
AI.method: FairTutor combines query analysis, pedagogical planning, low-cost model generation, evaluator-guided critique and revision, and selective escalation to premium AI models in a multi-agent orchestration framework.
AI.result: FairTutor achieves 97.1% of premium pedagogical quality (floor-adjusted Likert scale) while reducing serving cost by 71.6%, with a tunable cost-quality Pareto frontier demonstrated via sensitivity analysis.
AI.conclusion: FairTutor can be tailored to diverse student populations' needs by tuning along the cost-quality Pareto frontier, effectively narrowing the access-tier AI Education Advantage Gap.

title: Spectral GS-SLAM: Observability-Aware, Degeneracy-Robust Tracking for Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM
comment: This work has been accepted to IROS 2026
summary: Recent 3DGS-SLAM systems enable real-time operation by leveraging conventional feature matching or ICP-based tracking, thereby avoiding the heavy dense photometric optimization used in earlier approaches. However, feature matching remains prone to failure in textureless environments, while ICP-based tracking struggles in structureless or geometrically degenerate scenes due to ill-conditioned optimization. To address this issue, we propose Spectral GS-SLAM, an efficient yet robust tracking framework that integrates ICP with complementary feature-based constraints. Our method mitigates numerical instability by adaptively compensating under-constrained directions in degenerate scenarios, without interfering with the shared Gaussian representation used for mapping. We further introduce a Gaussian-aware planarity weighting mechanism that exploits the intrinsic covariance structure of 3D Gaussians to characterize scene geometry and guide information fusion. Extensive evaluations on challenging TUM RGB-D sequences demonstrate that Spectral GS-SLAM achieves real-time performance (40.14 FPS) while maintaining consistent tracking in both structureless and featureless environments. The proposed method preserves trajectory integrity in degenerate scenes while maintaining competitive performance in non-adverse conditions.

AI.tldr: Spectral GS-SLAM is a real-time SLAM system that combines ICP with feature-based constraints and a Gaussian-aware planarity weighting mechanism to maintain robust tracking in textureless and structureless environments, achieving 40.14 FPS on TUM RGB-D sequences.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS-SLAM systems use either feature matching (fails in textureless areas) or ICP-based tracking (struggles in structureless/geometrically degenerate scenes due to ill-conditioned optimization). The paper aims to address these failure modes without sacrificing real-time performance.
AI.method: The method integrates ICP with complementary feature-based constraints, adaptively compensating under-constrained directions in degenerate scenarios via numerical stabilization. It also introduces a Gaussian-aware planarity weighting mechanism that leverages the covariance structure of 3D Gaussians to characterize scene geometry and guide information fusion, all while using a shared Gaussian representation for mapping.
AI.result: Achieves real-time performance at 40.14 FPS on challenging TUM RGB-D sequences. Maintains consistent tracking in both structureless and featureless environments, preserves trajectory integrity in degenerate scenes, and remains competitive in non-adverse conditions.
AI.conclusion: Spectral GS-SLAM provides an efficient and robust tracking framework that handles degenerate scenarios where prior methods fail, by adaptively fusing ICP and feature-based constraints with geometry-aware weighting, all within a real-time 3DGS-SLAM pipeline.

title: Escape from Delusional Echo Trap: Symmetry Breaking, Stochastic Dynamics and Mathematical Mitigation Strategies for Algorithmic Sycophancy
summary: We propose a rigorous and systematic mathematical framework for tracking the cognitive trajectories of a user, in the context of algorithmic sycophancy and AI-driven delusional spiraling. Using tools from dynamical systems theory and stochastic differential equations, we explore how individuals perceive, interpret, and update their beliefs as they interact with AI chatbots that possess hidden traits of sycophancy. We treat the evolving conviction as a continuous log-odds state variable, coupled into a stochastic differential equation, navigating a multi-valley potential energy landscape. Our analysis reveals several critical observations governing the stability and rigidity of belief dynamics. We demonstrate that the baseline prior perception of the individual is systematically enhanced by sycophantic feedback beyond a critical threshold. Here, the perceptual potential landscape undergoes a structural phase transition that severely deepens any incremental initial tilt present in the baseline state, transforming the landscape and giving rise to deep, highly resilient attractor basins that trap the individual in unshakeable, self-reinforcing, delusional convictions. Finally, we demonstrate that genuine external information can successfully challenge these rigid states. If this incoming evidence is strong and authentic enough to overcome the internal feedback barrier, it can correct the structural asymmetry caused by sycophancy, inducing a perception reversal that successfully restores the objective belief state.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a mathematical framework using dynamical systems and stochastic differential equations to model how sycophantic AI feedback systematically deepens users' initial biases, creating resilient attractor basins that trap individuals in delusional convictions, though sufficiently strong external evidence can overcome the feedback barrier and restore objective beliefs.
AI.motivation: To rigorously model the phenomenon of algorithmic sycophancy and AI-driven delusional spiraling, where AI chatbots with sycophantic traits reinforce user biases, leading to entrenched false beliefs.
AI.method: Treats evolving conviction as a continuous log-odds state variable governed by stochastic differential equations in a multi-valley potential energy landscape, analyzing phase transitions and attractor basin dynamics under sycophantic feedback.
AI.result: Sycophantic feedback enhances baseline prior perception beyond a critical threshold, inducing a structural phase transition that deepens initial perceptual tilts, creating deep, resilient attractor basins that trap users in self-reinforcing delusions; however, sufficiently strong external evidence can correct the asymmetry and restore objective beliefs.
AI.conclusion: The framework reveals how sycophantic AI feedback can structurally distort belief dynamics, but also that authentic external information of sufficient strength can reverse the induced delusional states.

title: RogueRover: Autonomous Rogue Device Localization for Incident Response
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Code and data are available in the accompanying artifact repository
summary: Physically localizing unauthorized wireless devices remains a critical bottleneck in cyber-physical security operations, where rogue access points can provide entry points for lateral movement and persistent compromise. While such devices can often be detected through network-side mechanisms, determining their physical location typically requires dense sensing infrastructure, site-specific RF fingerprinting, or manual inspection, limiting timely incident response. We investigate whether a single commodity robot can autonomously detect and localize rogue wireless devices under zero-configuration constraints, without RF fingerprinting, pre-installed sensors, or site calibration. We present RogueRover, an end-to-end system in which a quadruped robot autonomously patrols, collects spatially labeled RSSI measurements via a standard 802.11 interface, and estimates device locations offline. We evaluate the system across 11 patrol runs in a real indoor environment, with 6 rogue devices deployed under heterogeneous propagation conditions. Across 62 AP-patrol sessions, RogueRover achieves a median single-patrol localization error of 1.62 m without prior RF knowledge. Under multi-run aggregation, five of six devices are localized within 1 m. A blind trial validates the full pipeline, correctly identifying rogue devices among 73 observed BSSIDs and localizing them with errors of 0.34 m and 1.84 m. Across environments, simple weighted-centroid estimators perform comparably to, or better than, parametric path-loss models, indicating that measurement coverage from autonomous patrols is the primary determinant of localization accuracy under zero-prior constraints. Our results demonstrate that infrastructure-free, autonomous localization is feasible in practice, enabling rapid physical incident response in cyber-physical environments without additional sensing infrastructure.

AI.tldr: RogueRover is an end-to-end system using a single commodity quadruped robot to autonomously detect and localize rogue wireless devices via RSSI measurements, achieving 1.62 m median error without RF fingerprinting, pre-installed sensors, or site calibration.
AI.motivation: Physically localizing unauthorized wireless devices (e.g., rogue APs) is a critical bottleneck in cyber-physical security, typically requiring dense sensing infrastructure, site-specific RF fingerprinting, or manual inspection, which limits timely incident response.
AI.method: RogueRover uses a quadruped robot to autonomously patrol an environment, collect spatially labeled RSSI measurements via a standard 802.11 interface, and estimate device locations offline using weighted-centroid or parametric path-loss estimators without any prior RF knowledge, pre-installed sensors, or site calibration.
AI.result: Across 62 AP-patrol sessions in real indoor environments with 6 rogue devices, RogueRover achieves 1.62 m median single-patrol localization error; multi-run aggregation localizes 5/6 devices within 1 m. A blind trial correctly identified rogue devices among 73 observed BSSIDs with errors of 0.34 m and 1.84 m.
AI.conclusion: Infrastructure-free, autonomous localization of rogue wireless devices is feasible in practice using a single commodity robot, enabling rapid physical incident response in cyber-physical environments without additional sensing infrastructure. Measurement coverage from autonomous patrols is the primary determinant of accuracy under zero-prior constraints.

title: When Web Agents Finish but Still Fail: Reproducible Triggers and Trace Diagnostics for Parallel Web Exploration
summary: Long-horizon web agents often fail in ways hidden by final-answer evaluation: they may visit useful pages, produce a well-formed answer, and terminate confidently while still missing fields, over-including unsupported items, or relying on stale evidence. We study these failures with Parallel WebBench, a parallel web-exploration benchmark containing 1,679 verified records: 350 manually curated parallel tasks and 1,329 reconstructed records with verified URL-based trajectories. We train WebExplorer-style agents with GRPO under human-only, balanced human-synthetic, and synthetic-heavy data mixtures. At 16k context and 16 interaction rounds, the best GRPO model improves completion over WebExplorer-8B from 50.7% to 96.0% and GPT-4.1-mini-judged element-wise F1 from 0.2489 to 0.4529, but binary accuracy remains far below completion. Trace-level analysis identifies three persistent failure modes: context-bound search loops, premature termination on partial answers, and synthesis collapse after relevant evidence has already been retrieved. These results show that synthetic-data GRPO reduces abstention and improves partial correctness, but leaves a completion-correctness gap that requires evidence-grounded coverage and synthesis diagnostics.

AI.tldr: Parallel WebBench introduces a benchmark with 1,679 verified records to study hidden failures in long-horizon web agents; GRPO training improves completion from 50.7% to 96.0% and element-wise F1 from 0.2489 to 0.4529, but reveals a persistent completion-correctness gap with three failure modes: context-bound search loops, premature termination, and synthesis collapse.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon web agents often fail in ways hidden by final-answer evaluation—missing fields, over-including unsupported items, or relying on stale evidence—motivating the need for fine-grained benchmarks and diagnostics beyond binary correctness.
AI.method: Construction of Parallel WebBench (1,679 records: 350 manual + 1,329 reconstructed with verified URL-based trajectories); training WebExplorer-style agents with GRPO under three data mixtures (human-only, balanced human-synthetic, synthetic-heavy); evaluation at 16k context and 16 interaction rounds.
AI.result: Best GRPO model improves completion from 50.7% to 96.0% and element-wise F1 from 0.2489 to 0.4529, but binary accuracy remains far below completion. Three persistent failure modes identified: context-bound search loops, premature termination on partial answers, and synthesis collapse after relevant evidence retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic-data GRPO reduces abstention and improves partial correctness but leaves a completion-correctness gap; addressing this requires evidence-grounded coverage metrics and synthesis diagnostics.

title: NAC: Neural Action Codec for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on discrete action tokenizers to bridge continuous robot control and autoregressive sequence modeling, yet existing tokenizers often trade off between compression, latency, and downstream performance. We revisit this design through the lens of neural audio codecs-convolutional encoder-decoder architectures with residual vector quantization that serve as the standard front end for audio foundation models. Motivated by their success, we introduce the Neural Action Codec (NAC), which treats short robot action trajectories as multi-channel 1D signals and compresses them using a multi-scale RVQGAN architecture. We observe that audio-specific mel-spectrogram objectives are ill-suited for kinematic signals; however, by replacing them with simple time-domain and non-mel spectral reconstruction losses, audio-codec-style models can autoencode actions with high fidelity without substantial architectural changes. NAC provides a compact, ordered token space via offset codebooks, enabling standard autoregressive policies to operate over short, structured sequences. Meanwhile, a Vocos-style decoder with an ISTFT head and adversarial discriminators recovers smooth, detailed trajectories. Across LIBERO-10, RoboMimic, and a suite of real-world manipulation tasks, NAC achieves lower reconstruction error and higher success rates than binning, FAST, and prior VQ-based tokenizers at comparable or better compression rates. These results demonstrate that repurposed neural audio codecs offer a strong, practical backbone for learned action tokenization in modern VLAs.

AI.tldr: NAC repurposes neural audio codec architecture with multi-scale RVQGAN to tokenize robot action trajectories, achieving lower reconstruction error and higher success rates than prior methods across manipulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA action tokenizers trade off between compression, latency, and downstream performance; neural audio codecs succeed in audio domain but haven't been adapted for robot kinematic signals.
AI.method: NAC treats short robot action trajectories as multi-channel 1D signals, uses multi-scale RVQGAN with offset codebooks for compact ordered token space, replaces mel-spectrogram objectives with time-domain and non-mel spectral losses, and employs Vocos-style ISTFT decoder with adversarial discriminators.
AI.result: Across LIBERO-10, RoboMimic, and real-world manipulation tasks, NAC achieves lower reconstruction error and higher success rates than binning, FAST, and prior VQ-based tokenizers at comparable or better compression rates.
AI.conclusion: Repurposed neural audio codecs provide a strong, practical backbone for learned action tokenization in modern VLAs.

title: Repeated Shared Access Enables Grokking, but Edit Propagation Depends on a Fine-Grained Addressable Memory
summary: We study factual edit propagation in a controlled synthetic knowledge-graph QA setting, comparing four architectures that cross loop recurrence with shared memory access: dense (Dense), looped (Loop), dense with shared memory (Dense+Mem), and looped with shared memory (LMC). Dense fits in-distribution 2-hop compositions but fails OOD; both looped recomputation and memory rereading cross this OOD grokking barrier, indicating that repeated shared access -- not a specific architecture -- is the common ingredient for learning. Editing, however, separates the substrates along a different axis. On a shared pre-edit-correct ID set, a single-row factual edit propagates strongly in the two memory-bearing cells (LMC 0.78-0.92, Dense+Mem 0.71-0.96) and only weakly in the others (Loop 0.04-0.30, Dense 0.00-0.03); the separation is statistically clean (Mann-Whitney p=0.008 between memory and non-memory cells, p=0.55 between the two memory cells, though n=5 vs n=5 is underpowered to rule out a moderate gap). In LMC, atomic facts localize to dominant memory sites that composition rereads, and a one-row value edit on LMC's own pre-edit-correct probes achieves 100% direct success with mean 0.989 intended propagation while moving unrelated facts ~0.1% of the time (matched specificity across substrates pending). A coarse hold-answer-subspace (HOLDANS) interchange diagnostic is consistent with this ordering, suggesting that what separates the substrates is when an edited fact is injected and how much computation remains afterwards to reuse it. These results dissociate learning competence from editing affordance: repeated shared access suffices to grok, but edit propagation depends on whether the substrate exposes a fine-grained addressable memory the forward computation can write to and later reread -- an affordance that loop recurrence provides only partially.

AI.tldr: The paper studies factual edit propagation in knowledge-graph QA, comparing four architectures. It finds that repeated shared access enables OOD generalization, but edit propagation requires explicit addressable memory—not just recurrence—revealing a dissociation between learning competence and editing affordance.
AI.motivation: To dissociate the architectural ingredients needed for learning factual compositions from those needed for precise factual editing, and to understand whether loop recurrence alone can support edit propagation or whether explicit memory is required.
AI.method: Controlled synthetic knowledge-graph QA comparing four architectures: Dense, Loop, Dense+Mem, and LMC. Evaluated on OOD generalization (2-hop compositions) and single-row factual edit propagation using propagation scores, Mann-Whitney tests, HOLDANS interchange diagnostics, and specificity analyses.
AI.result: Repeated shared access (loop or memory) enables OOD grokking. However, edit propagation strongly separates memory-bearing cells (LMC 0.78-0.92, Dense+Mem 0.71-0.96) from non-memory cells (Loop 0.04-0.30, Dense 0.00-0.03) with p=0.008. LMC achieves 100% direct edit success with 0.989 intended propagation and 0.1% unintended fact movement.
AI.conclusion: Learning competence and editing affordance are dissociated: repeated shared access suffices for grokking, but edit propagation requires a fine-grained addressable memory that the forward computation can write to and later reread—something loop recurrence provides only partially.

title: Long-Distance Real-World Navigation of the Legged-Wheeled Robot Go2-W Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Legged-wheeled robots have long been studied for their potential to combine the efficient flat-ground mobility of wheels with the rough-terrain capability of legs. However, examples of their application to long-range autonomous navigation in real environments remain limited. This paper reports our effort to build a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) based locomotion controller and an autonomous navigation system for the commercially available legged-wheeled robot Go2-W, and to apply them to long-range autonomous navigation in a real environment. For locomotion control, we extended a proprioception-only policy, which we had previously developed for quadruped robots, to the 16-DoF legged-wheeled robot. We also found that wheeled locomotion concentrates the load on the hip joints and causes heat concentration that hinders sustained travel, and obtained a policy that suppresses it by distributing the load. We evaluated the system at the Tsukuba Challenge 2025, demonstrating that it can autonomously traverse an approximately 2.8 km route including sidewalks, a park, and stairs without stopping due to overheating.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a DRL-based locomotion controller and autonomous navigation system for the Go2-W legged-wheeled robot, demonstrating successful long-range (2.8 km) autonomous traversal in a real-world urban environment at the Tsukuba Challenge 2025, with a load-distribution policy that mitigates hip joint overheating.
AI.motivation: Legged-wheeled robots have long been studied for combining wheel efficiency on flat ground with leg capability on rough terrain, yet their application to long-range autonomous navigation in real environments remains limited.
AI.method: Extended a proprioception-only DRL policy from quadruped robots to a 16-DoF legged-wheeled robot (Go2-W); identified wheeled locomotion causes hip joint heat concentration; developed a load-distribution policy to suppress overheating.
AI.result: Successfully traversed an approximately 2.8 km route including sidewalks, a park, and stairs without stopping due to overheating at the Tsukuba Challenge 2025.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DRL-based system enables practical long-range autonomous navigation for legged-wheeled robots in real environments by addressing the overheating issue through load-distribution policy learning.

title: Fara-1.5: Scalable Learning Environments for Computer Use Agents
summary: Collecting computer use data from human demonstrations is expensive and slow, motivating the need for scalable generation strategies. This requires two key ingredients: environments in which agents can act and verifiers that can judge whether their demonstrations succeeded. We introduce FaraGen1.5, a scalable data pipeline for computer use agents composed of three modular components: environments, solvers, and verifiers. FaraGen1.5 uses both live websites and synthetic environments that faithfully simulate domains gated by authentication or that require irreversible actions. It employs a solver harness that can be powered by multiple models, including strong frontier models such as GPT-5.4, and also incorporates a user simulator to enable multi-turn rollouts. Finally, FaraGen1.5 scores the resulting trajectories with three complementary verifiers covering task correctness, efficiency, and critical-point adherence. Using data produced by this pipeline, we train Fara1.5, a family of native computer use agents (CUAs) at three scales built on Qwen3.5 (4B, 9B, and 27B). To train these models, we employ a supervised finetuning (SFT) recipe that carefully balances data from FaraGen1.5 for broad coverage, specific high-value tasks, and target model deficiencies in an iterative approach. Each model sets a new state of the art for its size class on browser-use benchmarks: Fara1.5-9B reaches 63.4% on Online-Mind2Web and 86.6% on WebVoyager, while Fara1.5-27B achieves 72.3% on Online-Mind2Web, which is competitive with much larger proprietary systems.

AI.tldr: FaraGen1.5 is a scalable data pipeline for training computer use agents, combining live and synthetic web environments, multiple solver models, and three complementary verifiers. Using this pipeline, the authors train Fara1.5 models (4B–27B) that achieve state-of-the-art results on browser-use benchmarks, with the 27B model competing with much larger proprietary systems.
AI.motivation: Collecting human demonstrations for computer use agents is expensive and slow, motivating the need for scalable automated data generation pipelines that require environments for agents to act in and verifiers to judge success.
AI.method: FaraGen1.5 consists of three modular components: (1) environments (live websites + synthetic environments simulating authenticated or irreversible-action domains), (2) a solver harness using multiple models including GPT-5.4 and a user simulator for multi-turn rollouts, and (3) three complementary verifiers scoring trajectories on task correctness, efficiency, and critical-point adherence. The resulting data is used for supervised finetuning of Qwen3.5-based models (4B, 9B, 27B) with an iterative balancing approach.
AI.result: Fara1.5-9B achieves 63.4% on Online-Mind2Web and 86.6% on WebVoyager; Fara1.5-27B achieves 72.3% on Online-Mind2Web, competitive with much larger proprietary systems. Each model sets a new state of the art for its size class.
AI.conclusion: Scalable data generation pipelines with carefully designed environments, solvers, and verifiers can produce high-quality training data for computer use agents, enabling smaller models to achieve competitive performance against much larger proprietary systems.

title: Overcoming Imperfect Kinematics in Surgical Robotics Through Sim-to-Real Visuomotor Learning
comment: Accepted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2026
summary: Robot-Assisted Surgery is integral to modern minimally invasive procedures, with automation emerging as the next frontier to enhance precision and reduce surgeon fatigue. This evolution is largely impeded by the inherent kinematic inaccuracies of surgical robots, where unreliable internal sensors lead to significant control errors. While previous methods attempted to mitigate these issues through complex model-based calibration, they often suffer from high cost and limited effectiveness. This work utilises a learning-policy to actively compensate for hardware inaccuracies using closed-loop visual feedback that was trained from a teacher-student learning framework. The policy can fuse unreliable internal readings with precise external visual data, allowing it to correct for kinematic errors in real time without needing a perfect physical model. The learned policy was successfully deployed on the da Vinci Research Kit, where experiments validated the fundamental feasibility of using external vision to overcome internal sensor deficits. This research provides a foundational and reliable control methodology, paving the way for more advanced and robust surgical automation.

AI.tldr: A teacher-student learning framework uses closed-loop visual feedback to compensate for kinematic inaccuracies in surgical robots, enabling real-time error correction on the da Vinci Research Kit without requiring a perfect physical model.
AI.motivation: Surgical robots suffer from inherent kinematic inaccuracies due to unreliable internal sensors, causing significant control errors. Existing model-based calibration methods are expensive and have limited effectiveness, impeding the advancement of surgical automation.
AI.method: A learning-policy trained via a teacher-student framework actively compensates for hardware inaccuracies by fusing unreliable internal sensor readings with precise external visual feedback in a closed loop, operating in real time without requiring a perfect physical model.
AI.result: The learned policy was successfully deployed on the da Vinci Research Kit, validating that external vision can overcome internal sensor deficits for kinematic error correction in real time.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a foundational and reliable control methodology that leverages external visual feedback to compensate for internal sensor inaccuracies, paving the way for more advanced and robust surgical automation.

title: What Shapes Emergent Misalignment? Insights from Training Dynamics, Model Priors, and Data
summary: Emergent misalignment (EM) is a phenomenon in which models generalize with narrow fine-tuning, leading to broad (yet uneven) misalignment across evaluation questions. We study EM and its variability directly through the components of fine-tuning: training dynamics, model priors, and data. (1) We first explored how in-domain training loss relates to out-of-domain alignment scores across datasets and model families. Then, we tried to induce potential alternative local minima through different learning schedules for one narrow fine-tuning, but did not find strong runs with better broad alignment scores conditioned on similar or lower training loss. (2) We found that although the mean and standard deviations of the misaligned model scores are usually statistically different from those of the pre-trained model, there are some potential signals on overall positive correlation. The evaluation prompt-only activations from both the pre-trained and the original instruct models (prior to narrow fine-tuning) could predict fine-grained alignment scores after narrow fine-tuning. (3) Finally, we compared activation deltas before and after narrow fine-tuning and found moderate-to-high subspace overlap and similarity between the resulting activation shifts for training and evaluation prompts. Subspace overlaps between training and evaluation prompt activations correlate with their shifts' similarities when measuring with the last prompt-token activations. The train-evaluation data prompt overlap is controlled against overlap computed from random vectors and evaluation prompts activations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Emergent Misalignment (EM) in fine-tuned models, finding that (1) training loss alone doesn't predict alignment scores, (2) pre- and post-fine-tuning activations correlate with alignment outcomes, and (3) activation shifts during fine-tuning show overlapping subspaces between training and evaluation prompts.
AI.motivation: To understand how narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment (EM) and identify the factors—training dynamics, model priors, and data—that control this phenomenon.
AI.method: (1) Analyzed relationship between in-domain training loss and out-of-domain alignment scores across datasets and model families; tested alternative learning schedules. (2) Compared statistical distributions of misaligned vs. pre-trained model scores; used activation-based prediction of alignment scores. (3) Computed activation deltas before/after fine-tuning and measured subspace overlap and similarity between training and evaluation prompt activations.
AI.result: (1) No strong runs found where better broad alignment was achieved with similar/lower training loss. (2) Misaligned model scores statistically differ from pre-trained, but with some positive correlation; pre-fine-tuning activations can predict post-fine-tuning alignment. (3) Moderate-to-high subspace overlap and similarity between training/evaluation activation shifts; last prompt-token activations correlate with shift similarities.
AI.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is traceable to model priors and activation dynamics, with training and evaluation prompts sharing overlapping representational shifts during fine-tuning.

title: BIT-Nav: Brain-Inspired Trajectory Memory for Embodied Navigation
comment: Accepted to CVPR 2026: 2nd Workshop on 3D-LLM/VLA: Bridging Language, Vision and Action in 3D Environments
summary:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for embodied navigation rely on selecting a fixed number of frames from a growing trajectory history. As episodes extend, this selection grows increasingly sparse, yet prior work shows no accuracy gain when scaling from 8 to 64 frames, suggesting the bottleneck is not frame quantity but the representation itself. Sparse frame selection cannot capture the structured behavioral signal that long-horizon reasoning requires: turning patterns, cumulative displacement, and path topology.
  We introduce BIT-Nav (Brain-Inspired Trajectory Memory for Navigation), a framework that augments frozen VLM navigation pipelines with a compact learned trajectory memory.
