Motivated by hippocampal path integration, where spatial experience is compressed into structured episodic traces rather than stored as raw sensory replay, BIT-Nav trains a Bi-GRU encoder over action and relative pose sequences via a multi-positive InfoNCE contrastive objective on trajectory prefixes sharing the same behavioral intent. The resulting embedding is projected into the VLM token space via a lightweight MLP and injected as a single memory token at each decision step, conditioning the model on structured motion history at constant token cost regardless of episode length

AI.tldr: BIT-Nav introduces a learned trajectory memory that compresses action and pose sequences into a single token, enabling frozen VLMs to perform long-horizon navigation without sparsifying frame history.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs for embodied navigation select a fixed number of frames from growing trajectory histories, causing sparsity over long episodes; scaling frames (8→64) shows no accuracy gain, indicating the bottleneck is representation, not frame quantity.
AI.method: BIT-Nav trains a Bi-GRU encoder on action and relative pose sequences using a multi-positive InfoNCE contrastive objective on trajectory prefixes sharing behavioral intent. The embedding is projected via an MLP into VLM token space and injected as a single memory token at each decision step.
AI.result: The approach maintains constant token cost regardless of episode length, conditioning frozen VLMs on structured motion history (turning patterns, cumulative displacement, path topology) without sparsifying frame selection.
AI.conclusion: BIT-Nav demonstrates that hippocampal-inspired trajectory compression—rather than increasing frame count—is an effective strategy for enabling long-horizon reasoning in VLM-based embodied navigation.

title: Study on Quantitative Dynamic Epistemic Logic for Belief Revision
summary: Belief revision is a process in which an agent begins to believe in something she previously did not. I begin the paper by presenting, based on (Gärdenfors, 1998; Hansson, 1999), postulates for belief revision that constitute the basis of the AGM theory. I will then briefly show the semantics of a modal logic introduced in (van Ditmarsch, 2005), which I call `$P$'. This logic formalizes static epistemic states and has greater expressive power than AGM in doing so because it captures the quantitative notion of "degrees of conviction". The third step is to introduce revision operators on $P$ and, mostly following (van Ditmarsch, 2005), obtain the Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) I call `$P*$'. It models processes of belief revision in several ways. Original results are presented in the following two sections. The first one of these sections revolves around a formalization of AGM postulates within $P*$ by proving some theorems related to the satisfaction of those postulates by revisions defined in $P*$. The last section features an analysis of $P*$'s revisions that go beyond the mere satisfaction of postulates. I compare their formal behavior with respect to some philosophical criteria. At last, I conclude that the functions presented in (van Ditmarsch, 2005) are not good formalizations of the philosophical intuition behind AGM. Instead, it is captured by the function $*^0$ originally defined in this paper (but highly inspired by (van Benthem, 2007)). An implementation of this function is also provided.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques existing belief revision models in Dynamic Epistemic Logic (specifically van Ditmarsch's P*), showing they fail to capture the philosophical intuition behind AGM postulates, and proposes an alternative revision function (*⁰) that does, along with its implementation.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between formal belief revision models (AGM postulates) and Dynamic Epistemic Logic frameworks by identifying whether existing DEL revisions satisfy AGM's philosophical intuitions, not just its syntactic postulates.
AI.method: The paper first presents AGM postulates and the modal logic P (capturing degrees of conviction). It then defines revision operators on P to obtain P* (a DEL). Original results include: (1) formalizing AGM postulates within P* via theorems proving their satisfaction, and (2) analyzing P* revisions against philosophical criteria beyond mere postulate satisfaction.
AI.result: van Ditmarsch's (2005) revision functions do not adequately formalize the philosophical intuition behind AGM. Instead, the function *⁰ (originally defined in this paper, inspired by van Benthem 2007) successfully captures it. An implementation of *⁰ is provided.
AI.conclusion: Not all formally AGM-satisfying revision operators align with AGM's philosophical foundations; the proposed *⁰ function resolves this discrepancy.

title: Robot Self-Improvement via Human-Video Dynamics Models
summary: A central question in robot learning is how to acquire skills from the kinds of data that humans learn from: passive observation, embodied practice, and the experience of failure. Human videos provide the first of these in abundance, and prior work has shown they can initialize useful policies. Far less clear is whether they can support the second and third: whether priors extracted from human videos can ground a robot's own attempts well enough to evaluate them, correct them, and improve from them. In this work, we show that human videos can be used to learn embodiment-agnostic action, dynamics, and value representations that transfer across robot embodiments, providing the predictive foundation required for robots to autonomously improve from their own rollouts and failures. We introduce Dynamics-Guided Action Correction (DGAC), a training-free approach that leverages these adapted models to repair failed states: each failure becomes a query for which the learned models propose and rank corrective actions, turning failures into supervision for the next policy update. Across seven real-world manipulation tasks spanning both a mobile manipulator and a static manipulator arm, our approach improves success rates from 40% to 81% across multiple policy backbones, demonstrating cross-embodiment robot self-improvement from human-video priors. These results show that human priors and robot failures can be combined to enable scalable autonomous policy improvement. Project page: https://ethz-mrl.github.io/robot-self-improvement-website/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DGAC, a training-free method that uses human videos to learn embodiment-agnostic representations, enabling robots to autonomously improve from their own failures by proposing and ranking corrective actions. Across 7 real-world tasks with two different manipulators, success rates improved from 40% to 81%.
AI.motivation: To determine whether human videos can support not just initial policy initialization but also the full learning loop of embodied practice, self-evaluation, correction, and improvement from failures, enabling scalable autonomous policy improvement across robot embodiments.
AI.method: DGAC (Dynamics-Guided Action Correction): A training-free approach that learns embodiment-agnostic action, dynamics, and value representations from human videos, then transfers them to robot embodiments. Failed states are treated as queries where learned models propose and rank corrective actions, turning failures into supervision for policy updates.
AI.result: Across 7 real-world manipulation tasks on a mobile manipulator and a static manipulator arm, success rates improved from 40% to 81% across multiple policy backbones, demonstrating cross-embodiment robot self-improvement from human-video priors.
AI.conclusion: Human priors and robot failures can be combined to enable scalable autonomous policy improvement, showing that human videos can ground robots' own attempts for evaluation, correction, and improvement.

title: Process-Reward Tactic Evolution for Long-Horizon Bioinformatics Workflows
summary: LLM agents can write code and call tools, but reliable bioinformatics work requires long-horizon interaction with workflow software, typed data objects, provenance, and biological checks. We study this setting through Galaxy workflow execution. The agent must explore task data, construct or adapt an executable workflow DAG, bind inputs and dataset collections, monitor execution, debug failures, and validate biological outputs. We propose Process-Reward Tactic Evolution, a Galaxy-based training framework that turns verified workflow rollouts into reusable \tactics. During training, agents practice on curriculum-organized Galaxy tasks in Agent Gym; process verifiers score workflow construction, software interaction, execution, and biological correctness; successful and failed traces are distilled into a tactic library. At inference, the trained executor, Process-Reward Tactic Evolution, uses this library to execute held-out peer reviewed Galaxy workflow converted BioWorkflow Bench and BioAgent Bench tasks in isolated environments. The paper evaluates whether process-supervised tactic accumulation improves long-horizon bioinformatics workflow completion, biological correctness, and execution efficiency over no-memory and reflection-style baselines.

AI.tldr: PRTE is a Galaxy-based training framework using Process-Reward Tactic Evolution that turns verified workflow rollouts into reusable tactics, improving long-horizon bioinformatics workflow completion, biological correctness, and execution efficiency over baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle with reliable bioinformatics work requiring long-horizon interaction with workflow software, typed data objects, provenance, and biological checks—capabilities current agents lack when executing complex Galaxy workflows.
AI.method: Proposes Process-Reward Tactic Evolution (PRTE) framework: trains agents on curriculum-organized Galaxy tasks in Agent Gym with process verifiers scoring workflow construction, software interaction, execution, and biological correctness; successful/failed traces are distilled into a tactic library used at inference by the trained executor.
AI.result: Evaluated on held-out peer-reviewed Galaxy workflows converted to BioWorkflow Bench and BioAgent Bench tasks, measuring workflow completion, biological correctness, and execution efficiency against no-memory and reflection-style baselines.
AI.conclusion: Process-supervised tactic accumulation improves long-horizon bioinformatics workflow execution, with PRTE outperforming baselines on completion, biological correctness, and efficiency metrics.

title: Temporal logics and formal synthesis for robot planning and control
summary: As robots move from controlled environments into real-world settings, it becomes increasingly crucial to ensure that they perform as expected. A key step toward that goal is a rigorous specification of the desired robot behavior, capturing intricate temporal, spatial, and logical requirements. Complementing this, plan and control synthesis methods are needed to fulfill these specifications with provable guarantees. This manuscript presents temporal logics - particularly linear and signal temporal logic - as expressive specification languages for robot behavior over time. We then discuss principles of formal synthesis, from discrete graph- and game-based approaches to sampling-based motion planning, trajectory optimization, and control-certificate-based synthesis. Finally, we outline challenges in deploying formal synthesis in real-world robotics, emphasizing the interplay between modeling fidelity, computational tractability, and the types of rigorous guarantees that can be achieved.

AI.tldr: This manuscript presents temporal logics (LTL and STL) as specification languages for robot behavior and reviews formal synthesis methods—including graph/game-based planning, sampling-based motion planning, trajectory optimization, and control certificate synthesis—while discussing challenges in deploying these methods in real-world robotics.
AI.motivation: As robots move from controlled environments to real-world settings, it is crucial to ensure they perform as expected, which requires rigorous specification of desired behavior and synthesis methods with provable guarantees.
AI.method: The paper surveys temporal logics (LTL and STL) for specification, and formal synthesis approaches including discrete graph/game-based methods, sampling-based motion planning, trajectory optimization, and control-certificate-based synthesis.
AI.result: A comprehensive overview of how temporal logics and formal synthesis methods can be applied to specify and guarantee robot behavior, along with identification of key challenges in real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: Deploying formal synthesis in real-world robotics faces challenges in balancing modeling fidelity, computational tractability, and the types of rigorous guarantees achievable.

title: SignVLA: Real-Time Sign Language-Guided Robotic Manipulation via Attention LSTM and Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable robots to execute manipulation tasks from natural-language instructions grounded in visual observations. However, existing VLA interfaces primarily rely on speech or text input, limiting accessibility for deaf, hard-of-hearing, and speech-impaired users. We present SignVLA, a real-time sign-language-guided VLA framework for accessible human-robot interaction. The system introduces a modular sign-to-text interface that converts visual sign gestures into semantic instructions compatible with downstream VLA policies. Given video streams, SignVLA extracts hand landmark features and employs an attention-enhanced Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to capture temporal gesture dynamics for alphabet- and command-level sign recognition. A temporal stabilization module further improves prediction consistency in real-time interaction settings.The generated instruction sequence is then passed to a downstream VLA policy for sign-conditioned robotic manipulation. Experimental results demonstrate stable real-time sign recognition and successful execution of manipulation tasks driven by sign-language inputs. Our findings suggest that lightweight temporal sign recognition can serve as an effective and practical accessibility layer for multimodal embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: SignVLA is a real-time sign-language-guided Vision-Language-Action (VLA) framework that converts sign gestures into semantic instructions for robotic manipulation, using hand landmark extraction, attention-enhanced LSTM for temporal gesture recognition, and a temporal stabilization module, enabling accessible human-robot interaction for deaf, hard-of-hearing, and speech-impaired users.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA interfaces rely on speech or text input, limiting accessibility for deaf, hard-of-hearing, and speech-impaired users.
AI.method: A modular sign-to-text interface using hand landmark extraction, attention-enhanced LSTM for temporal gesture dynamics, and a temporal stabilization module for real-time prediction consistency.
AI.result: Stable real-time sign recognition and successful execution of manipulation tasks driven by sign-language inputs.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight temporal sign recognition can serve as an effective and practical accessibility layer for multimodal embodied intelligence.

title: Manipulider: A Multi-Engine Buoyancy-Controlled Robot for Thrusterless Underwater Gliding and Manipulation
summary: The Manipulider is a buoyancy-actuated underwater robot that enables thrusterless, glide-like locomotion and attitude-based manipulation, while providing a magnetic modular interface for rapid payload swapping (e.g., a gripper or sensors). Four syringe-based buoyancy engines distributed around the body jointly regulate net buoyancy and the center of buoyancy, allowing the vehicle to maintain large tilt angles through static force balance without continuous thrust and to avoid propeller entanglement risks. We present the mechanical and electrical design, calibration procedure, and control architecture. Experiments with a gripper attached (no external payload) show a controllable buoyancy-displacement range of 40 mL per engine ({\approx}160 g total buoyancy authority), maximum statically stable tilts of 64.6° (single-engine) and 61.8° (dual-engine), and representative vertical and tilt-transition dynamics. We further demonstrate tilt regulation, controlled ascent/descent primitives, and a proof-of-concept gripper-based payload-transport sequence without thrusters.

AI.tldr: The Manipulider is a buoyancy-actuated underwater robot with four syringe-based engines for thrusterless locomotion, attitude-based manipulation, and a magnetic modular interface for payload swapping. Experiments show 40 mL buoyancy displacement per engine, max tilts of 64.6° (single-engine) and 61.8° (dual-engine), and proof-of-concept gripper payload transport without thrusters.
AI.motivation: To develop an underwater robot that achieves thrusterless glide-like locomotion and attitude-based manipulation while avoiding propeller entanglement risks, using buoyancy control for static stability and a modular magnetic interface for rapid payload swapping.
AI.method: Four syringe-based buoyancy engines distributed around the body jointly regulate net buoyancy and center of buoyancy; magnetic modular interface enables payload swapping; calibration procedure and control architecture are presented.
AI.result: 40 mL buoyancy-displacement range per engine (~160 g total authority), maximum statically stable tilts of 64.6° (single-engine) and 61.8° (dual-engine), demonstrated vertical/tilt-transition dynamics, tilt regulation, ascent/descent primitives, and gripper-based payload transport without thrusters.
AI.conclusion: Buoyancy-actuated underwater robots can achieve static stability at large tilt angles and perform manipulation tasks without thrusters, offering a safe alternative for environments where propeller entanglement is a concern.

title: When Do Intrinsic Rewards Work for Code Reasoning? A Comprehensive Study
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has driven substantial progress in large language model reasoning, but relies on ground-truth supervision that is costly or infeasible, especially in coding tasks. Recent work addresses this by deriving rewards from a model's own signals, such as majority voting or confidence-based scores, achieving notable success on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. However, code generation poses distinct challenges: programs are structurally complex, semantically equivalent solutions may differ syntactically, and verification typically requires execution. Whether these intrinsic reward methods transfer effectively to code remains unexplored. In this work, we present a systematic empirical study of intrinsic reward methods for code generation. We conduct extensive experiments on LiveCodeBench, systematically evaluating representative certainty-based Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback (RLIF) approaches under different training scenarios and hyperparameter settings. Our experiments reveal that certainty-based methods yield early gains but inevitably collapse: models progressively shorten outputs and lose reasoning capability, with collapse speed sensitive to sample size and temperature. When used to initialize RLVR training, RLIF pre-training offers no significant improvement over training from scratch. We also provide actionable recommendations for using intrinsic rewards for training code reasoning models. Our study shows both the promise and limitations of intrinsic reward methods for code, informing future work on code models and agents.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies intrinsic reward methods (certainty-based RLIF) for code generation, finding they cause early gains but inevitable training collapse (output shortening, reasoning loss), and offer no benefit over scratch training when used to initialize RLVR.
AI.motivation: RLVR relies on ground-truth supervision which is costly/infeasible for code tasks. While intrinsic reward methods succeed on math reasoning, it's unexplored whether they transfer to code generation due to code's structural complexity, syntactic diversity, and execution-based verification needs.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study on LiveCodeBench evaluating certainty-based RLIF (Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback) methods under various training scenarios and hyperparameters, comparing against RLVR and scratch training baselines.
AI.result: Certainty-based methods show early performance gains but inevitably collapse—models shorten outputs and lose reasoning capability. Collapse speed is sensitive to sample size and temperature. RLIF pre-training offers no significant improvement over training from scratch when used to initialize RLVR.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic reward methods have both promise and limitations for code generation; the paper provides actionable recommendations for training code reasoning models with intrinsic rewards.

title: ASCII Art Turns LLMs into VLA Controllers
summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) controllers are often built by extending vision--language models (VLMs) with action supervision, relying on multimodal backbones with large data and compute requirements. We demonstrate that a text-only large language model (LLM) can be adapted into a VLA-style controller when visual observations are rendered into a text input using an ASCII representation. This ASCII-as-vision interface enables existing training and deployment stacks for LLMs to efficiently condition on visual state, follow natural-language instructions, and produce constrained, executable actions. We fine-tune and compare multiple LLMs and VLMs across model families and scales, using both expert demonstrations from a planning-based teacher, as well as DAgger for iterative improvement. In a 2D manipulation benchmark, in both simulation and on a physical manipulator, the resulting controllers can identify task-relevant entities and plan feasible action sequences. Our results suggest that ASCII rendering can serve as a lightweight, interpretable modality bridge from images to text, complementing conventional VLA pipelines, and opening directions for VLA research with text-only backbones.

AI.tldr: Text-only LLMs can be turned into VLA-style controllers by rendering visual observations as ASCII text, enabling lightweight, interpretable vision-to-text bridging that competes with conventional VLA pipelines in 2D manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: VLA controllers built by extending VLMs require large multimodal backbones with high data and compute costs. The authors explore whether a text-only LLM, combined with ASCII-rendered visual input, can serve as a more lightweight and interpretable alternative.
AI.method: Visual observations are converted into ASCII text representations, which are fed as text input to LLMs. The LLMs are fine-tuned on expert demonstrations (from a planning-based teacher) and improved via DAgger. Multiple LLMs and VLMs across different scales are compared in a 2D manipulation benchmark, both in simulation and on a real physical manipulator.
AI.result: The ASCII-based LLM controllers can identify task-relevant entities and plan feasible action sequences in both simulated and physical 2D manipulation settings, achieving competitive performance against VLM-based VLA controllers.
AI.conclusion: ASCII rendering offers a lightweight, interpretable modality bridge from images to text, complementing conventional VLA pipelines and opening new directions for VLA research using text-only backbones.

title: Neurosymbolic Clinical Trial Matching via LLM-Driven Abduction and Logical Verification
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising path to automate Clinical Trial Matching (CTM), but still struggle with the deterministic verification required for complex eligibility criteria. Conversely, purely symbolic methods provide formal rigour but break down when faced with incomplete patient records and noisy clinical evidence. To bridge this gap, we investigate a hybrid framework for CTM combining LLMs with logical verification. In particular, we introduce an abductive neurosymbolic CTM framework (αNeSy-CTM), which leverages the linguistic and world knowledge in LLMs to support reasoning over noisy and underspecified clinical text. Extensive evaluation demonstrates that αNeSy-CTM substantially outperforms standalone LLM baselines, achieving up to 30% relative improvement over zero-shot baselines. In addition, our analyses confirm the impact of abductive reasoning on CTM, with αNeSy-CTM exhibiting improved accuracy, specificity, and robustness over a non-abductive neurosymbolic setting. Furthermore, αNeSy-CTM and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning prove highly complementary, highlighting the potential for a hybrid routing policy. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates the impact of neurosymbolic methods for automating CTM, providing a path toward the next generation of auditable, LLM-driven clinical applications.

AI.tldr: αNeSy-CTM is a hybrid neurosymbolic framework combining LLMs with abductive logical reasoning for Clinical Trial Matching, outperforming standalone LLMs by up to 30% and complementing Chain-of-Thought reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with deterministic verification for complex eligibility criteria in CTM, while purely symbolic methods fail on incomplete/noisy clinical data. A hybrid approach is needed to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The authors propose αNeSy-CTM, an abductive neurosymbolic framework that integrates LLMs' linguistic and world knowledge with formal logical verification to reason over noisy and underspecified clinical text for clinical trial matching.
AI.result: αNeSy-CTM achieves up to 30% relative improvement over zero-shot LLM baselines, and outperforms non-abductive neurosymbolic settings in accuracy, specificity, and robustness. It is also highly complementary with Chain-of-Thought reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid neurosymbolic methods are effective for automating CTM, offering a path toward auditable, LLM-driven clinical applications with improved reasoning capabilities.

title: Decoupling the Declarative from the Procedural in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Deploying generalist robotic agents in the real world requires transferable skills. Specifically, a policy trained to clone a behavior from object-specific demonstrations must generalize beyond that object, otherwise data collection requirements become intractable. Recently, fine-tuning of pre-trained billion-parameter Vision-Language Models (VLMs), initially on large-scale robot datasets and then on fewer scenario-specific demonstrations, has emerged as the predominant paradigm for designing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. While these policies achieve state-of-the-art manipulation performance in-distribution, they remain brittle to minor spatial, semantic, and task variations. In this work, we address the inability of current models to decouple the declarative (i.e., concepts and entity semantics) from the procedural knowledge (i.e., how to do something) encoded in their parameters, which is a fundamental bottleneck for zero-shot skill transfer to novel objects. To address this, we propose w$^{2}$VLA, a new VLA model with restructured information flow. Rather than feeding all multimodal tokens from the VLM encoder into a large, opaque transformer-based action expert, our approach modulates the robot state sequence with visual, spatial, and skill information in a compositional and interpretable manner. Unlike popular, state-of-the-art VLAs, we show that our modular approach successfully decouples knowledge representations, enabling robust behavior cloning and unprecedented zero-shot skill transfer capabilities across dissimilar, unseen objects.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes w²VLA, a Vision-Language-Action model that restructures information flow to decouple declarative knowledge (concepts/entities) from procedural knowledge (how-to), enabling zero-shot skill transfer to novel objects by modulating robot state sequences with visual, spatial, and skill information in a compositional manner.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models struggle to generalize beyond in-distribution scenarios because they fail to decouple declarative (concept/entity semantics) from procedural (how-to) knowledge. This coupling makes policies brittle to spatial, semantic, and task variations, creating a fundamental bottleneck for zero-shot skill transfer to novel objects.
AI.method: w²VLA restructures information flow by replacing the large opaque transformer-based action expert with a modular approach that compositionally modulates the robot state sequence using visual, spatial, and skill information, rather than feeding all multimodal tokens from the VLM encoder directly into the action head.
AI.result: The modular approach successfully decouples knowledge representations, enabling robust behavior cloning and achieving unprecedented zero-shot skill transfer capabilities across dissimilar, unseen objects, outperforming popular state-of-the-art VLA models.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly separating declarative and procedural knowledge representations through compositional information flow is a viable path toward achieving transferable robotic manipulation skills without requiring extensive object-specific demonstrations.

title: Root Cause Analysis with Latent Confounders using Partial Ancestral Graphs
summary: Finding the source of failures, known as Root Cause Analysis (RCA), is essential for identifying the root causes of anomalies and maintaining the reliability of complex systems. While causal theory has advanced data-driven RCA, existing frameworks assume causal sufficiency, failing to account for the unobserved latent variables prevalent in real-world environments. To address this gap, we propose PAG-RCA. This framework models system failures as parametric interventions over Partial Ancestral Graphs (PAGs) to perform RCA in the presence of latent variables. We use standard causal identification algorithms to find the source of failures by quantifying causal effects over the PAG. When an effect is identifiable, candidate root causes are ranked based on their exact intervention effects. When effects are structurally unidentifiable, our framework (for the first time in the RCA literature) integrates partial identification to evaluate and score candidates using analytical causal bounds. By integrating latent variables and partial identification at once our framework ensures robust RCA even under data scarcity and latent-variable scenarios where traditional methods degrade. Evaluations on synthetic data, microservice anomaly benchmarks and power-grid cascading failures demonstrate that PAG-RCA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data-driven baselines. By improving data-driven RCA performance under data scarcity, this methodology advances reliable automated diagnostics in partially observable complex networks.

AI.tldr: PAG-RCA is a novel framework that uses Partial Ancestral Graphs to perform Root Cause Analysis under latent variables, combining causal identification with partial identification methods to handle structurally unidentifiable effects, outperforming baselines on synthetic, microservice, and power-grid datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven RCA frameworks assume causal sufficiency, failing to account for unobserved latent variables that are prevalent in real-world complex systems, leading to degraded performance under data scarcity and latent-variable scenarios.
AI.method: The framework (1) models system failures as parametric interventions over Partial Ancestral Graphs (PAGs); (2) uses standard causal identification algorithms to quantify causal effects over PAGs; (3) ranks candidates by exact intervention effects when identifiable; (4) integrates partial identification to evaluate candidates using analytical causal bounds when effects are structurally unidentifiable.
AI.result: Evaluations on synthetic data, microservice anomaly benchmarks, and power-grid cascading failures show PAG-RCA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data-driven baselines, especially under data scarcity and latent-variable conditions.
AI.conclusion: By integrating latent variables and partial identification, PAG-RCA advances reliable automated diagnostics in partially observable complex networks, ensuring robust RCA where traditional methods degrade.

title: UniviewVLA: A Unified Multiview Vision-Language-Action Model with World Modeling
summary: Occluded tasks remain a bottleneck in robot manipulation. Existing solutions either deploy additional physical cameras requiring training-inference camera parity, or rely on explicit 3D reconstruction with high computational cost. Moreover, both approaches rely on standard agent-view and wrist-view observations, while failing to capture occlusion information and future scene evolution. To this end, we propose UniviewVLA, a unified multiview Vision-Language-Action model with world modeling, which infers multiview scene evolution for action prediction from only standard two-camera observations. We demonstrate that by leveraging generated multiview future views from the world model, UniviewVLA reveals occluded cues and models future scene evolution, improving action prediction and removing the need for extra hardware or explicit reconstruction. Besides, to accelerate inference while preserving prediction accuracy, UniviewVLA develops Motion-Informative Token Compression, which compresses each generated view from 625 to 16 tokens and reduces per-view latency from 6-7s to 0.2-0.3s. UniviewVLA also proposes training-free Action-Entropy View Selection, which dynamically identifies the most action-informative view at different inference stages. Extensive experiments show that UniviewVLA achieves 95.8% on LIBERO and 4.60 on CALVIN ABCD to D, both standard occlusion-free benchmarks. On customized occlusion-focused tasks, it improves success rate from 40.0% to 73.3%, and average real-robot success rate by 33.4 points, demonstrating stronger occlusion-focused performance without sacrificing standard occlusion-free benchmarks.

AI.tldr: UniviewVLA is a unified multiview Vision-Language-Action model that generates future multiview scene predictions from only two standard camera inputs, using world modeling to handle occlusions without extra hardware or explicit 3D reconstruction. It introduces Motion-Informative Token Compression (reducing tokens from 625→16 per view, latency 6-7s→0.2-0.3s) and training-free Action-Entropy View Selection. It achieves 95.8% on LIBERO, 4.60 on CALVIN, and improves occlusion-task success from 40.0%→73.3%.
AI.motivation: Occlusion remains a major bottleneck in robot manipulation. Existing solutions require extra physical cameras (demanding training-inference parity) or explicit 3D reconstruction (high computational cost), and both rely on standard agent/wrist views that miss occlusion information and future scene evolution.
AI.method: UniviewVLA uses a world model to generate multiview future scene evolutions from only two standard camera views, revealing occluded cues. It employs Motion-Informative Token Compression (reducing tokens per view from 625 to 16 via motion-aware compression) for fast inference, and training-free Action-Entropy View Selection to dynamically pick the most action-relevant view at different inference stages.
AI.result: 95.8% on LIBERO, 4.60 on CALVIN ABCD→D (occlusion-free). On customized occlusion tasks, success rate improved from 40.0% to 73.3%. Real-robot average success rate improved by 33.4 points.
AI.conclusion: UniviewVLA demonstrates that leveraging generated multiview future views from a world model effectively reveals occluded cues and models future scene evolution, improving action prediction without extra hardware or explicit reconstruction, and without sacrificing standard occlusion-free performance.

title: Power Systems Agent Benchmark: Executable Evaluation of AI Agents in Electric Power Engineering
comment: 19 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/trashchenkov/power-systems-agent-benchmark ; archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20753046
summary:
Executable evaluation -- checking the consequences of an agent's actions with a program rather than grading its prose -- has become a prominent way to assess tool-using AI agents in software settings. Electric power engineering has not yet had an analogous benchmark: language-model use is still dominated by retrieval and text question answering, while agents acting on power-system artifacts remain mostly academic prototypes. We introduce the Power Systems Agent Benchmark, an executable benchmark for power-engineering agents. An agent receives a structured task and returns a structured solution; a deterministic evaluator recomputes the engineering quantities, checks operational constraints, and returns a feasibility flag, a normalized score, and explicit violations.
  The benchmark contains 41 task families across eight areas of power engineering, from power flow and protection to stability, microgrids, reliability, power quality, and forecasting. Each task is grounded in a citable source, standard, or documented engineering formulation. To resist contamination, held-out cases are synthesized on demand by per-family generators from private seeds: the construction is inspectable, but the instances remain private. In a reference evaluation with three command-line agents, the strongest score near the compact tier's ceiling, a smaller open model trails, and public and held-out performance are broadly consistent; a separate public-split grid with OpenCode and Aider probes harness effects. The reference evaluation doubles as quality control: unanimous failures flag candidate task or evaluator defects, and it exposed a latent evaluator bug missed by self-consistency checks. The evaluators are compact deterministic surrogates, but the task contract allows their internals to be upgraded to simulator-backed checks without changing how tasks are posed or solved.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Power Systems Agent Benchmark (PSAB), an executable benchmark for evaluating tool-using AI agents in power engineering. It comprises 41 task families across 8 areas, with deterministic evaluation, contamination-resistant private instances, and reference evaluations revealing the strongest agents near ceiling performance while exposing a latent evaluator bug. The benchmark is designed to be upgradable to simulator-backed checks.
AI.motivation: Electric power engineering lacks an executable benchmark for tool-using AI agents, unlike other software domains. Current language-model use in this field is limited to retrieval and text QA, while agent-based approaches remain academic prototypes. A standardized, executable evaluation framework is needed to advance AI agent research in power systems.
AI.method: The benchmark defines a task contract where agents receive structured tasks and return structured solutions, evaluated by deterministic evaluators that recompute engineering quantities, check operational constraints, and return feasibility flags, normalized scores, and explicit violations. It includes 41 task families across 8 power engineering areas with per-family generators that synthesize held-out cases on demand from private seeds. Reference evaluation tested three command-line agents.
AI.result: The strongest agent scored near the compact tier's ceiling, a smaller open model lagged behind, and public vs. held-out performance was broadly consistent. The reference evaluation doubled as quality control, exposing a latent evaluator bug missed by self-consistency checks. A separate public-split grid with OpenCode and Aider probes revealed harness effects.
AI.conclusion: The Power Systems Agent Benchmark provides a robust, contamination-resistant, and upgradable evaluation framework for AI agents in power engineering. The deterministic evaluators can be upgraded to simulator-backed checks without changing the task interface, ensuring long-term utility.

title: A Stitch in Time Saves Nine: Preserving Policy Compatibility Under Perception Updates in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: 12 pages, 9 tables, 5 figures; T-ITS under review
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving systems tightly couple perception and decision-making through latent representations. Consequently, updates to perception models can alter these representations and degrade the performance of downstream policies that remain fixed. Existing solutions typically rely on policy retraining or architectural decoupling, both of which incur substantial computation and validation costs. In this paper, we formulate the model stitching problem for end-to-end autonomous driving and test the hypothesis that policy compatibility can be preserved through lightweight latent-space alignment. We study low-complexity model stitching methods, including linear and convolutional stitchers, for restoring compatibility between updated perception modules and frozen downstream policy modules. Experiments demonstrate that stitching effectively preserves downstream driving behavior under diverse perception updates, including changes in random initialization, sensor configuration, and training domain. In the most challenging cross-domain setting from nuScenes to CARLA, convolutional stitching retains over 91\% of the no-shift driving score while reducing adaptation time from \SI{22.18}{h} to \SI{0.91}{h}. These results suggest that model stitching provides an effective and computationally efficient alternative to retraining or fine-tuning for maintaining end-to-end autonomous driving systems. The model will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance at https://github.com/SCP-CN-001/model-stitching to support further research and development in autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes lightweight model stitching (linear and convolutional stitchers) to align latent representations between updated perception modules and frozen downstream policy modules in end-to-end autonomous driving, preserving performance without costly retraining. Convolutional stitching retains over 91% of the no-shift driving score in cross-domain settings (nuScenes to CARLA), reducing adaptation time from 22.18h to 0.91h.
AI.motivation: Updates to perception models in end-to-end autonomous driving alter latent representations, degrading downstream policy performance. Existing solutions require costly policy retraining or architectural decoupling, motivating the need for a lightweight, efficient alternative to maintain system compatibility.
AI.method: Formulates the model stitching problem for end-to-end autonomous driving and tests low-complexity stitchers (linear and convolutional) that align latent spaces between updated perception encoders and frozen downstream policy modules, enabling compatibility without retraining the policy.
AI.result: Stitching preserves driving behavior under diverse perception updates (random initialization, sensor configuration, training domain changes). In the cross-domain setting (nuScenes to CARLA), convolutional stitching retains over 91% of the no-shift driving score while reducing adaptation time from 22.18h to 0.91h.
AI.conclusion: Model stitching is an effective and computationally efficient alternative to retraining or fine-tuning for maintaining end-to-end autonomous driving systems, enabling rapid adaptation at minimal cost.

title: Generative Responsible AI Data Evaluation Schema (GRAIDES) for AI Assurance in Local Government
summary: Trust in the application of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) relies on well-governed measurable evidence of performance and safety. In practice, however, evaluation data is often fragmented across systems, inconsistently structured and difficult to compare. We introduce the Generative Responsible AI Data Evaluation Schema (GRAIDES) as a lightweight open-source data model for centralising AI observability across popular vendors. Practical blueprints for code, architecture and statistical evaluation are shared as guidance about how to approach generative system assurance at the organisational level. Illustrative case study results are reported from Westminster City Council's AI catalogue with a focus on measuring human-model alignment including detecting systematic disagreement between evaluators. By framing evaluations as a data modelling problem, GRAIDES provides a practical pathway toward more consistent and reproducible benchmarking, tuning and assurance activities for generative AI systems.

AI.tldr: GRAIDES is a lightweight open-source data model for centralizing AI observability across vendors, providing practical blueprints for code, architecture, and statistical evaluation to enable consistent benchmarking, tuning, and assurance for generative AI systems.
AI.motivation: Evaluation data for generative AI is often fragmented across systems, inconsistently structured, and difficult to compare, undermining trust that requires well-governed measurable evidence of performance and safety.
AI.method: The authors introduce GRAIDES as an open-source data model for centralizing AI observability, provide practical blueprints for code, architecture, and statistical evaluation, and report illustrative case study results from Westminster City Council's AI catalogue measuring human-model alignment and detecting systematic disagreement between evaluators.
AI.result: Case study results from Westminster City Council's AI catalogue demonstrate the ability to measure human-model alignment and detect systematic disagreement between evaluators.
AI.conclusion: By framing evaluations as a data modeling problem, GRAIDES provides a practical pathway toward more consistent and reproducible benchmarking, tuning, and assurance activities for generative AI systems.

title: LOGOS: LiDAR-Only Gaussian Elevation Splatting for Unified Tiny Obstacle Segmentation
summary: Robust obstacle segmentation is essential for the safety of intelligent robots, where LiDAR-based perception systems play a fundamental role in the robot-environment interaction. While extensive LiDAR-based approaches have demonstrated high performance on common obstacles in urban scenarios, their results on tiny obstacles such as curbs, gravel, and potholes remain unsatisfactory due to the significant similarity between tiny obstacles and inherent road undulations. Moreover, their segmentation accuracy even deteriorates sharply when the LiDAR scans suffer from degradation in challenging off-road scenes. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose LOGOS, a LiDAR-only unified tiny obstacle segmentation system, which models the road surface as a continuous mixture of 2D Gaussian primitives and distinguishes tiny obstacles via high-presicion elevation estimation. Unlike existing Gaussian splatting methods that rely on iterative RGB training, LOGOS is a backpropagation-free LiDAR-only approach. It directly estimates Gaussian parameters via a freespace-aware initialization by incrementally pruning non-road primitives using smoothness constraints. Subsequently, pointwise signed distances are computed via a novel normal-aware elevation splatting function, ensuring robustness to both flat and sloped terrains. We evaluate LOGOS on a highly heterogeneous benchmark of point cloud frames collected from urban mobility scenarios and mining haulage off-road environments. These data are practically acquired using different LiDAR sensors and exhibit large variations in point density, terrain roughness, and obstacle types. Experiments on the road and off-road scenes demonstrate that LOGOS significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, particularly in degraded point cloud regions and challenging off-road scenarios, while maintaining real-time efficiency.

AI.tldr: LOGOS is a LiDAR-only, backpropagation-free tiny obstacle segmentation system that models road surfaces as continuous 2D Gaussian primitives with freespace-aware initialization and normal-aware elevation splatting, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both urban and off-road terrains in real-time.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR-based methods struggle with tiny obstacles (curbs, gravel, potholes) due to their similarity to road undulations, and segmentation accuracy deteriorates sharply in degraded LiDAR scans from challenging off-road scenes.
AI.method: LOGOS models road surfaces as a continuous mixture of 2D Gaussian primitives, uses freespace-aware initialization with smoothness constraints to prune non-road primitives, and computes pointwise signed distances via a novel normal-aware elevation splatting function.
AI.result: LOGOS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on heterogeneous benchmarks from urban and off-road mining environments, especially in degraded point cloud regions and challenging off-road scenarios, while maintaining real-time efficiency.
AI.conclusion: LOGOS provides a robust, real-time LiDAR-only solution for tiny obstacle segmentation that is resilient to terrain variations and sensor degradation, demonstrating strong generalization across diverse environments.

title: AutoACSL: Synthesizing ACSL Specifications by Integrating LLMs with CPG-Based Static Analysis
summary: Generating formal specifications for C programs remains a challenge in formal verification due to the manual effort, expertise, and semantic precision required. While recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) offer promise in automating specification synthesis, current approaches often lack semantic depth and produce unverifiable or incomplete contracts. To address these limitations, we introduce AutoACSL, a novel framework that integrates LLM prompting with semantic features extracted from Code Property Graphs (CPGs). AutoACSL performs static analyses to extract key semantic elements, including arithmetic operations, loop and recursion structures, and return value propagation, which are encoded into structured prompts. These prompts enable the LLM not only to generate normal behavioral specifications but also to include constraints that prevent inputs leading to runtime errors. AutoACSL employs a feedback-driven synthesis loop, where candidate specifications are verified using Frama-C/WP and refined iteratively until verification succeeds or a termination condition is met. Evaluated on 604 programs drawn from diverse datasets, AutoACSL achieves a 98% specification generation success ratio and a 96% full proof ratio when paired with Gemini-3. Compared to a code-only baseline, AutoACSL improves the full proof ratio by 24.7% to 51.7% across four LLMs (GPT-o4 Mini, GPT-5.2, Grok-4.1, and Gemini-3), demonstrating that integrating large language models with CPG-based static analysis substantially enhances both generation robustness and verification effectiveness for automated ACSL specification synthesis.

AI.tldr: AutoACSL integrates LLMs with Code Property Graph (CPG) semantic analysis to automatically generate verifiable ACSL formal specifications for C programs. Evaluated on 604 programs, it achieves 98% specification generation success and 96% full proof ratio with Gemini-3, improving full proof ratios by 24.7%-51.7% over code-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Generating formal specifications for C programs remains a challenge due to high manual effort, required expertise, and need for semantic precision. Current LLM-based approaches lack semantic depth and produce unverifiable or incomplete contracts.
AI.method: AutoACSL performs static analyses on Code Property Graphs (CPGs) to extract semantic elements (arithmetic operations, loop/recursion structures, return value propagation), encodes them into structured prompts, feeds them to LLMs for specification synthesis, and employs a feedback-driven loop where Frama-C/WP verifies and refines candidates iteratively.
AI.result: On 604 programs, AutoACSL achieves 98% specification generation success ratio and 96% full proof ratio with Gemini-3. It improves full proof ratio by 24.7%-51.7% over code-only baselines across GPT-o4 Mini, GPT-5.2, Grok-4.1, and Gemini-3.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLMs with CPG-based static analysis substantially enhances both generation robustness and verification effectiveness for automated ACSL specification synthesis.

title: Robot Critics that Sweat the Small Stuff
summary: Large vision-language models contain several priors about the world and object interactions, making them useful critics during inference to steer robot policies towards success. However, closed-loop robot manipulation requires judging small visual differences between success and failure, which remains a challenge for current VLMs. We introduce a method to fine-tune critics by constructing pairwise progress supervision using success and failure rollouts obtained from a policy. Our fine-tuned critic excels at fine-grained progress reasoning and subtle failure detection, outperforming prior progress reasoning baselines. Additionally, we use an action-conditioned video model to predict the visual effect of several candidate actions sampled from a policy, and show that our critic can correctly identify successful candidates to execute, improving the average policy success rate by 11% across real-world tasks and 5.9% across simulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning vision-language models with pairwise progress supervision from policy rollouts improves fine-grained failure detection and robot manipulation success by up to 11%.
AI.motivation: Large VLMs struggle to judge small visual differences between success and failure in closed-loop robot manipulation, limiting their usefulness as critics during inference.
AI.method: Construct pairwise progress supervision from success/failure policy rollouts to fine-tune a critic; use an action-conditioned video model to predict visual effects of candidate actions, then apply the critic to identify the best action.
AI.result: Outperforms prior progress reasoning baselines on fine-grained failure detection; improves average policy success rate by 11% on real-world tasks and 5.9% on simulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned critics with pairwise progress supervision effectively steer robot policies by leveraging VLMs' priors while overcoming their limitations in judging subtle visual differences.

title: How Should Agents Read Demonstrations? Hierarchical Structure Beats Flat Action Logs
comment: Accepted at the 5th Deep Learning for Code (DL4C) Workshop, ICML 2026. 8 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Programming by Demonstration (PbD) offers a human-centered way to author procedural knowledge for LLM agents: users communicate what they want by showing rather than by writing prompts or code, making agent authoring accessible to non-programmers. The natural output of a PbD recording is a flat action log, but how this log is organized before being passed to the agent is an open design question with significant consequences for plan quality. We propose grouping recorded actions into labeled, hierarchical subgoals and evaluate the effect of this organizational structure in a controlled experiment. Across 85 web automation tasks, we compare a zero-shot baseline against four demonstration formats that share identical action sequences but differ in structure. On 43 natural-language tasks with vague descriptions, hierarchically grouped demonstrations improve pass rates from 76.7\% to 90.7\% (paired permutation test $p{=}0.034$; win-loss 6:0), while flat demonstrations show a smaller, non-significant improvement. On 42 tasks with precise descriptions, no format provides any benefit, confirming that the hierarchical advantage arises specifically when descriptions leave procedural details ambiguous. Ablation shows that subgoal grouping alone drives the effect: preconditions, postconditions, and parameter annotations add no measurable benefit. These results offer a concrete design recommendation for PbD pipelines and, more broadly, for any system that feeds procedural context to an LLM agent: segment action sequences into named subgoal groups rather than presenting flat step lists.

AI.tldr: Grouping demonstration actions into labeled, hierarchical subgoals significantly improves LLM agent performance on vague tasks (76.7% to 90.7% pass rate), while flat action logs show minimal benefit. The effect is driven solely by subgoal grouping—not by preconditions, postconditions, or parameter annotations.
AI.motivation: Programming by Demonstration (PbD) makes agent authoring accessible to non-programmers by letting users demonstrate tasks instead of writing prompts or code. However, the natural output of PbD is a flat action log, and it's unclear how best to organize that log before feeding it to an LLM agent—an open design question with significant consequences for plan quality.
AI.method: Controlled experiment across 85 web automation tasks comparing a zero-shot baseline against four demonstration formats sharing identical actions but differing in structure (flat, hierarchical with labeled subgoals, with/without preconditions/postconditions/parameter annotations). Evaluated on 43 vague-description tasks and 42 precise-description tasks.
AI.result: Hierarchical subgoal grouping improved pass rates from 76.7% to 90.7% on vague tasks (p=0.034; win-loss 6:0). Flat demonstrations showed smaller, non-significant improvement. No format benefited precise-description tasks. Ablation confirmed subgoal grouping alone drives the effect.
AI.conclusion: Concrete design recommendation: segment action sequences into named subgoal groups rather than presenting flat step lists for PbD pipelines and any system feeding procedural context to an LLM agent.

title: Conflict-Aware Switching for CBF-CLF-Based Multi-Goal Navigation
summary: Quadratic programs (QPs) using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and Control Lyapunov Functions (CLFs) are widely used for safe control in reach-and-avoid navigation. However, the inherently conflicting nature of CBF and CLF constraints can lead to performance degradation, including slowdowns and deadlocks. This issue is exacerbated in multi-goal scenarios, where multiple nominal control objectives must be satisfied under shared safety constraints. Existing approaches for preemptive safety are often computationally expensive or overly conservative, while methods that relax or switch between nominal objectives are not well-suited for sequential goal-to-goal navigation. To address these limitations, we propose a conflict-aware switching strategy that detects high-conflict conditions and switches between available nominal control objectives to reduce constraint conflict. We apply this approach to multi-agent, multi-goal reach-and-avoid scenarios under CBF-CLF-QP control. Compared to a baseline sequential goal traversal strategy, our method reduces both completion time and timeout rates, demonstrating improved performance in satisfying all nominal control objectives while respecting safety constraints.

AI.tldr: A conflict-aware switching strategy is proposed to resolve CBF-CLF constraint conflicts in multi-agent, multi-goal reach-and-avoid navigation, reducing completion time and timeout rates compared to baseline sequential goal traversal.
AI.motivation: CBF-CLF-QP controllers suffer from performance degradation (slowdowns, deadlocks) due to conflicting safety and control objectives, especially in multi-goal scenarios; existing methods are either computationally expensive, overly conservative, or ill-suited for sequential goal-to-goal navigation.
AI.method: A conflict-aware switching strategy that detects high-conflict conditions and dynamically switches between available nominal control objectives to reduce CBF-CLF constraint conflict in multi-agent, multi-goal reach-and-avoid scenarios.
AI.result: The proposed method reduces both completion time and timeout rates compared to a baseline sequential goal traversal strategy in multi-agent, multi-goal settings under CBF-CLF-QP control.
AI.conclusion: Conflict-aware switching between nominal objectives effectively mitigates CBF-CLF conflicts, improving performance in satisfying all nominal control objectives while respecting safety constraints.

title: BioInsight: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Interactive Biomedical Knowledge Discovery
summary: Biomedical researchers increasingly use AI-generated analyses and reports to interpret protein-level signals, but static outputs are often insufficient for research decision-making, where users need to inspect evidence, assess uncertainty, compare mechanisms, and refine hypotheses. We present \textsc{BioInsight}, a multi-agent system that moves from static biomedical report generation to interactive evidence-centered interactive interface generation. Given a disease name, a protein association table, and optional cohort metadata, BioInsight organizes disease-specific evidence through typed intermediate artifacts, including ranked pathways, literature evidence packets, protein-level reasoning notes, citation-grounded reports, dashboard schemas, and rendered interactive interfaces. The system decomposes evidence retrieval from mechanistic reasoning, normalizes citations through deterministic components, and converts the same structured evidence used in the report into an interactive interface. We evaluate BioInsight on standardized biomedical QA, challenging protein-function reasoning, and end-to-end biomedical evidence synthesis. Results show that BioInsight achieves best, and suggest that biomedical AI systems should move beyond text-only and static reports toward provenance-preserving, interactive evidence artifacts.

AI.tldr: BioInsight is a multi-agent system that transforms static biomedical report generation into interactive, evidence-centered interfaces. It processes disease names, protein association tables, and cohort metadata to produce ranked pathways, literature evidence, reasoning notes, citation-grounded reports, dashboard schemas, and interactive interfaces. By decoupling evidence retrieval from mechanistic reasoning and using deterministic citation normalization, it enables users to inspect evidence, assess uncertainty, compare mechanisms, and refine hypotheses. Evaluations on biomedical QA, protein-function reasoning, and evidence synthesis show state-of-the-art performance, advocating for provenance-preserving interactive artifacts over text-only static reports.
AI.motivation: Biomedical researchers need interactive tools to inspect evidence, assess uncertainty, compare mechanisms, and refine hypotheses, but current AI systems produce only static, text-based reports that are insufficient for research decision-making.
AI.method: BioInsight is a multi-agent system that, given a disease name, protein association table, and optional cohort metadata, organizes evidence through typed intermediate artifacts: ranked pathways, literature evidence packets, protein-level reasoning notes, citation-grounded reports, dashboard schemas, and rendered interactive interfaces. It decomposes evidence retrieval from mechanistic reasoning, normalizes citations via deterministic components, and converts structured evidence into interactive interfaces.
AI.result: BioInsight achieves state-of-the-art results on standardized biomedical QA, challenging protein-function reasoning, and end-to-end biomedical evidence synthesis tasks.
AI.conclusion: Biomedical AI systems should move beyond text-only, static reports toward provenance-preserving, interactive evidence artifacts to better support research decision-making.

title: VQActFlow: Vector-Quantized Action Mode Steering for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
summary: Multi-task robot manipulation policies are challenging to learn from demonstration because traditionally a single network must select among qualitatively different action modes from a multimodal demonstration distribution, conditioned on language and visual context. A wrong mode selection means executing the wrong task or an action infeasible in the scene. Tokenizing continuous actions into a learned discrete codebook separates these modes at the representation level, offering structural advantages for multi-task learning. We propose VQActFlow, a multi-task manipulation policy that tokenizes action chunks and generates code sequences via Variational Flow Matching. VQActFlow maintains an explicit preference over action modes throughout generation. Inference-time guidance acts on this preference to steer mode commitment. We instantiate this with classifier-free guidance over language conditioning, which steers the policy toward the instructed action mode, and a learned codebook critic that supplies a complementary feasibility signal. We evaluate VQActFlow on three platforms: the LIBERO simulation benchmarks, a Unitree G1 humanoid performing whole-body pick-and-place, and an ALOHA-style bimanual platform performing contact-rich tasks. Across these benchmarks, VQActFlow outperforms both continuous and discrete baselines.

AI.tldr: VQActFlow tokenizes continuous actions into a discrete codebook and generates code sequences via Variational Flow Matching, using inference-time guidance (classifier-free guidance and a learned codebook critic) to steer action mode commitment. It outperforms continuous and discrete baselines on LIBERO, Unitree G1 humanoid, and ALOHA-style bimanual platforms.
AI.motivation: Multi-task robot manipulation policies are hard to learn from demonstration because a single network must select among qualitatively different action modes from a multimodal demonstration distribution, conditioned on language and visual context. Wrong mode selection leads to executing the wrong task or infeasible actions.
AI.method: Tokenizes continuous actions into a learned discrete codebook to separate action modes at the representation level, then generates code sequences via Variational Flow Matching. Inference-time guidance uses classifier-free guidance over language conditioning to steer toward the instructed action mode, plus a learned codebook critic to supply a complementary feasibility signal.
AI.result: Outperforms both continuous and discrete baselines on three platforms: LIBERO simulation benchmarks, Unitree G1 humanoid performing whole-body pick-and-place, and ALOHA-style bimanual platform performing contact-rich tasks.
AI.conclusion: Discrete action tokenization with flow matching and inference-time guidance provides a robust framework for multi-task robot manipulation, effectively handling multimodal action distributions and improving mode selection accuracy.

title: Building Agent Harnesses for Scientific Curation from Multimodal Sources
summary: Scientific discovery workflows often depend on structured curation from the literature. This is difficult for current agents because the key evidence is scattered across long text, dense tables, and figures, and the final records often require reasoning across multiple evidence fragments rather than copying a single span. We study scientific curation from multimodal sources and introduce Beaver, an agent harness that extracts structured information from scientific papers while preserving provenance to the supporting evidence. Beaver combines a frontier agent with multimodal evidence tooling, task scaffolding, and artifact-grounded autoresearch. These components turn curation into a staged, auditable workflow and enable an iterative evaluate--diagnose--revise loop, where persistent run artifacts expose stage-localized failures and guide harness updates. Experiments show that Beaver reaches 81.0 on Gold-Referenced Attribute Score (GRAS), an attribute-level measure of agreement with gold curated records, outperforming frontier agents by over 23 absolute points. Ablations show that task scaffolding, multimodal evidence tooling, and provenance traces each contribute meaningfully to performance, while attribute-level analysis shows the largest gains on high-value attributes that require cross-modal reasoning and normalization. These results show that, for scientific curation from papers with multimodal evidence, harness design is a central determinant of agent performance.

AI.tldr: Beaver is an agent harness for scientific curation from multimodal literature that achieves 81.0 GRAS, outperforming frontier agents by 23+ points through staged, auditable workflows with multimodal evidence tooling, task scaffolding, and provenance tracking.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery workflows require structured curation from literature, but current agents struggle because key evidence is scattered across long text, dense tables, and figures, and final records often require reasoning across multiple evidence fragments rather than simple copying.
AI.method: Beaver combines a frontier agent with multimodal evidence tooling, task scaffolding, and artifact-grounded autoresearch. It structures curation as a staged, auditable workflow with an iterative evaluate-diagnose-revise loop, where persistent run artifacts expose stage-localized failures and guide harness updates.
AI.result: Beaver achieves 81.0 on Gold-Referenced Attribute Score (GRAS), outperforming frontier agents by over 23 absolute points. Ablations confirm task scaffolding, multimodal evidence tooling, and provenance traces each contribute meaningfully, with largest gains on high-value attributes requiring cross-modal reasoning and normalization.
AI.conclusion: For scientific curation from papers with multimodal evidence, harness design is a central determinant of agent performance, rather than just the capability of the underlying model.

title: Energy-based Compositional Diffusion Planning
summary: Compositional diffusion planners aim to solve long-horizon robotic tasks using short training trajectories. Yet, current approaches often rely on the heuristic stitching of local predictions. We show that the resulting stitched update is generally a non-conservative field} that does not mathematically correspond to any valid global trajectory log-density function. We propose Energy-based Compositional Diffuser (ECD), a framework that formulates the global trajectory as the minimizer of the sum of local bridge potentials. This energy-based perspective defines a conservative correction field and contains a boundary reaction term that heuristic stitching omits. To enable efficient inference, we further introduce a Markov-based score approximation that computes the reaction term via a single block-tridiagonal solve, maintaining time complexity linear in the planning horizon. Empirically, ECD achieves state-of-the-art success rates on a range of OGBench stitching tasks, while nearly matching the inference speed of heuristic stitching methods. Code is available at https://github.com/GradientSpaces/ECD.

AI.tldr: ECD reformulates compositional diffusion planning as an energy-based optimization with a conservative correction field and boundary reaction term, achieving SOTA results on OGBench with linear-time inference.
AI.motivation: Heuristic stitching of local diffusion predictions produces a non-conservative field that does not correspond to any valid global trajectory log-density, leading to suboptimal long-horizon planning.
AI.method: ECD defines the global trajectory as the minimizer of the sum of local bridge potentials, introducing a conservative correction field and a boundary reaction term. A Markov-based score approximation enables computing the reaction term via a single block-tridiagonal solve with linear time complexity.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art success rates on OGBench stitching tasks while nearly matching the inference speed of heuristic stitching methods.
AI.conclusion: The energy-based formulation with conservative correction and reaction terms is both theoretically sound and practically efficient for compositional diffusion planning.

title: Closure of Self-Determining System Based on Causal and Constitutive Relations
summary: A self-determining system is defined as one in which causes originating within the system influence the system itself. This definition raises the question of how to specify system boundaries. Although the concept of "closure" is commonly used for this purpose, defining boundaries solely in terms of causal relations introduce challenges, such as how to handle external causes and circular causality. To address this issue, we introduce two types of asymmetric relations: causal and constitutive. We propose that system boundaries can be defined as closures of loops formed by these relations, referred to as causal-constitutive loops. By constraining constitutive relations, the resulting system necessarily includes internal causes and thereby satisfies self-determination. Furthermore, to prevent reduction to supervenience, constitutive relations must involve at least two independent variables. This minimal requirement leads to two interdependent loops, which implies a dual-process organization.

AI.tldr: The paper defines self-determining systems through causal-constitutive loops, requiring dual-process organization to avoid supervenience.
AI.motivation: The concept of "closure" for defining system boundaries faces challenges with external causes and circular causality. The authors aim to address these issues by introducing asymmetric relations (causal and constitutive) to define self-determining systems.
AI.method: The authors propose using closures of loops formed by causal and constitutive relations (causal-constitutive loops) to define system boundaries. They impose two constraints: (1) constitutive relations must be constrained to ensure internal causes, and (2) constitutive relations must involve at least two independent variables to prevent reduction to supervenience.
AI.result: System boundaries can be defined as closures of causal-constitutive loops. Constraining constitutive relations ensures self-determination. The minimal requirement of two independent variables leads to interdependent loops and a dual-process organization.
AI.conclusion: Self-determining systems require a dual-process organization with interdependent causal-constitutive loops, preventing reduction to supervenience while maintaining internal causality.

title: Online Learning of Robust Legged Odometry with Minimal Exteroceptive Supervision
summary: Robust locomotion and navigation for legged robots relies heavily on dependable odometry. Traditional multi-sensor fusion for such state estimation requires meticulous sensor calibration and platform-specific kinematic modeling, which complicates deployment. Industrially packaged exteroceptive sensors can provide accurate motion tracking but remain vulnerable to perceptually degraded conditions. We thus develop a plug-and-play, robust legged odometry system that eliminates the need for explicit exteroceptive-to-proprioceptive calibration or system kinematic modeling. Our approach leverages established exteroceptive motion pipelines as a continuous supervisory signal to train an online learned velocity neural network directly from proprioceptive data. An Invariant EKF (InEKF) is then used to fuse the learned proprioceptive or exteroceptive velocity (if any) and IMU data. When exteroception fails due to environmental degradation, the system seamlessly falls back to using the learned proprioceptive model, yielding a resilient legged odometry that readily adapts to new hardware. We demonstrate the platform-agnostic, easily deployable nature of our approach on different quadruped platforms, showcasing promising results in maintaining robust motion estimation across challenging scenarios.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play legged odometry system that eliminates the need for sensor calibration or kinematic modeling. It uses exteroceptive motion pipelines to supervise training of a proprioceptive velocity neural network, fused with IMU via Invariant EKF, with automatic fallback to learned model when exteroception fails.
AI.motivation: Traditional multi-sensor fusion for legged robot odometry requires meticulous sensor calibration and platform-specific kinematic modeling, complicating deployment. Exteroceptive sensors are accurate but vulnerable to perceptually degraded conditions.
AI.method: (1) Train an online learned velocity neural network from proprioceptive data using exteroceptive motion pipelines as supervisory signal. (2) Fuse learned proprioceptive or exteroceptive velocity with IMU via Invariant EKF (InEKF). (3) Automatic fallback to learned proprioceptive model when exteroception fails.
AI.result: Demonstrated platform-agnostic performance on different quadruped platforms, maintaining robust motion estimation across challenging scenarios without explicit calibration or kinematic modeling.
AI.conclusion: The system provides a resilient, easily deployable legged odometry solution that adapts to new hardware and degrades gracefully under perceptual failures.

title: Agentic Time Machine as an Infrastructure for Future-Event Forecasting
summary: Forecasting future events is a critical challenge for large language model (LLM) agents, spanning domains from elections and monetary policy to financial markets. However, evaluating progress on this task presents a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and environment fidelity. While live evaluation benchmarks suffer from an inherently slow feedback loop, existing retrospective replays typically restrict agents to static, pre-frozen databases that sacrifice the environmental realism of actual deployments. To tackle this issue, we introduce Agentic Time Machine (TM), an infrastructure that approximately reconstructs the web state at any chosen past time by filtering post-cutoff content. Leveraging this evaluation infrastructure, we further propose a planner-solver-aggregator multi-agent framework that breaks each question into diverse analytical angles, gathers evidence in parallel, and combines the results into a single forecast. Experiments show that offline scores under TM correlate strongly with live FutureX scores, validating that TM offers a fast and reliable sandbox for forecasting-agent evaluation. On FutureX-Past and Polymarket evaluated under TM, our framework achieves the highest score among strong closed-book, tool-augmented, and self-consistency baselines. On the official FutureX live leaderboard, our system achieves the best average rank over four consecutive weeks, including 1st place in May Week 1. As of June 17, it also ranks 1st on FutureX's official eight-week overall leaderboard.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Agentic Time Machine (TM), an infrastructure that reconstructs past web states for evaluating forecasting agents, along with a planner-solver-aggregator multi-agent framework. TM achieves strong correlation with live benchmarks, and the proposed framework achieves top rankings on FutureX leaderboards.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLM forecasting agents faces a trade-off between efficiency (live benchmarks are slow) and environment fidelity (retrospective replays use static databases lacking realism). The authors aim to provide both fast and realistic evaluation.
AI.method: (1) Agentic Time Machine (TM): reconstructs past web states by filtering post-cutoff content. (2) Planner-solver-aggregator multi-agent framework: breaks questions into analytical angles, gathers evidence in parallel, aggregates results. (3) Validation via correlation between offline TM scores and live FutureX scores.
AI.result: Offline TM scores strongly correlate with live FutureX scores. The proposed framework achieves highest scores on FutureX-Past and Polymarket under TM.
