Achieves best average rank over four weeks on FutureX live leaderboard, including 1st in May Week 1 and 1st on eight-week overall leaderboard as of June 17.
AI.conclusion: TM provides a fast and reliable sandbox for forecasting-agent evaluation. The multi-agent framework demonstrates strong forecasting performance, validated both offline and live.

title: Imitation from Heterogeneous Demonstrations using Grounded Latent-Action World Models
summary: Imitation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning visuomotor policies, but its generalisation and stability are limited by the scale and quality of demonstration data needed. A promising direction is to leverage more abundant but heterogeneous data sources, which differ in action space and often lack action labels altogether. Existing co-training approaches that combine heterogeneous data sources rely on heuristic and hand-engineered alignment techniques. In contrast, we argue that action representations should be grounded in prediction: actions that produce the same effect on the environment should share the same representation, regardless of their sources. To this end, we instantiate this principle by using a grounded latent-action world model (GLAM), a pair of generative models with a shared latent action space across data sources that is grounded by predicting future observations consistently across sources. This latent action space is used to train downstream behavioural cloning (BC) policies which map observations to latent actions and decode them back to robot actions, providing a paradigm for learning from heterogeneous data. Empirically, we demonstrate that GLAM successfully learns an aligned latent action space that facilitates action transfer across data sources with and without action labels. Across five manipulation tasks in simulation and in the real world, GLAM-aligned policies significantly outperform BC baselines and prior latent-action methods, achieving an average of +48% improvement in task success rate with the same data-scarce setting. Videos and code are available at https://viccccciv.github.io/glam/.

AI.tldr: GLAM uses a grounded latent-action world model to learn aligned action representations across heterogeneous data sources by grounding actions in their environmental effects, enabling effective imitation learning from mixed-quality, unlabeled data and achieving +48% average improvement in task success rate over baselines.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning suffers from limited generalization and stability due to the need for large-scale, high-quality demonstration data. The authors aim to leverage more abundant but heterogeneous data sources (differing action spaces, often lacking action labels) without relying on heuristic hand-engineered alignment techniques.
AI.method: GLAM (grounded latent-action world model) uses a pair of generative models with a shared latent action space across data sources, grounded by predicting future observations consistently across sources. This latent space is used to train downstream BC policies mapping observations to latent actions, then decoding back to robot actions.
AI.result: Across five manipulation tasks in simulation and real world, GLAM-aligned policies significantly outperform BC baselines and prior latent-action methods, achieving an average of +48% improvement in task success rate in data-scarce settings.
AI.conclusion: Action representations grounded in prediction (shared latent action space based on environmental effects) enable effective learning from heterogeneous data sources, providing a scalable paradigm for imitation learning without hand-engineered alignment.

title: The AI Evaluability Gap: The Missing Layer for Managing Risk and Sustaining Value
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Conceptual framework paper introducing the AI Evaluability Gap, Evaluability as evidence sufficiency for governance decisions, Operational Certification, Investment Certification, and a six-property evidence lifecycle for AI governance
summary:
Organizations deploying AI face two fundamental governance challenges: managing AI risk and sustaining AI value. Both depend on evidence whose sufficiency cannot be taken for granted. We call the shared underlying challenge the AI Evaluability Gap: the condition in which organizations lack sufficient evidence to support high-confidence governance decisions regarding either risk or value.
  We argue that this gap reflects a category error in current practice. Existing governance approaches focus primarily on properties of systems, such as safety, fairness, reliability, compliance, and value, while paying comparatively little attention to the evidentiary foundations required to justify decisions about those properties. We further argue that AI governance encompasses both operational decisions regarding whether a system may operate and investment decisions regarding whether it merits continued organizational resources.
  To address this problem, we introduce Evaluability, defined as the capability of a system to generate, maintain, and renew evidence sufficient to support high-confidence governance decisions over time. We formalize governance decisions as functions of calibrated confidence Conf(D|E) and identify six properties of evaluable evidence: observability, attributability, intervenability, verifiability, calibration, and temporal validity.
  The framework distinguishes Operational Certification, which relies primarily on structural evidence to justify deployment decisions, from Investment Certification, which relies primarily on causal evidence to justify continued resource allocation. We argue that evidence sufficiency is a missing layer of AI governance and that closing the AI Evaluability Gap is a prerequisite for both managing risk and sustaining value in AI-enabled organizations.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies the "AI Evaluability Gap" — organizations' lack of sufficient evidence to make high-confidence governance decisions about AI risk and value — and proposes a framework centered on "Evaluability" (a system's capability to generate, maintain, and renew evidence) with six properties of evaluable evidence, distinguishing operational vs. investment certification.
AI.motivation: Organizations face dual challenges of managing AI risk and sustaining AI value, yet existing governance approaches focus on system properties (safety, fairness, etc.) while neglecting the evidentiary foundations needed to justify decisions about those properties.
AI.method: The authors identify a category error in current AI governance practice, formalize governance decisions as functions of calibrated confidence Conf(D|E), define six properties of evaluable evidence (observability, attributability, intervenability, verifiability, calibration, temporal validity), and introduce a framework distinguishing Operational Certification (structural evidence for deployment) from Investment Certification (causal evidence for resource allocation).
AI.result: A conceptual framework defining the AI Evaluability Gap, the Evaluability construct, six properties of evaluable evidence, and a two-tier certification distinction (Operational vs. Investment).
AI.conclusion: Evidence sufficiency is a missing layer of AI governance; closing the AI Evaluability Gap is a prerequisite for both managing risk and sustaining value in AI-enabled organizations.

title: Shape-programmable Magnetic Soft Membranes for Mechanically Active Microchannels
comment: Supplementary video can be requested from dakyildiz@wisc.edu
summary: The capability to encode spatially distinct magnetization patterns within soft materials enables remote control over complex deformations. This characteristic is especially important for microfluidic platforms, where limited dynamic control of channel boundaries and laminar flow conditions usually restrict fluid transport and interactions. The present study introduces a shape-programmable magnetic soft membrane actuator as an active microchannel component that can dynamically modulate its shape under magnetic fields and therefore the microfluidic environment. The membrane is magnetically programmed using a template-based approach, which allows it to be controllably deformed in the form of a sinusoid under the influence of an external magnetic field. The membrane's integration into a microchannel converts a passive channel wall into a dynamically changeable interface, allowing active fluid manipulation and enhancing micromixing in laminar flow conditions. The proposed approach establishes a versatile platform for wirelessly controlled deformable interfaces in next-generation microfluidic and lab-on-chip systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a shape-programmable magnetic soft membrane actuator that can dynamically modulate its shape under magnetic fields, serving as an active microchannel component for fluid manipulation and enhanced micromixing in laminar flow conditions.
AI.motivation: Limited dynamic control of channel boundaries and laminar flow conditions in microfluidic platforms restrict fluid transport and interactions, motivating the need for wirelessly controllable deformable interfaces.
AI.method: A magnetic soft membrane is programmed using a template-based approach, enabling controllable sinusoidal deformation under external magnetic fields. The membrane is integrated into a microchannel to convert a passive wall into a dynamically changeable interface.
AI.result: The membrane actuator achieves shape-programmable deformation (e.g., sinusoidal patterns) under magnetic fields, enabling active fluid manipulation and enhanced micromixing in laminar flow.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a versatile platform for wirelessly controlled deformable interfaces in next-generation microfluidic and lab-on-chip systems.

title: Negative Knowledge as Failure-aware Shared Memory for AutoResearch
summary: AI-assisted research systems generate many failed attempts, but those failures rarely become a durable, shared knowledge asset. We propose a negative knowledge memory layer: a curator agent converts each failed attempt into a bounded, typed record in a shared bank, and a downstream research agent explicitly adopts or rejects those records before proposing its next experiment. We evaluate this layer in two settings: same-task retry on ScienceAgentBench and cross-task scientific research on two nonlinear math-physics PDE problems. The negative knowledge layer outperforms vanilla AutoResearch baselines while using fewer tokens; agents with the negative knowledge bank solve new tasks that all baselines fail to solve in PDE systems research. We also show that the previous negative knowledge bank can transfer and enhance AutoResearch on different PDE problems. These results suggest that structured negative knowledge is a knowledge asset that should be explicitly maintained in broader AI-engaged scientific research beyond a memory-compression or debugging aid, alongside positive findings, as a collective infrastructure for scientific memory. Code is available at https://github.com/hch-wang/Negative_Knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a negative knowledge memory layer that curates failed experimental attempts into structured records, enabling AI research agents to learn from past failures. This approach improves performance on ScienceAgentBench and complex PDE problems, even transferring knowledge across tasks, while using fewer tokens than vanilla baselines.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted research produces many failed attempts that are typically discarded rather than reused. The authors argue these failures should become a durable, shared knowledge asset rather than being treated as transient debugging aids.
AI.method: A curator agent converts failed attempts into bounded, typed records stored in a shared negative knowledge bank. A downstream research agent explicitly adopts or rejects these records before proposing the next experiment, creating a structured memory of what does not work.
AI.result: The negative knowledge layer outperforms vanilla AutoResearch baselines while using fewer tokens, solves tasks that all baselines fail on, and demonstrates transfer learning where negative knowledge from previous problems enhances research on different PDE problems.
AI.conclusion: Structured negative knowledge is a valuable knowledge asset that should be explicitly maintained alongside positive findings as collective infrastructure for scientific memory in AI-engaged research.

title: Programmable magnetic soft robots with controlled locomotion and directional liquid cargo release
comment: This manuscript has been accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Magnetically programmable soft elastomers enable complex shape morphing and locomotion dynamics in small scale soft robots under external magnetic fields. Benefiting from their programmed deformation and wireless actuation capabilities, magnetic soft robots have emerged as promising platforms for targeted drug delivery, especially in human gastrointestinal tract. However, achieving controlled directional liquid cargo release toward desired tissue interface while preserving the encoded shape morphing and locomotion capabilities remain a significant challenge. Here, we report a new design strategy that employs an optimized magnetization profile to enable controlled directional release of aqueous cargo without compromising shape morphing and locomotion capabilities. Magnetic soft robots with a specific spatially distributed magnetization profile allow directional alignment of the release interface with the orientation of the external magnetic field. This orientation control ensures active alignment of the release interface toward the intestinal wall prior to drug release. An interconnected microporous elastomer is embedded within the robot for aqueous cargo storage, while a thin microcrystalline wax layer seals the release opening hole to isolate the stored liquid cargo from external environment during transport. Triggered release is achieved by mechanically rupturing the wax sealing layer under a higher magnitude external magnetic field. Controlled directional flipping, locomotion, and triggered release are decoupled through external magnetic field's direction and strength. The controlled directional release strategy reported here integrates directional targeted liquid cargo release, shape morphing, and locomotion, which establishes the groundwork for target drug delivery in gastrointestinal tract applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a magnetically programmable soft elastomer robot that enables controlled directional liquid cargo release, shape morphing, and locomotion for targeted drug delivery in the gastrointestinal tract, using an optimized magnetization profile and a microcrystalline wax sealing layer that can be mechanically ruptured under a higher magnetic field.
AI.motivation: Achieving controlled directional liquid cargo release toward desired tissue interfaces while preserving shape morphing and locomotion capabilities remains a significant challenge in magnetic soft robots for targeted drug delivery in the gastrointestinal tract.
AI.method: The authors use an optimized magnetization profile to enable directional alignment of the release interface with the external magnetic field. An interconnected microporous elastomer stores aqueous cargo, and a thin microcrystalline wax layer seals the release opening. Triggered release is achieved by mechanically rupturing the wax layer under a higher magnitude magnetic field.
AI.result: Controlled directional flipping, locomotion, and triggered release are decoupled through external magnetic field direction and strength, enabling directional alignment of the release interface toward the intestinal wall prior to drug release.
AI.conclusion: The controlled directional release strategy integrates directional targeted liquid cargo release, shape morphing, and locomotion, establishing groundwork for target drug delivery in gastrointestinal tract applications.

title: Coherence Under Commitment: Probing Generalization and Vacuous Memorization in LLM Logical Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed for logical reasoning in knowledge-intensive domains exhibit a subtle but critical failure: coherence can be vacuously achieved through systematic abstention. A model that withholds commitment to either entailment or refutation satisfies negation consistency while providing no utility. We introduce Coherence Under Commitment (CUC), a dual-query evaluation paradigm that jointly measures consistency and decisiveness. CUC contributes three innovations: (1) a commitment score $c(\varphi) = p(\varphi) + p(\lnot\varphi)$ quantifying probability mass allocated to decisive outcomes; (2) a \textbf{deterministic elicitation protocol} via normalized YES/NO log probabilities, eliminating sampling variance; and (3) a 3-way decision framework (True/False/Uncertain) operationalizing the coherence-commitment trade-off into metrics. Experiments on four open-weight LLMs (1B-3B) across 204 FOLIO examples expose a sharp frontier. Qwen2.5-3B achieves near-zero contradiction ($\mathbb{E}[v_{\mathrm{neg}}]{=}0.025$) but only $7.4\%$ coverage, while TinyLlama-1.1B reaches $79.4\%$ coverage with violations on every example. Coherence-only evaluation would rank the abstaining model first; CUC exposes this as vacuous, and the frontier generalizes to LogiQA~v2 ($ρ{=}0.97$). We argue that evaluation must report both coherence and non-vacuous commitment and release a toolkit for standardized assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Coherence Under Commitment (CUC), a dual-query evaluation paradigm that jointly measures LLM consistency and decisiveness in logical reasoning. Experiments on four small LLMs show a sharp trade-off: models can be conflict-free by abstaining (near-zero coverage) or decisive but contradictory. Coherence-only evaluation rewards vacuous abstention; CUC exposes this failure.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed for logical reasoning in knowledge-intensive domains can achieve apparent coherence by systematically abstaining (withholding commitment to entailment or refutation). This satisfies negation consistency but provides no utility, making standard coherence evaluation misleading.
AI.method: CUC is a dual-query evaluation paradigm with three innovations: (1) a commitment score c(φ) = p(φ) + p(¬φ) measuring probability mass on decisive outcomes; (2) a deterministic elicitation protocol using normalized YES/NO log probabilities to eliminate sampling variance; (3) a 3-way decision framework (True/False/Uncertain) operationalizing the coherence-commitment trade-off into metrics.
AI.result: On 204 FOLIO examples across four 1B-3B open-weight LLMs, Qwen2.5-3B achieves near-zero contradiction (𝔼[v_neg]=0.025) but only 7.4% coverage, while TinyLlama-1.1B reaches 79.4% coverage with violations on every example. The frontier generalizes to LogiQA v2 (ρ=0.97).
AI.conclusion: Evaluation must jointly report both coherence and non-vacuous commitment. The paper releases a toolkit for standardized assessment using the CUC framework.

title: RoverDevKit: An open, physics-grounded tradespace toolkit for conceptual design of lunar micro-rovers
summary: Pre-Phase-A design of lunar micro-rovers is dominated by tightly coupled mobility, power, thermal, and mass trades, yet conceptual-design tooling for the rapidly growing sub-50 kg class is typically proprietary, weakly benchmarked, or too slow to drive optimization. We contribute RoverDevKit, an open analytical evaluator coupling terramechanics, mass, power, thermal survival, and traverse that runs in 30ms per mission, fast enough to serve directly as a multi-objective optimizer's fitness function. Across mare, polar, highland, and crater-rim scenarios, NSGA-II Pareto fronts show that the binding design trade changes with mission profile within a single mass class: energy storage dominates at high latitude, slope traction on loose highland regolith, and traverse range on mare and crater-rim missions. Notably, rigid four-wheel layouts Pareto-dominate the full modeled mass range under smooth-regolith range-mass-slope objectives, contrary to the expectation that six-wheel architectures become optimal at heavier masses; six-wheel rocker-bogie layouts enter the Pareto set only once missions impose an obstacle-navigation requirement. The evaluator performance is benchmarked using both component and system checks: the terramechanics kernel matches measured single-wheel drawbar pull within the literature model-form band on two independent datasets, the bottom-up mass model predicts published in-class (5-50 kg) rover masses to 13.3% median absolute error, and a rediscovery check places real micro-rovers near the optimizer's fronts. Propagating the measured terramechanics error through the optimizer leaves the qualitative design rules unchanged. The tool, data, validation artifacts, and figure-generation scripts are released openly.

AI.tldr: RoverDevKit is an open analytical evaluator for sub-50 kg lunar micro-rovers that runs in 30ms per mission, enabling direct use as a multi-objective optimizer's fitness function. NSGA-II Pareto fronts reveal mission-dependent design trades, and rigid four-wheel layouts dominate across most scenarios, with six-wheel designs only needed for obstacle navigation.
AI.motivation: Pre-Phase-A design of lunar micro-rovers involves tightly coupled mobility, power, thermal, and mass trades, but existing conceptual-design tools for the sub-50 kg class are proprietary, weakly benchmarked, or too slow for optimization.
AI.method: Developed RoverDevKit, an open analytical evaluator integrating terramechanics, mass, power, thermal survival, and traverse modeling, running in 30ms per mission. Used NSGA-II multi-objective optimization across mare, polar, highland, and crater-rim scenarios, and validated against measured drawbar pull data, published rover masses, and real micro-rover rediscovery checks.
AI.result: Binding design trade changes with mission profile: energy storage dominates at high latitude, slope traction on loose highland regolith, traverse range on mare and crater-rim missions. Rigid four-wheel layouts Pareto-dominate across the mass range under smooth-regolith objectives; six-wheel rocker-bogie layouts only appear when obstacle navigation is required. Terramechanics kernel matches measured data within model-form band, bottom-up mass model predicts in-class rover masses to 13.3% median absolute error.
AI.conclusion: RoverDevKit enables fast, open, and validated conceptual design optimization for micro-rovers, revealing that optimal architecture depends strongly on mission profile rather than mass alone, and that four-wheel rigid layouts outperform six-wheel designs except when obstacle traversal is required.

title: Repeated post-training is not Self-improving: Diagnosing Scientific Amnesia in Continual DPO Pipelines
summary: Industrial LLM teams often ship behavior updates by repeatedly DPO-training a base model on sequences of related preference-data campaigns. The dominant failure mode in this regime is not always classical catastrophic forgetting: a pipeline may preserve previously learned behaviors while still failing to accumulate reusable methodological knowledge about how to train the next campaign. We call this failure mode scientific amnesia. This paper turns that practitioner intuition into a measurable industrial problem. We contribute: (i) a diagnostic suite for amnesia, (ii) a Program-based pipeline that chains FSDP-sharded DPO checkpoints across Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct runs, (iii) a 30-campaign HumanEval subdomain benchmark, and (iv) a comparative diagnostic study of five strategy proposers: random memory, rule-based scheduling, retrieval-only memory, warm-start Bayesian optimization, and MSCL, a meta-scientific memory and reasoner candidate. Across a single-seed 5-condition * 3-step real-LM chain, 4 of 5 candidates degrade in step-level peak pass@1, including MSCL; only the deliberately conservative rule-based schedule improves. Follow-up pilots qualify rather than overturn this finding: in a heterogeneous chain, MSCL is the only completed candidate that improves, whereas in a small multi-seed homogeneous sweep, retrieval-only has the best mean Delta and no pairwise candidate gap is statistically distinguishable. The contribution is therefore diagnostic, not a claim that MSCL solves the problem: scientific amnesia is observable in a production-like continual-DPO pipeline, and conclusions about interventions depend sharply on chain regime, evaluator design, and seed coverage.

AI.tldr: Industrial LLM teams updating behavior via continual DPO training suffer from "scientific amnesia" — failing to accumulate reusable methodological knowledge across campaigns, not just classical forgetting. This paper provides a diagnostic suite, benchmark, and comparative study showing that amnesia is measurable and that intervention conclusions depend heavily on chain regime, evaluator design, and seed coverage.
AI.motivation: Practitioners observe that continual DPO pipelines degrade not by forgetting old behaviors but by failing to accumulate methodological knowledge about how to train subsequent campaigns. This gap lacks formal measurement and systematic study.
AI.method: The authors construct a diagnostic suite, a Program-based pipeline with FSDP-sharded DPO checkpoints over Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, a 30-campaign HumanEval benchmark, and compare five strategy proposers (random memory, rule-based scheduling, retrieval-only memory, warm-start Bayesian optimization, and MSCL) in a 5-condition × 3-step real-LM chain.
AI.result: In a single-seed 5-condition × 3-step chain, 4/5 candidates degrade (including MSCL); only the conservative rule-based schedule improves. In a heterogeneous chain, MSCL is the only completed candidate that improves. In a multi-seed homogeneous sweep, retrieval-only achieves best mean Delta but no pairwise gaps are statistically distinguishable.
AI.conclusion: Scientific amnesia is measurable in production-like continual DPO pipelines. No single strategy universally solves it; conclusions are sensitive to chain regime, evaluator design, and seed coverage. The contribution is diagnostic rather than a solution claim.

title: A Novel Bio-Inspired Fish Robot with Tunable Stiffness via Particle Jamming
summary: Fish achieve efficient swimming across varied speeds through active modulation of their body flexibility. To explore the effects of tunable stiffness on swimming performance, we present a bio-inspired freely swimming fish robot with a rapidly tunable particle-jamming body. This design enables rapid stiffness adjustments with negligible changes in shape or volume, achieving a 54% variation in flexural rigidity across vacuum pressures of 0 to -40 kPa. We visualize the midline of the oscillating body under both low- and high-stiffness conditions, and the comparison confirms that the body curvature varies with stiffness. We further experimentally evaluate the tunable stiffness body's effects on swimming performance using velocity and cost of transport (CoT) measurements obtained via a motion tracking system. Results show that active stiffness tuning is essential for sustaining efficient and high-speed swimming across beating frequencies of 1-3 Hz. At low frequencies (1-1.5 Hz), a softer body (0 kPa) maximizes velocity and minimizes CoT, whereas at high frequencies (2.5-3 Hz), a stiffer body (-40 kPa) delivers superior velocity and reduced transport cost. These findings highlight stiffness modulation as a key strategy for adaptive and efficient propulsion in bio-inspired robotic swimmers.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a bio-inspired fish robot with a rapidly tunable particle-jamming body that achieves 54% variation in flexural rigidity. Experimental results show that softer bodies maximize velocity and minimize cost of transport at low frequencies (1-1.5 Hz), while stiffer bodies perform better at high frequencies (2.5-3 Hz), demonstrating that active stiffness tuning is essential for efficient swimming across different speeds.
AI.motivation: Fish achieve efficient swimming across varied speeds through active modulation of body flexibility, and the authors aim to explore the effects of tunable stiffness on swimming performance in a bio-inspired robotic system.
AI.method: A freely swimming fish robot with a rapidly tunable particle-jamming body was designed, enabling rapid stiffness adjustments with negligible shape/volume changes. The body's midline oscillation was visualized under low- and high-stiffness conditions, and swimming performance was evaluated via velocity and cost of transport (CoT) measurements using a motion tracking system across beating frequencies of 1-3 Hz and vacuum pressures of 0 to -40 kPa.
AI.result: The design achieved a 54% variation in flexural rigidity. Body curvature varied with stiffness. At low frequencies (1-1.5 Hz), softer bodies (0 kPa) maximized velocity and minimized CoT; at high frequencies (2.5-3 Hz), stiffer bodies (-40 kPa) delivered superior velocity and reduced transport cost.
AI.conclusion: Active stiffness tuning is essential for sustaining efficient and high-speed swimming across different frequencies, highlighting stiffness modulation as a key strategy for adaptive and efficient propulsion in bio-inspired robotic swimmers.

title: Self-Improvement Can Self-Regress: The Rise-and-Collapse Failure Mode of LLM Self-Training
summary:
Self-improvement can self-regress. In REINFORCE post-training for code, a model can quickly improve on its optimized metric and then collapse within the same training campaign. We study this in a controlled multi-seed testbed using Qwen-2.5-3B and Qwen-2.5-7B, trained on competitive-programming tasks with binary CodeGrader reward across 10 sequential 20-step campaigns. Across campaigns, pass@1 shows a robust rise-then-collapse pattern: it peaks within tens of gradient steps and then falls back, sometimes to near zero. This is not cross-task catastrophic forgetting, but within-task policy over-optimization on a fixed distribution; KL- and EWC-style constraints do not prevent it.
  We ask where the control loop should sit. We compare three levels: CARE, a between-campaign memory mechanism with a capability posterior, transfer gate, and regression-aware belief revision; ES, a within-campaign early-stop rule that rolls forward the peak checkpoint and sets the next budget to peak_step+3; and GRPO, which changes the RL update using group-relative reward normalization.
  The answer is regime-dependent. On Qwen-2.5-3B, where naive REINFORCE is fragile, CARE v2 nearly doubles end-of-chain pass@1 from 4.9% to 9.5%, with paired bootstrap 95% CI [+0.4,+8.9] and gains in 4/5 seeds. On Qwen-2.5-7B, CARE reaches parity with naive REINFORCE, 13.8% vs. 11.8%, while ES reaches 22.2% [14.1,28.0]. Out-of-the-box GRPO reaches 20.7% [15.7,25.1], nearly matching REINFORCE+ES.
  GRPO raises the floor but does not remove the cliff. Its 7B gain mainly comes from better between-campaign carryover, while the within-campaign peak-to-end gap remains about 17 points under both REINFORCE and GRPO. GRPO+ES gives mixed evidence: 2/3 seeds improve, but one final cliff lowers the mean to 17.0% [0.0,28.1]. A Gemma-3-4B pilot shows the same signature, suggesting the phenomenon is not limited to Qwen.

AI.tldr: Self-improvement via REINFORCE in code post-training can cause rapid performance gains followed by collapse (rise-then-cliff pattern). Three control strategies (CARE, ES, GRPO) are tested across Qwen-2.5-3B/7B, with regime-dependent results: CARE helps fragile 3B models, ES and GRPO help 7B models, but GRPO does not eliminate within-campaign collapse.
AI.motivation: To investigate and characterize the phenomenon where REINFORCE-based self-improvement for code generation leads to initial gains followed by performance collapse, and to identify where in the training loop control mechanisms should be placed to mitigate this.
AI.method: Multi-seed testbed with Qwen-2.5-3B/7B on competitive-programming tasks using binary CodeGrader reward across 10 sequential 20-step campaigns. Compared three control levels: CARE (between-campaign memory with capability posterior and belief revision), ES (within-campaign early-stop rolling forward peak checkpoint), and GRPO (group-relative reward normalization).
AI.result: On Qwen-2.5-3B, CARE v2 nearly doubles end-of-chain pass@1 from 4.9% to 9.5%. On Qwen-2.5-7B, ES reaches 22.2% and GRPO 20.7%, vs. naive REINFORCE 11.8%. GRPO raises the floor but within-campaign peak-to-end gap remains ~17 points. GRPO+ES shows mixed results due to final cliff. Gemma-3-4B pilot replicates the pattern.
AI.conclusion: The optimal control loop placement is regime-dependent: between-campaign memory (CARE) benefits smaller/fragile models, while within-campaign early-stop (ES) or GRPO benefits larger models. GRPO mitigates but does not eliminate collapse; the rise-then-cliff phenomenon is general across model families.

title: Rotation-Aware Point-Cloud Embeddings for Vision-Based In-Hand Reorientation
summary: Point-cloud goals provide a direct way to specify dexterous in-hand reorientation: instead of defining an object-specific pose frame or estimating 6D pose at test time, the policy is given the desired 3D geometry of the object. Yet raw point-cloud goal conditioning is poorly conditioned for policy learning. Current and goal clouds are unordered, independently sampled, and often visibility-dependent, so their discrepancy entangles object rotation with permutation, resampling, and unstable correspondence structure. For this reason, prior point-cloud manipulation methods typically add structure outside the representation itself, such as explicit pose or relative-pose inputs, dense flow features, or distillation from privileged teachers. We close this gap by learning a rotation-aware point-cloud embedding whose Euclidean latent distance is calibrated to the SO(3) geodesic error between object orientations. The resulting representation turns current-goal comparison into a smooth control signal, allowing a model-free RL policy to act from current and goal point-cloud embeddings, proprioception, and centroid metadata, without object pose, relative pose, dense flow, or teacher-action supervision. In in-hand reorientation experiments, this interface matches privileged-state and distillation-based baselines while avoiding brittle test-time computation of structured pose or flow inputs. These results suggest that point-cloud goals become practical for this task when the representation, rather than an external module, encodes the task-relevant geometry of rotation. We also show evidence that generic visual point-cloud pretraining is insufficient for such a current-goal comparison because it discards the task-relevant state and preserves only shape features.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a rotation-aware point-cloud embedding that enables model-free RL policies to perform dexterous in-hand reorientation from point-cloud goals alone, without requiring explicit pose, flow, or teacher supervision.
AI.motivation: Point-cloud goal conditioning is poorly conditioned for policy learning because current and goal clouds are unordered, independently sampled, and visibility-dependent, making their discrepancy entangle object rotation with permutation, resampling, and unstable correspondence structure. Prior methods compensate by adding external structure (pose, flow, distillation).
AI.method: A rotation-aware point-cloud embedding is learned whose Euclidean latent distance is calibrated to the SO(3) geodesic error between object orientations. This representation converts current-goal comparison into a smooth control signal for model-free RL, using current/goal embeddings, proprioception, and centroid metadata only.
AI.result: The method matches privileged-state and distillation-based baselines in in-hand reorientation tasks while avoiding brittle test-time computation of structured pose or flow inputs. Generic visual point-cloud pretraining is shown insufficient for such current-goal comparison.
AI.conclusion: Point-cloud goals become practical for dexterous in-hand reorientation when the representation itself, rather than an external module, encodes the task-relevant rotation geometry.

title: Answer Engineering: Local Trajectory Editing for Protocol-Constrained Decision Making in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models can produce confident but protocol-invalid answers in domains where procedural compliance is critical. This paper presents Answer Engineering, a deterministic runtime and authoring layer that applies localized rule-guided interventions to the visible reasoning trajectory during standard autoregressive generation, without retraining, modifying model weights, or performing global search. The method is evaluated on a controlled clinical benchmark for sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL), where correct management depends on protocol-consistent interpretation of symptom timing, Weber/Rinne tuning-fork findings, and otoscopic findings. In the benchmark, step-by-step reasoning shifted rather than eliminated errors: compliant outcomes for SSNHL decreased from 54.5% under unguided generation to 25.1%, while acceptance on the conductive contrast condition increased from 1.6% to 58.9%. Local trajectory editing increased SSNHL compliance to 83.5% and conductive-case adherence to 77.9%, raising balanced accuracy from 42.0% under reasoning-only generation to 80.7%. The results support a systems-level view in which protocol adherence can be improved through auditable runtime control of reasoning trajectories, while also identifying limitations caused by rule coverage, trigger reliability, and persistent diagnosis-first generation dynamics.

AI.tldr: Answer Engineering is a deterministic runtime layer that applies rule-guided interventions to LLM reasoning trajectories, improving protocol compliance on a clinical SSNHL benchmark from 42.0% to 80.7% balanced accuracy without retraining or weight modification.
AI.motivation: Large language models produce confident but protocol-invalid answers in domains requiring procedural compliance (e.g., clinical diagnosis). Existing methods (retraining, weight modification, global search) are costly or impractical. There is a need for lightweight, auditable runtime control to enforce domain-specific protocols during generation.
AI.method: Answer Engineering: a deterministic runtime and authoring layer that applies localized rule-guided interventions to the visible reasoning trajectory during standard autoregressive generation, without retraining, modifying weights, or global search. Evaluated on a controlled clinical benchmark for sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) with protocol-consistent interpretation of symptom timing, Weber/Rinne findings, and otoscopic findings.
AI.result: Unguided reasoning shifted errors: SSNHL compliance dropped from 54.5% to 25.1%; conductive-case acceptance rose from 1.6% to 58.9%. Local trajectory editing increased SSNHL compliance to 83.5%, conductive-case adherence to 77.9%, and balanced accuracy from 42.0% (reasoning-only) to 80.7%.
AI.conclusion: Protocol adherence can be improved through auditable runtime control of reasoning trajectories. Limitations remain due to rule coverage, trigger reliability, and persistent diagnosis-first generation dynamics. Supports a systems-level view of compliance in LLM outputs.

title: THREAD: Trajectory Planning for Hybrid Rigid-Soft Manipulators with Environment-Aware Diffusion
summary: Manipulation in confined environments, such as threading a manipulator through narrow apertures, remains a fundamental challenge, especially for conventional rigid robots. Hybrid rigid-soft manipulators offer promise but face two compounding planning challenges: backbone shapes feasible in free space become infeasible under environmental contact, and planning rigid and soft segments independently ignores their kinematic coupling. We present THREAD, the first diffusion-based trajectory planner for hybrid manipulation, learning a generative prior over physically realizable backbone trajectories conditioned on local environment geometry, with physics-inspired losses encoding curvature, smoothness, and collision constraints jointly across both segments. Trained in simulation, THREAD achieves 92.4% task success with 5x fewer collisions than the strongest baseline. We show cross-embodiment real-world transfer with minimal online updates, successfully threading through apertures as small as 1.3x the soft segment diameter.

AI.tldr: THREAD is a diffusion-based trajectory planner for hybrid rigid-soft manipulators that learns a generative prior over physically realizable backbone trajectories conditioned on local environment geometry, achieving 92.4% task success with 5x fewer collisions than baselines and real-world transfer through apertures as small as 1.3x the soft segment diameter.
AI.motivation: Manipulation in confined environments (e.g., threading through narrow apertures) remains challenging for conventional rigid robots. Hybrid rigid-soft manipulators show promise but face two compounding planning challenges: backbone shapes feasible in free space become infeasible under environmental contact, and planning rigid and soft segments independently ignores their kinematic coupling.
AI.method: THREAD is a diffusion-based trajectory planner that learns a generative prior over physically realizable backbone trajectories conditioned on local environment geometry. It uses physics-inspired losses encoding curvature, smoothness, and collision constraints jointly across both rigid and soft segments.
AI.result: Achieves 92.4% task success with 5x fewer collisions than the strongest baseline. Demonstrates cross-embodiment real-world transfer with minimal online updates, successfully threading through apertures as small as 1.3x the soft segment diameter.
AI.conclusion: THREAD effectively addresses the coupled planning challenges of hybrid rigid-soft manipulators in confined spaces by using a diffusion-based generative approach with physics-inspired joint constraints, enabling high success rates and real-world transfer.

title: PulseCX: Breaking the Closed-World Assumption in Real-Time CX
summary: Conversational AI agents in Customer Experience (CX) typically suffer from a Closed-World Constraint, ignoring high-velocity external shifts like viral trends or outages. Ad-hoc web search attempts to bridge this gap but often introduce prohibitive latency and context poisoning. We introduce PulseCX, a framework that decouples knowledge acquisition from consumption. Adopting a structure-first paradigm, PulseCX employs an asynchronous agent to linearize signals into a Decay-Aware Temporal Knowledge Graph (DA-TKG) governed by reinforcement--decay dynamics to actively manage information lifecycles. By coupling this self-evolving memory with hierarchical intent gating, PulseCX removes synchronous search bottlenecks (<10ms overhead) and drives significant gains in Intent Resolution (IRR) and Customer Satisfaction (s-CSAT) in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: PulseCX introduces a framework that decouples knowledge acquisition from consumption using a Decay-Aware Temporal Knowledge Graph with reinforcement-decay dynamics and hierarchical intent gating, achieving <10ms overhead and significant improvements in Intent Resolution and Customer Satisfaction for dynamic CX environments.
AI.motivation: Conversational AI agents in Customer Experience suffer from a Closed-World Constraint, ignoring high-velocity external shifts (e.g., viral trends, outages). Ad-hoc web search attempts to bridge this gap but introduces prohibitive latency and context poisoning.
AI.method: PulseCX decouples knowledge acquisition from consumption using a structure-first paradigm: an asynchronous agent linearizes signals into a Decay-Aware Temporal Knowledge Graph (DA-TKG) governed by reinforcement-decay dynamics for active lifecycle management, coupled with hierarchical intent gating to remove synchronous search bottlenecks.
AI.result: The framework achieves <10ms overhead and drives significant gains in Intent Resolution (IRR) and Customer Satisfaction (s-CSAT) in dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: PulseCX effectively addresses the Closed-World Constraint in conversational AI agents by decoupling knowledge pipelines, enabling low-latency, adaptive responses to real-world shifts without context poisoning.

title: SurGE: Surrogate Gradient-guided Evolution for Co-design of Legged Robots with Parallel Elasticity
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication at IROS 2026. Website at https://arcad-lab-um.github.io/surge-codesign/
summary: Co-design of legged robots with elastic elements is challenging due to the non-differentiability of contact dynamics and mechanism engagement. This paper presents SurGE, a framework that computes surrogate gradients of the design objective through a differentiable pipeline consisting of a kinodynamic single-rigid-body (Kino-SRB) model and a design-aware control policy, and injects them into CMA-ES via mean shift with cosine-annealed step decay. On a 4-DOF design space of a hopping robot with unidirectional parallel spring, SurGE achieves 6 times lower cross-seed standard deviation and 18% tighter population concentration compared to vanilla CMA-ES, while matching or improving the best objective. Hardware experiments on a 2D design subspace show that, starting from a hand-tuned initial design, SurGE reduces the design objective by 37.65% on hardware, with the improvement trend identified in simulation transferring consistently to the physical system. SurGE provides the potential to accelerate non-differentiable co-design problems in legged robots via surrogate model gradients.

AI.tldr: SurGE is a framework that uses surrogate gradients from a differentiable kinodynamic model and design-aware control policy to guide CMA-ES optimization for co-designing legged robots with elastic elements, achieving lower variance, tighter convergence, and successful hardware transfer.
AI.motivation: Co-design of legged robots with elastic elements is challenging due to the non-differentiability of contact dynamics and mechanism engagement, making gradient-based optimization infeasible.
AI.method: SurGE computes surrogate gradients through a differentiable pipeline (Kino-SRB model + design-aware control policy) and injects them into CMA-ES via mean shift with cosine-annealed step decay.
AI.result: On a 4-DOF hopping robot design space, SurGE achieves 6× lower cross-seed standard deviation and 18% tighter population concentration vs. vanilla CMA-ES. On hardware (2D subspace), it reduces the design objective by 37.65% from a hand-tuned initial design.
AI.conclusion: SurGE accelerates non-differentiable co-design problems in legged robots by leveraging surrogate model gradients, with simulation trends transferring consistently to physical hardware.

title: Learning Burst-Aware Early Warning Models for Capacity Stress under AI Workload Surges in Hyperscale Data Centers
summary: The rapid growth of large-scale AI workloads, particularly Large Language Model (LLM) training and inference, is fundamentally reshaping the operational dynamics of hyperscale data centers. Unlike traditional cloud workloads, AI-driven jobs exhibit bursty, high-intensity, and rapidly shifting resource demands, often leading to sudden capacity stress that cannot be effectively handled by reactive threshold-based mechanisms. In this paper, we propose a deployment-oriented, burst-aware early warning framework for proactive capacity stress prediction under AI workload surges. We formulate the problem as a high-recall forecasting task over multivariate telemetry windows, with the explicit goal of enabling operational intervention before system degradation occurs. The proposed framework integrates workload intensity, temporal variation, and system pressure signals, and employs a lightweight tree-based learning model to capture nonlinear interactions in highly imbalanced environments. To evaluate the system under realistic conditions, we introduce an AI workload surge injection methodology that simulates burst-driven demand patterns observed in large-scale AI systems. Our XGBoost-based model achieves an ROC AUC of 0.697 and an AP of 0.670, significantly outperforming baseline methods. Under deployment-oriented threshold selection, the framework achieves a Recall of 0.914, enabling the detection of the majority of stress-prone periods with acceptable false-alarm cost. Beyond predictive performance, we show how the proposed framework can be integrated into operational control loops to support proactive actions such as workload throttling and resource scaling. Our results highlight the practical value of high-recall, learning-based early warning systems in enabling resilient and adaptive data center operations in the era of AI-driven workloads.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a burst-aware early warning framework using XGBoost to proactively predict capacity stress in hyperscale data centers caused by AI workload surges, achieving 0.914 recall and enabling preemptive operational interventions like throttling and scaling.
AI.motivation: AI workloads (LLM training/inference) exhibit bursty, high-intensity resource demands that reactive threshold-based mechanisms cannot handle effectively, causing sudden capacity stress in hyperscale data centers.
AI.method: A deployment-oriented, burst-aware early warning framework that formulates capacity stress prediction as a high-recall forecasting task over multivariate telemetry windows. Uses XGBoost to model nonlinear interactions between workload intensity, temporal variation, and system pressure signals. Includes an AI workload surge injection methodology for realistic evaluation.
AI.result: XGBoost model achieves ROC AUC of 0.697 and AP of 0.670. Under deployment-oriented threshold selection, Recall reaches 0.914, detecting most stress-prone periods with acceptable false-alarm cost.
AI.conclusion: The framework can be integrated into operational control loops for proactive actions like workload throttling and resource scaling, demonstrating the practical value of high-recall learning-based early warning systems for resilient AI-driven data center operations.

title: Predictive Gaze Is Preserved but Reorganized toward Monitoring during Robot-Mediated Manipulation
summary: Goal-directed eye movements are a fundamental component of visuomotor control, enabling humans to anticipate and guide their actions. Whether this anticipatory and task-driven behavior is preserved when actions are executed through a robot rather than through one's own body remains unclear. Here we address this question by investigating gaze behavior during goal-directed telemanipulation to determine how visuomotor control adapts to altered embodiment. Our findings show that gaze remains strongly aligned with task goals, preserving its predictive role even during robot-mediated manipulation. At the same time, teleoperation systematically redistributes visual attention toward the robotic end-effector and manipulated objects, increasing online monitoring. These findings show that predictive gaze is not lost under altered embodiment, but reorganized in response to changes in sensory feedback and control demands. More broadly, they reveal the flexibility of the human visuomotor system when the natural sensorimotor coupling is disrupted and identify gaze as an informative signal for inferring action intentions in human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: Gaze remains predictive and task-aligned during robot-mediated teleoperation, but visual attention shifts more toward the robotic end-effector and objects, indicating reorganization rather than loss of predictive gaze under altered embodiment.
AI.motivation: To determine whether anticipatory, goal-directed gaze behavior—a key feature of natural visuomotor control—is preserved when actions are executed through a robot rather than one's own body.
AI.method: Investigated gaze behavior during goal-directed telemanipulation tasks, comparing visuomotor control under natural and robot-mediated conditions.
AI.result: Gaze remains strongly aligned with task goals and preserves its predictive role; however, teleoperation redistributes visual attention toward the robotic end-effector and manipulated objects, increasing online monitoring.
AI.conclusion: Predictive gaze is not lost under altered embodiment but reorganized in response to changes in sensory feedback and control demands. Gaze is an informative signal for inferring action intentions in human-robot interaction.

title: Trip+: Benchmarking Agents in Personalized Interactive Travel Planning
summary: Interactive travel planning has become a popular use case for language models. Agents are deployed to manage evolving preferences and unexpected disruptions over multiple turns. Such settings require models to make complex, profile-conditioned planning decisions. However, existing benchmarks often evaluate feasibility, personalization, or interaction in relatively isolated settings. We therefore introduce Trip+ to measure the ability of agents to plan travel holistically. In Trip+, given traveler profiles and dynamic interactions, agents must generate and revise minute-level itineraries. End-to-end traveler experiences are evaluated via an LLM-based simulator, enabling the assessment of subjective metrics like fatigue. Our scenarios range from simple request resolutions to complex environment-driven replanning. We evaluate 18 LMs and find a consistent gap in experiential quality. Models favor technically feasible but exhausting itineraries that diverge sharply from profiled traveler preferences.

AI.tldr: Trip+ is a new benchmark for evaluating language model agents on holistic, interactive travel planning with profile-conditioned, minute-level itinerary generation and revision, evaluated via an LLM simulator on feasibility, personalization, and experiential quality.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate feasibility, personalization, or interaction in relatively isolated settings, lacking a holistic measure of travel planning agents' ability to handle evolving preferences and unexpected disruptions over multiple turns.
AI.method: Trip+ uses traveler profiles and dynamic interactions, requiring agents to generate and revise minute-level itineraries. An LLM-based simulator evaluates end-to-end traveler experiences, including subjective metrics like fatigue. Scenarios range from simple request resolutions to complex environment-driven replanning.
AI.result: Evaluated 18 language models and found a consistent gap in experiential quality. Models favor technically feasible but exhausting itineraries that diverge sharply from profiled traveler preferences.
AI.conclusion: Current language models struggle to balance feasibility with subjective experiential quality in interactive travel planning, tending toward exhausting itineraries that ignore traveler profiles.

title: CoRDE: Concept-Prior Routed Diffusion Experts for Structural Generalization in Robot Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: Diffusion models excel at capturing multi-modal action distributions in robot imitation learning. However, in multi-task and long-horizon scenarios, monolithic architectures lack structural generalization capabilities, suffering from gradient conflicts between distinct semantic sub-stages. While pure data-driven Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) methods introduce labor division, they frequently trigger routing collapse, and instantiating full-scale experts causes parameter explosion and high expansion costs. To address these issues, we propose Concept-prior Routed Diffusion Experts (CoRDE), a structure-guided variational distillation framework. CoRDE extracts semantic distributions from a frozen concept encoder to guide the variational posterior responsibility via a learnable soft mapping matrix. This mechanism introduces an entropy-controlled responsibility inference process that encourages confident routing under reliable semantic predictions while preserving the stochastic diffusion term for behavioral diversity. To overcome parameter inflation, CoRDE employs a parameter-efficient expert pool using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a shared frozen backbone. Theoretical analysis shows that the mixture score discrepancy is bounded by responsibility-weighted local expert errors, supporting high-fidelity generation under low-rank expert adaptation. Empirical evaluations confirm that, compared to existing baselines, CoRDE systematically reduces routing collapse, forming robust, semantically aligned expert allocations while achieving superior action quality and incremental learning efficiency.

AI.tldr: CoRDE proposes a concept-prior routed diffusion expert framework that uses semantic guidance from a frozen concept encoder to prevent routing collapse in Mixture-of-Experts for robot imitation learning, while employing LoRA-based parameter-efficient experts to avoid parameter explosion.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion models for robot imitation learning lack structural generalization in multi-task and long-horizon scenarios due to gradient conflicts between distinct semantic sub-stages; pure MoE methods suffer from routing collapse and parameter explosion.
AI.method: CoRDE extracts semantic distributions from a frozen concept encoder to guide variational posterior responsibility via a learnable soft mapping matrix, uses entropy-controlled responsibility inference, and employs a parameter-efficient expert pool via LoRA on a shared frozen backbone.
AI.result: CoRDE systematically reduces routing collapse, forms robust semantically aligned expert allocations, and achieves superior action quality and incremental learning efficiency compared to existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed structure-guided variational distillation framework with concept-prior routing and LoRA-based experts effectively addresses structural generalization and parameter efficiency in multi-task robot imitation learning.

title: Whistleblowing and the machine -- towards a considered position
comment: Presented at AAMAS-26 Workshop on Rebellion and Disobedience in AI, see https://sites.google.com/view/rad-ai/rad-ai/cfp?authuser=0
summary: Artificial intelligent agents and autonomous systems are embedded in our environments. They are both a commercial product and a personal tool that generates a lot of data and can draw conclusions from it: machines generate and keep secrets. But should machines protect all secrets? It has been shown that artificial agents are able to whistleblow and it has been argued that digital multi-agent environments should allow for agents in them to whistleblow. We argue that machine whistleblowing must be normative and principled and routed in the existing understanding of whistleblowing as an important rule-breaking mechanism in society. We also argue that there is a need for government regulators to formulate an informed stance on both what machines should be allowed to whistleblow on and how to legally protect those who develop whistleblowing machines

AI.tldr: This paper argues that machine whistleblowing in AI systems must be principled, normative, and grounded in existing whistleblowing theory, while calling for government regulation to define what machines can whistleblow on and legally protect developers of such systems.
AI.motivation: AI agents generate and keep secrets, and while prior work shows agents can whistleblow, there is a lack of normative grounding and regulatory framework for this capability.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis drawing on existing whistleblowing theory and its application to artificial agents in multi-agent environments.
AI.result: The paper establishes that machine whistleblowing must be principled and normative, and identifies the need for regulatory stances on what machines should whistleblow about and legal protections for developers.
AI.conclusion: Government regulators must formulate an informed stance on machine whistleblowing, including permissible targets and legal protections for whistleblowing machine developers.

title: RARM: Confidence-Gated Progress Reward Modeling for RL in Manipulation
summary: Reinforcement learning for robot manipulation is often bottlenecked by reward design, especially in long-horizon tasks: sparse success rewards provide weak supervision, while hand-crafted dense rewards are tedious to design and generalize poorly across tasks. Progress-based reward models offer a promising alternative by estimating how far an observation has advanced toward task completion, but existing approaches often require task-specific demonstrations or progress labels, and can assign high rewards to visually plausible but physically incorrect states. We introduce the Reference-Anchored Reward Model (RARM), a lightweight visual comparator that converts a single successful demonstration into a dense, progress-aware reward. RARM is trained once on general-purpose videos with a contrastive temporal objective, requiring no robot-specific data, task-specific reward labels, or per-task reward engineering. At deployment, RARM matches rollout clips to reference clips and rewards only confident forward progress, suppressing uncertain matches that may otherwise produce false-positive rewards. Across 9 simulated manipulation tasks from LIBERO and MetaWorld and 4 real-world tasks, RARM achieves the best overall success rates in subsequent RL training, with particularly large gains on long-horizon tasks such as cloth folding, where unreliable progress estimates are especially harmful.

AI.tldr: RARM is a lightweight visual comparator that converts a single successful demonstration into a dense, progress-aware reward for robot manipulation RL. It is trained once on general-purpose videos with a contrastive temporal objective, requires no task-specific data or reward engineering, and achieves best success rates across 9 simulated and 4 real-world tasks, with large gains on long-horizon tasks like cloth folding.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for robot manipulation is bottlenecked by reward design: sparse success rewards provide weak supervision in long-horizon tasks, while hand-crafted dense rewards are tedious to design and generalize poorly.
AI.method: RARM is a lightweight visual comparator trained once on general-purpose videos using a contrastive temporal objective. At deployment, it matches rollout clips to reference clips from a single successful demonstration and rewards only confident forward progress, suppressing uncertain matches that could produce false-positive rewards.
AI.result: Across 9 simulated manipulation tasks (LIBERO, MetaWorld) and 4 real-world tasks, RARM achieves the best overall success rates in RL training, with particularly large gains on long-horizon tasks such as cloth folding.
AI.conclusion: RARM provides an effective, generalizable alternative to hand-crafted dense rewards or sparse rewards by converting a single demonstration into a dense progress signal without task-specific engineering or data requirements.

title: ARCO: Adaptive Rubric with Co-Evolution for Multi-Step LLM-Based Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning for multi-step LLM agents often relies on scalar rewards that indicate success but cannot explain why a trajectory is good or bad. Rubric-based rewards improve interpretability through natural-language criteria, but existing methods score at the trajectory level and freeze the scorer behind a closed-source judge, leaving step-level credit assignment unresolved and the judge itself static. We propose ARCO (Adaptive Rubric CO-evolution), a rubric framework in which a same-scale model $μ$ shares a backbone with two heads: a generation head that produces per-step criteria, and a score head that predicts rubric-conditioned step-level rewards. A trajectory decomposition constraint ties the sum of step rewards to the terminal outcome, enabling credit assignment without step-level labels, while $μ$ and the policy $π$ are jointly updated on on-policy data so that the rubric content and the scoring function co-evolve at the parameter level. Across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with two open-source backbones, ARCO improves the best EM in every setting over strong outcome-, rubric-, and process-reward baselines, and analyses show that its rubrics are step-specific, robust to design choices, and useful for diagnosing agent behavior. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/zihangtian/ARCO.

AI.tldr: ARCO introduces an adaptive rubric co-evolution framework where a shared-backbone model jointly learns to generate per-step criteria and predict rubric-conditioned step-level rewards, enabling parameter-level co-evolution with the policy via a trajectory decomposition constraint, achieving state-of-the-art results on multi-hop QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing rubric-based rewards improve interpretability over scalar rewards but score at trajectory level using a frozen closed-source judge, failing to provide step-level credit assignment and lacking adaptability.
AI.method: ARCO uses a same-scale model μ with a shared backbone and two heads: a generation head producing per-step criteria and a score head predicting rubric-conditioned step-level rewards. A trajectory decomposition constraint ties sum of step rewards to terminal outcome, enabling step-level credit without labels. μ and policy π are jointly updated on on-policy data for parameter-level co-evolution.
AI.result: ARCO achieves the best EM across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with two open-source backbones, outperforming outcome-, rubric-, and process-reward baselines.
AI.conclusion: ARCO's rubrics are step-specific, robust to design choices, and useful for diagnosing agent behavior; the framework solves step-level credit assignment while enabling adaptive co-evolution of both rubric content and scoring function.

title: Deep RL- Tuned Mo del-Free Adaptive Control for Lower-Limb Exoskeletons During Sit-to-Stand Transitions
summary: Sit-to-stand (STS) transitions impose significant joint-loading demands on elderly individuals, making them a primary target for lower-limb exoskeleton assistance. However, accurate trajectory tracking during STS is challenging due to complex, time-varying human exoskeleton interaction dynamics and inter-subject variability that render model-based control approaches difficult to apply in practice. This paper presents an intelligent model free adaptive backstepping control strategy for a bilateral lower-limb exoskeleton during STS motion. The proposed controller design uses an ultra-local second-order model to avoid explicit system identification, while a Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) neural network estimates the unknown lumped dynamics online. To further improve phase-aware tracking performance, a Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) reinforcement learning agent is integrated as a supervisory gain scheduler that adaptively adjusts controller gains across the distinct phases of STS motion. The proposed controller is evaluated through co-simulation in MATLAB/Simulink and Simscape Multibody using OpenSim-derived reference trajectories and benchmarked against state-of-the-art controllers. Results demonstrate that the proposed controller achieves the lowest average RMSE of 0.078 degree across all joints, representing improvements of 60.2%, 54.4%, 48.7%, and 42.6% over proportional integral derivative (PID), model-free adaptive control (MFAC), linear quadratic regulator (LQR), and sliding-mode control (SMC), respectively. TD3 integration further reduces tracking error by 35%, 33%, and 79% at the hip, knee, and ankle joints compared to the standalone RBF-MFAC baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed controller design for assistive exoskeleton control during STS transitions.

AI.tldr: An intelligent model-free adaptive backstepping controller with RBF neural network and TD3 reinforcement learning gain scheduling is proposed for lower-limb exoskeleton control during sit-to-stand transitions, achieving 60.2% better RMSE (0.078°) than PID and substantial improvements over other controllers in co-simulation.
AI.motivation: Sit-to-stand transitions impose high joint-loading demands on elderly individuals, making them a key target for exoskeleton assistance. However, accurate trajectory tracking is challenging due to complex, time-varying human-exoskeleton interaction dynamics and inter-subject variability, which render model-based control impractical.
AI.method: An intelligent model-free adaptive backstepping control strategy is designed using: (1) an ultra-local second-order model to avoid explicit system identification, (2) a Gaussian RBF neural network for online estimation of unknown lumped dynamics, and (3) a TD3 reinforcement learning agent as a supervisory gain scheduler to adaptively adjust controller gains across distinct STS motion phases.
AI.result: The proposed controller achieves the lowest average RMSE of 0.078° across all joints, outperforming PID (60.2%), MFAC (54.4%), LQR (48.7%), and SMC (42.6%). TD3 integration reduces tracking error by 35% (hip), 33% (knee), and 79% (ankle) over the standalone RBF-MFAC baseline in co-simulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model-free, learning-based controller demonstrates effectiveness and robustness for assistive exoskeleton control during STS transitions, offering a practical solution that avoids system identification while adapting to phase-varying dynamics.

title: Towards Dys-XAI: Influence-Based Explanations for Dysarthria Severity Assessment
summary: Dysarthria severity assessment is essential for therapy planning and longitudinal monitoring, yet manual perceptual rating is time-consuming and variable across clinicians. Although deep learning models achieve strong performance, their black-box nature limits clinical adoption. Existing speech explainability methods typically provide acoustic feature importance scores that are difficult for end-users to interpret. We propose an influence-based, instance-level explainability framework that explains each decision through supportive and competing training samples. Using gradient-based influence approximations, we compute per-utterance influence scores to identify supportive and competing training samples for each prediction. Controlled deletion experiments from 5 to 20 percent validate the explanations, showing that removing highly influential samples systematically shifts predictions. This approach provides auditable explanations by linking decisions to perceptible reference cases.

AI.tldr: Proposes an influence-based explainability framework for dysarthria severity assessment that explains decisions via supportive and competing training samples, enabling auditable explanations through reference cases.
AI.motivation: Manual perceptual rating of dysarthria severity is time-consuming and variable; deep learning models are black-box, limiting clinical adoption; existing speech explainability methods provide hard-to-interpret acoustic feature importance scores.
AI.method: Gradient-based influence approximations to compute per-utterance influence scores, identifying supportive and competing training samples for each prediction; controlled deletion experiments (5-20%) validate explanations.
AI.result: Removing highly influential samples systematically shifts predictions, validating the explanation quality through controlled deletion experiments.
AI.conclusion: Provides auditable, clinically interpretable explanations by linking model decisions to perceptible reference cases, enhancing trustworthiness for clinical adoption.

title: A Multimodal Tiltwing Framework for Bioinspired Aerial Robots
summary: Tailless flapping-wing micro-aerial vehicles (FWMAVs) mimic the impressive flight performance of hummingbirds, utilising unsteady aerodynamic effects. However, existing designs are still limited and purpose-built with a restricted flight envelope and poor endurance. We therefore propose an adaptable tiltwing framework enabling bioinspired aerial robots to switch between hovering flight, high-speed directional flight, and energy-efficient gliding flight. The proposed framework utilises thrust vectoring with a wide actuation range via two fully independent propulsion units, each flapping a single wing, for effective control and enhanced manoeuvrability. For this, we developed a hybrid Scotch-yoke-based flapping mechanism that ensures a symmetric motion profile with a modular design guaranteeing an arbitrarily wide flapping angle to exploit the lift-enhancing clap-and-fling effect. Additionally, we implemented a passive wing-rotation mechanism, which, in combination with our dual-wing thrust-vectoring approach, allows unprecedented wing-design freedom, unlocking potential for precise optimisation. A contactless leading-edge tracking sensor provides accurate feedback on the wing's orientation and, in the gliding mode, enables dihedral-angle control, augmenting the active wing-pitch control. Extensive testing of a propulsion unit was conducted with a six-axis force/torque sensor, demonstrating the flapping mechanism's performance while optimising transmission efficiency and the passive wing-pitch mechanism. At full throttle, the average lift force generated by a single wing, flapping with a 188° amplitude, was 21.1 gf for a small 3.1 g 1S BLDC motor. Additional tests covering the full range of the wide-angle tilting capability showed an effective thrust-vectoring control architecture with a linear and symmetric response curve of the moments generated.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptable tiltwing framework for tailless flapping-wing micro-aerial vehicles (FWMAVs) that enables switching between hovering, high-speed directional flight, and energy-efficient gliding. The framework uses thrust vectoring via two independent propulsion units with a hybrid Scotch-yoke flapping mechanism, passive wing rotation, and contactless tracking sensors. Experimental results show 21.1 gf lift from a single wing at full throttle with a 188° flapping amplitude.
AI.motivation: Existing tailless FWMAVs are limited by purpose-built designs with restricted flight envelopes and poor endurance. The goal is to develop a versatile platform that can transition between multiple flight modes (hover, high-speed, glide) to expand operational capabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose a tiltwing framework with two independent propulsion units (each flapping a single wing) for thrust vectoring. A hybrid Scotch-yoke mechanism provides symmetric motion and wide flapping angles for the clap-and-fling effect. Passive wing rotation and a contactless leading-edge tracking sensor enable wing-orientation feedback and dihedral-angle control in gliding mode.
AI.result: At full throttle, a single wing with 188° flapping amplitude generated 21.1 gf average lift using a 3.1 g 1S BLDC motor. Thrust-vectoring testing showed linear and symmetric moment response across the full tilting range, validating effective control architecture.
AI.conclusion: The proposed tiltwing framework with dual independent flapping units and thrust vectoring offers a promising approach to achieving multi-modal flight (hover, directional, glide) in tailless FWMAVs, with demonstrated lift performance and control linearity.

title: Social World Model for Lifelong Social Intelligence
summary:
Social intelligence is a core competency for language agents, yet current research primarily focuses on static capability evaluation rather than how these skills are continuously shaped and accumulated. This gap calls for a shift toward sustainable learning paradigms. Currently, two methodological pain points exist: social interaction trajectories lack unified structured representations to form iterable learning signals, and capability improvement and retention are typically studied in isolation, hindering the assessment of continuous evolution.
  To bridge this gap, we propose the Social World Model. We decompose social interaction into five dimensions (scene setting, observation, mental state, action, and dialogue) to build a closed-loop learning framework. In this setup, agents collect interaction experiences, convert them into preference signals for model updating, and redeploy the updated policy for continued learning. Additionally, we provide a reusable data synthesis mechanism and a lifelong learning benchmark, transforming social capabilities from an "object of evaluation" into an "object of sustainable training".
  Validating our framework on the ASCENT-Bench, the interactively trained Qwen2.5-7B model outperforms its baseline across all five core metrics. Notably, it matches the closed-source Gemini 3 Flash in completion rate, exceeds it in pass rate, and achieves zero forgetting across three difficulty levels. Unlike prior works that merely report static comparisons or capability decay, this end-to-end approach provides a trainable, verifiable, and retainable pathway, demonstrating that small open-source models can sustainably acquire competitive social coordination capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Social World Model that decomposes social interaction into five dimensions to create a closed-loop learning framework, enabling sustainable training of language agents. Using a reusable data synthesis mechanism and lifelong learning benchmark, the Qwen2.5-7B model trained on ASCENT-Bench outperforms baselines across all metrics, matches Gemini 3 Flash in completion rate, exceeds it in pass rate, and achieves zero forgetting.
AI.motivation: Current research focuses on static capability evaluation of social intelligence in language agents rather than sustainable learning paradigms. Two pain points exist: (1) social interaction trajectories lack unified structured representations for iterable learning signals, and (2) capability improvement and retention are studied in isolation, hindering assessment of continuous evolution.
AI.method: The Social World Model decomposes social interaction into five dimensions: scene setting, observation, mental state, action, and dialogue. It builds a closed-loop learning framework where agents collect interaction experiences, convert them into preference signals for model updating, and redeploy the updated policy for continued learning. Also provides a reusable data synthesis mechanism and lifelong learning benchmark.
AI.result: On ASCENT-Bench, interactively trained Qwen2.5-7B outperforms its baseline across all five core metrics, matches Gemini 3 Flash in completion rate, exceeds it in pass rate, and achieves zero forgetting across three difficulty levels.
AI.conclusion: This end-to-end approach provides a trainable, verifiable, and retainable pathway for sustainable social capability acquisition. Demonstrates that small open-source models can sustainably acquire competitive social coordination capabilities, transforming social intelligence from an "object of evaluation" into an "object of sustainable training."

title: GeoFlow-SLAM++: A Robust Multi-Camera Visual-Inertial SLAM System with Relocalization
