Results show AgentCAT achieves effective ability estimation, and its selection strategy balances difficulty adaptation and instructional coherence, aligning with human pedagogical intuition.

AI.tldr: AgentCAT is a multi-agent LLM-based simulation system for Computerized Adaptive Testing that overcomes limitations of static offline data and isolated component optimization by modeling the complete dynamic testing process with examinee, selection, and supervisor agents.
AI.motivation: Existing CAT research is limited by static offline data with partial labels and isolated component optimization (e.g., selection or diagnosis), failing to model the holistic dynamic interaction process of adaptive testing.
AI.method: AgentCAT uses three LLM-based modules: (1) examinee agent with memory retrieval and Chain-of-Thought reasoning for response simulation; (2) selection agent using coarse-to-fine bucketing and knowledge graph exploration for balanced difficulty and coverage; (3) supervisor agent with dual-auditing and robust update for convergence and validity.
AI.result: On two real-world datasets across macro-level ability convergence, micro-level interaction logic, and data sparsity resilience, AgentCAT achieves effective ability estimation and selection strategies that balance difficulty adaptation with instructional coherence.
AI.conclusion: AgentCAT demonstrates that multi-agent LLM simulation can effectively model dynamic CAT processes, producing results aligned with human pedagogical intuition while overcoming previous static data constraints.

title: Any-Body Guard: Universal Safeguarding for Manipulation Policies via Action Masking
summary: Ensuring safety of learning-enabled robotic manipulation across diverse embodiments and tasks still requires significant manual engineering. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristically designed fallback controllers or complex forward invariance assessments. These methods are often too conservative for task success, too computationally expensive for real-time execution, too heuristic to provide useful safety guarantees, or too engineering-heavy to transfer between setups. In this paper, we propose a universal safeguarding approach, X-Safe, which reasons directly in the robot's configuration space to provide formal probabilistic guarantees for collision avoidance. By operating in the configuration space, our method transfers across embodiments while relying solely on an object-based, quasi-static scene representation and a forward kinematics model of the robotic manipulator. Thus, X-Safe provides useful formal safety guarantees without requiring additional data, or engineering effort for different embodiments or scenes. We demonstrate X-Safe for diverse embodiments and policies, both in simulation and on hardware. We observe less degradation in task performance compared to state-of-the-art safeguarding, no collisions on hardware experiments, and empirically corroborate our formal guarantees.

AI.tldr: X-Safe is a universal safeguarding approach for robotic manipulation that provides formal probabilistic collision-avoidance guarantees by reasoning directly in configuration space, requiring only a quasi-static scene representation and forward kinematics, thus transferring across embodiments without additional engineering.
AI.motivation: Existing safety methods for learning-enabled robotic manipulation are either too conservative, computationally expensive, heuristic, or engineering-heavy to transfer across different embodiments and tasks.
AI.method: X-Safe operates in the robot's configuration space, using an object-based quasi-static scene representation and a forward kinematics model to provide formal probabilistic guarantees for collision avoidance.
AI.result: Demonstrated across diverse embodiments and policies in simulation and hardware; less task performance degradation vs. state-of-the-art safeguarding, zero collisions in hardware experiments, and empirical corroboration of formal guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Configuration-space reasoning enables effective, transferable safety guarantees for robotic manipulation without requiring additional data or engineering per embodiment or scene.

title: Measuring What Persists: Conditioning Mechanisms and a Geometric Framework for AI Agent Identity
summary:
AI agents in long-context applications drift from their specified identity. Current methods detect this only after qualitative degradation is visible. We present a geometric framework for measuring identity structure using $\sqrt{\mathrm{JSD}}$ metric spaces and magnitude homology from enriched category theory, where identity is non-geodesic structure and drift is its relaxation toward the geodesic.
  Validated on a persistent AI agent, the framework's strongest empirical finding is a two-mechanism conditioning structure: cross-condition distances reveal an identity-vacuum cluster where the identity specification fills a behavioral void, and a safety-basin cluster where it displaces from post-training attractors. An equilateral probe baseline confirms that the identity specification creates measurable behavioral richness (55 unique response patterns vs. 1 for the base model) at maximum probe separation. A first-order perturbation theory for equilateral configurations predicts magnitude changes from perimeter changes alone, with shape perturbations first-order cancelled by the $S_n$ symmetry; the formula is self-consistent at the observed perturbation amplitudes.
  A drift experiment measuring magnitude decrease under context pressure was subsequently found to reflect repetitive-padding artifacts rather than genuine context-length drift; diverse padding produces no measurable deformation through 150K tokens. The magnitude homology framework's full diagnostic promise -- detecting anisotropic contraction and structural collapse via homological simplification -- is architecturally grounded in the perturbation theory and selection rules but remains empirically unconfirmed.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a geometric framework using √JSD metric spaces and magnitude homology to detect identity drift in AI agents. It identifies two behavioral mechanisms (identity-vacuum and safety-basin clusters), shows identity creates behavioral richness (55 vs. 1 patterns), but finds that observed drift was actually padding artifacts rather than genuine context-length drift. The full diagnostic framework remains empirically unconfirmed.
AI.motivation: Current methods detect identity drift in long-context AI agents only after qualitative degradation is already visible; there is no formal geometric framework for early detection or structural characterization of identity deviation.
AI.method: Uses √JSD metric spaces and magnitude homology from enriched category theory to model identity as non-geodesic structure and drift as relaxation toward the geodesic. Validated on a persistent AI agent with equilateral probe baselines and first-order perturbation theory under S_n symmetry.
AI.result: Identified two conditioning mechanisms: identity-vacuum and safety-basin clusters. Identity specification creates 55 unique response patterns vs. 1 for base model. However, observed drift magnitude decrease was due to repetitive-padding artifacts, not genuine context-length drift; diverse padding shows no deformation through 150K tokens. Perturbation theory is self-consistent at observed amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: The magnitude homology framework's diagnostic potential (detecting anisotropic contraction, structural collapse) is theoretically grounded but empirically unconfirmed. The paper demonstrates the framework's richness but its central drift-detection claim was undermined by experimental artifacts.

title: FlowDPG: Deterministic Policy Gradient on Flow Matching Policies for Real-World Manipulation
summary: Real-world reinforcement learning for robotic manipulation remains challenging, and this difficulty is amplified for flow matching policies: applying policy gradient methods to these policies is fundamentally limited by the need to backpropagate through time(BPTT) along the multi-step ODE that maps noise to actions, which is computationally prohibitive and numerically fragile. We propose FlowDPG, a DDPG-style method specifically designed for flow matching policies that distills the critic gradient into the velocity field at training time, bypassing BPTT entirely. Intuitively, FlowDPG combines two complementary vectors: the demonstration-driven velocity that keeps the action feasible, and the critic-driven correction that steers it toward higher value. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a BPTT-free distillation framework that enables stable DDPG-style policy improvement on flow matching policies, (2) a formal connection between the FlowDPG update direction and vanilla Deterministic Policy Gradient via three explicit approximations, and (3) real-world validation on a long-horizon, multi-stage, dual-arm AirPods assembly task, where FlowDPG attains a 92% end-to-end success rate, substantially outperforming recent RL methods spanning value-conditioning, auxiliary-module adaptation, and adjoint-based critic-gradient approaches. Videos and more results are provided on the project page https://flowdpg.github.io.

AI.tldr: FlowDPG is a DDPG-style reinforcement learning method for flow matching policies in robotic manipulation that avoids backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) by distilling critic gradients into the velocity field at training time, achieving 92% success on a dual-arm AirPods assembly task.
AI.motivation: Applying policy gradient methods to flow matching policies is fundamentally limited by the need to backpropagate through time (BPTT) along the multi-step ODE that maps noise to actions, which is computationally prohibitive and numerically fragile.
AI.method: FlowDPG: A DDPG-style method that distills the critic gradient into the velocity field at training time, bypassing BPTT entirely. It combines demonstration-driven velocity (for feasibility) with critic-driven correction (for higher value). The method establishes a formal connection to vanilla DPG via three explicit approximations.
AI.result: 92% end-to-end success rate on a long-horizon, multi-stage, dual-arm AirPods assembly task, substantially outperforming recent RL methods including value-conditioning, auxiliary-module adaptation, and adjoint-based critic-gradient approaches.
AI.conclusion: FlowDPG provides a BPTT-free distillation framework for stable DDPG-style policy improvement on flow matching policies, validated through real-world robotic manipulation.

title: ForEx: A Formal Verification Framework for Explainable Reasoning in Logical Fallacy Detection and Annotation
comment: 2026 IEEE 27th International Conference on Information Reuse and Integration for Data Science
summary: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) on logical fallacy detection focus on predicted labels, but do not establish whether those labels are supported by the reasoning the models provide. We propose ForEx (Formal Verification for Explainable Reasoning), a framework that translates LLM-generated explanations into Lean4 and verifies whether the translated rationale is derivable under encoded premises, not the logical validity of the original natural language argument. To distinguish prediction outcomes from the formal status of the supporting reasoning, we introduce the LLM Argument Verification Matrix, which separates label consistency from formal verification status. Experiments on LOGIC-Climate show that over 90% of LLM outputs can be translated into formal reasoning chains that pass verification, while agreement with human annotations remains around 20%. These results expose a systematic gap between formal derivability and label agreement, a distinction invisible to prediction-based metrics. ForEx moves LLM evaluation beyond label correctness toward machine-checkable analysis of formalized reasoning chains.

AI.tldr: ForEx translates LLM-generated explanations for logical fallacy detection into Lean4 and formally verifies whether the reasoning is derivable, revealing that over 90% of outputs pass formal verification while agreement with human labels remains only ~20%.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of LLMs on logical fallacy detection only assess predicted labels without checking whether the models' supporting reasoning is logically sound.
AI.method: ForEx translates LLM-generated explanations into Lean4 formal proofs and verifies derivability under encoded premises. It introduces the LLM Argument Verification Matrix to separate label correctness from formal reasoning validity.
AI.result: Over 90% of LLM outputs translate into formally verifiable reasoning chains, but human-annotated label agreement is only around 20%, exposing a gap between formal derivability and label correctness.
AI.conclusion: ForEx moves LLM evaluation beyond label-based metrics toward machine-checkable, formal verification of reasoning chains.

title: EmbodiedUS-FS: Fast Slow Intelligence for Ultrasound Robotics
summary: Robotic ultrasound scanning in real clinical environments requires both high-level clinical workflow reasoning and low-level closed-loop execution. Physicians natural-language instructions often contain implicit anatomical targets, procedural logic, image-quality requirements, and safety constraints, while execution is affected by patient motion, contact variations, and target drift. We propose a fast and slow hierarchical embodied ultrasound system for safe and interpretable robotic ultrasound assistance. The Slow Brain performs intent parsing and stage-wise task planning with knowledge augmentation from an API and handbook corpus, and generates executable plans through task-graph construction and structured plan verification. The Fast Brain fuses multimodal feedback, including ultrasound images, robot pose and force states, and patient-motion information, to refine local actions and perform image-quality-guided recovery behaviors. The system further integrates a Safety Shield and a hierarchical escalation policy to constrain risky actions and trigger replanning or human confirmation under persistent failures or safety-bound violations. Experiments on planning evaluation, closed-loop execution under dynamic perturbations, and safety-mechanism validation demonstrate that the proposed hierarchical design improves task success rates while reducing safety violations.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical fast-and-slow embodied ultrasound system (Slow Brain for planning, Fast Brain for execution) with Safety Shield and escalation policy that improves task success and reduces safety violations in real clinical environments.
AI.motivation: Robotic ultrasound in real clinical settings requires both high-level clinical workflow reasoning (interpreting implicit instructions, procedural logic) and low-level closed-loop execution (handling patient motion, contact variations, target drift), which existing systems handle inadequately.
AI.method: Slow Brain: intent parsing + stage-wise task planning with API/handbook knowledge augmentation, task-graph construction, and structured plan verification. Fast Brain: multimodal fusion (US images, robot pose/force, patient motion) for local action refinement and image-quality-guided recovery. Safety Shield + hierarchical escalation policy for risky action constraint, replanning, or human confirmation.
AI.result: Experiments on planning, closed-loop execution under dynamic perturbations, and safety validation show improved task success rates and reduced safety violations.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical fast-slow design with safety mechanisms effectively enables safe and interpretable robotic ultrasound assistance in real clinical settings.

title: AgentRiskBOM: A Risk-Scoping Security Bill of Materials for Agentic AI Systems
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Cybersecurity and AI-Based Systems (Cyber-AI 2026)
summary: Agentic AI systems retrieve private context, invoke tools, write files, call external services, coordinate with other agents, and may act without human approval. Existing bill of materials artifacts improve transparency for dependencies, model metadata, and training provenance, but leave an agentic transparency gap: capability opacity, the absence of a structured account of what a deployed agent can access, remember, change, delegate, and prove afterward. This paper introduces AgentRiskBOM, a security BOM for risk-scoping tool-using AI agents. It is an additive layer over SBOM, AIBOM, and MLBOM artifacts, referencing them where authoritative while adding fields for runtime authority: autonomy, tool permissions, memory, credential scope, approval gates, audit signals, inter-agent communication, and external action capability. We implement AgentRiskBOM as a JSON-schema artifact with a reproducible corpus, risk scenarios, scorer, diff detector, control mapper, and reports. We evaluate AgentRiskBOM on 13 open-source agents spanning coding, RAG, and multi-agent archetypes, plus 52 risk scenarios across 14 categories. The schema validates all 13 corpus artifacts. Coverage analysis gives AgentRiskBOM a native-equivalent score of 14 across 16 capability dimensions, vs. 1 for SBOM, 1.5 for AIBOM and 2 for MLBOM. Across modeled risk categories, AgentRiskBOM exposes 100% risk-category visibility vs. 10.5% for SBOM-like and 20.9% for AIBOM-like views. To test agentic authority drift, we inject 33 structured deployment mutations; the diff detector identifies the correct change type for all mutations. A secondary penalty-based scorer yields a Spearman correlation of 0.73 with the primary scorer, supporting rank-level consistency while showing that thresholds require human calibration. The results show that agentic AI security needs a machine-readable authority-and-risk artifact before incidents occur.

AI.tldr: AgentRiskBOM is a new security BOM artifact that fills the agentic transparency gap by providing structured information about AI agent runtime authority (autonomy, permissions, memory, credentials, etc.). Evaluated on 13 open-source agents and 52 risk scenarios, it achieves 100% risk-category visibility (vs. ~10-21% for existing BOMs), detects all 33 deployment mutations correctly, and shows strong rank consistency (Spearman 0.73) with a penalty-based scorer.
AI.motivation: Existing BOM artifacts (SBOM, AIBOM, MLBOM) capture dependencies, model metadata, and training provenance but fail to address capability opacity—the lack of a structured account of what a deployed agent can access, remember, change, delegate, and prove after acting. This gap leaves agentic AI systems with no machine-readable risk-scoping mechanism before incidents occur.
AI.method: The paper introduces AgentRiskBOM as an additive JSON-schema layer over existing BOMs, adding fields for runtime authority (autonomy, tool permissions, memory, credential scope, approval gates, audit signals, inter-agent communication, external action capability). It includes a reproducible corpus, risk scenarios, scorer, diff detector, control mapper, and reports. Evaluation covers 13 open-source agents across coding, RAG, and multi-agent archetypes with 52 risk scenarios across 14 categories and 33 structured deployment mutations.
AI.result: Schema validates all 13 corpus artifacts. Coverage analysis: AgentRiskBOM scores 14/16 capability dimensions vs. 1 (SBOM), 1.5 (AIBOM), 2 (MLBOM). Risk-category visibility: 100% vs. 10.5% (SBOM-like) and 20.9% (AIBOM-like). The diff detector identifies correct change type for all 33 deployment mutations. Secondary penalty-based scorer yields Spearman 0.73 with primary scorer.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI security requires a machine-readable authority-and-risk artifact deployed before incidents occur. AgentRiskBOM demonstrates that existing BOM paradigms are insufficient for agentic systems, and the proposed additive layer provides comprehensive risk visibility and drift detection, though threshold calibration still needs human judgment.

title: Tactile Genesis: Exploring Tactile Sensors at Scale for Learning Dexterous Tasks
summary: Tactile sensing is critical for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, yet it remains unclear which tactile abstractions a policy needs and when richer tactile fields justify their hardware cost. This is hard to study empirically: each sensor effectively defines a new robot, and no lab can replicate the same learning experiment across all of them. We present Tactile Genesis, a GPU-parallel tactile sensor simulation platform that exposes binary contact, contact depth, per-taxel kinematic force/torque, elastomer marker displacement, geometry-aware proximity, contact audio, and a voxelized temperature field (the first of its kind in robot learning physics simulation platforms) under a common interface, with configurable placement, resolution, and a realistic noise model (drift, hysteresis, dead taxels, crosstalk). It scales past 20,000 parallel environments and 1,000 taxels on a single GPU, improving throughput by 3 to 20 times over previous tactile simulators. We train teacher-student policies on three dexterous tasks, ablating sensor type, placement, resolution, and noise, and verify transfer to the real XHand1. Proprioception alone is insufficient on every task. Sensor placement dominates sensor type: fingertip-only coverage trails whole-hand coverage by a wide margin, while adding the palm and proximal phalanges closes most of the gap to the privileged teacher. Resolution matters far less than coverage: placing 200 taxels across the whole hand suffices across tasks. We find that force/torque per taxel is consistently the most useful sensor type. These results give concrete guidance for both future tactile hardware design for improving robot hands and policy-side observation choice in dexterous manipulation. https://neuroagents-lab.github.io/2026-tactile-genesis/

AI.tldr: Tactile Genesis is a GPU-parallel tactile sensor simulation platform supporting up to 20,000 parallel environments and 1,000 taxels, enabling systematic ablation studies across sensor types, placements, resolutions, and noise models. Key findings: proprioception alone is insufficient, sensor placement dominates sensor type, force/torque per taxel is the most useful modality, and coverage matters far more than resolution.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear which tactile abstractions a policy needs and whether richer tactile fields justify their hardware cost, as each sensor defines a new robot and no lab can replicate learning experiments across all sensor types.
AI.method: Developed Tactile Genesis, a GPU-parallel simulation platform with binary contact, contact depth, per-taxel force/torque, marker displacement, proximity, audio, and voxelized temperature field under a common interface with configurable placement, resolution, and noise model. Trained teacher-student policies on three dexterous tasks with ablations over sensor type, placement, resolution, and noise, with real-world transfer to XHand1.
AI.result: Platform scales past 20,000 parallel environments and 1,000 taxels on a single GPU, improving throughput 3-20× over prior simulators. Proprioception alone insufficient; sensor placement dominates sensor type; fingertip-only trails whole-hand coverage; 200 taxels across whole hand suffices; force/torque per taxel is the most useful sensor type.
AI.conclusion: Provides concrete guidance for tactile hardware design and policy-side observation choices in dexterous manipulation: prioritize whole-hand coverage over resolution, and force/torque sensing over other modalities.

title: Learning the ARTS of Search for Automated Discovery
summary: Scientific discovery can be formulated as an iterative search process over the space of hypotheses and experiments. Contemporary methods navigate this space using heuristics such as MCTS. These algorithms conflate the merit of a hypothesis with the quality of its experimental execution. A promising hypothesis with preliminary execution is therefore ranked below a modest hypothesis whose execution is refined. Moreover, prior methods prune the search logs as the search progresses because the accumulated history outgrows the context window. We propose Agentic Reasoning for Tree Search (ARTS), where we deploy a reasoning language model to navigate this space. The model inspects prior execution logs, diagnoses whether earlier failures arose from faulty implementations or bad hypotheses, and selects the hypothesis to build on next. To mitigate challenges with context length, ARTS uses test-time training to instill the knowledge of search tree in the model weights. Across 22 tasks from MLGym and MLEBench, we show that ARTS outperforms leading algorithms, with over 15.3% relative improvement in the normalized score. With test-time training we show that a Qwen3-4B agent can match performance with closed-source frontier models like Gemini-3 Pro and GPT o3-reasoning with upto 5x lower inference cost. We further observe that on partially observable RL tasks, the test-time trained Qwen3-4B scientist surpasses ARTS with the o3 scientist by rediscovering the human-best recurrent-memory solution that heuristic methods prune away.

AI.tldr: ARTS uses a reasoning LLM agent with test-time training to navigate the hypothesis-experiment search space, outperforming heuristic methods like MCTS by distinguishing hypothesis merit from execution quality and avoiding search log pruning. It achieves 15.3% relative improvement, and a 4B parameter model matches frontier models at 5x lower cost, even rediscovering human-best solutions in RL tasks that heuristics miss.
AI.motivation: Prior methods (e.g., MCTS) conflate hypothesis merit with execution quality, ranking promising hypotheses with preliminary execution below modest ones with refined execution. They also prune search logs as history grows, losing valuable information.
AI.method: ARTS deploys a reasoning LLM that inspects prior execution logs, diagnoses whether failures stem from faulty implementations or bad hypotheses, and selects which hypothesis to build on next. It uses test-time training to encode search tree knowledge into model weights, avoiding context window limitations.
AI.result: ARTS outperforms leading algorithms across 22 tasks with >15.3% relative improvement in normalized score. A Qwen3-4B agent with test-time training matches Gemini-3 Pro and GPT o3-reasoning at up to 5x lower inference cost. On partially observable RL tasks, the test-time trained Qwen3-4B surpasses ARTS with o3 scientist by rediscovering the human-best recurrent-memory solution that heuristic methods prune away.
AI.conclusion: Test-time training enables small models to match or exceed frontier closed-source models in scientific discovery search, while avoiding the pruning pitfalls of heuristic methods like MCTS.

title: Multi-AUV Marine Life Tracking with Single Hydrophone Payloads via a Hidden Markov Model Equipped Particle Filter
summary: Researchers tag and track marine animals to study migration patterns, human impacts on behavior, and behavioral shifts due to climate change. Accurate data collection often requires tagging individual animals to collect spatio-temporal state estimates of the animal's geo-position and depth. Acoustic transmitters are prominent due to their continuous communication without requiring retrieval or surfacing to collect data. These transmitters emit underwater acoustic pulses that can be detected by hydrophones. However, the frequent movement of aquatic animals results in high data loss when the animal moves out of the detection range of a stationary hydrophone. Autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) systems offer a solution for localizing transmitters with higher resolution over longer periods of time. Such systems previously deployed have often required multiple hydrophones mounted on a large frame carried by the AUV. This increases drag, limiting the speed at which the AUV can track highly mobile animals. This work provides an alternative by equipping multiple AUVs with a single compact hydrophone payload. A particle filter algorithm equipped with a hidden Markov model (HMM) behavioral motion model fuses measurements from multiple AUVs to estimate the transmitter's position. Real-world data shows a root mean square error (RMSE) of approximately 10 meters for short-term deployments, and a larger simulated dataset shows an RMSE of approximately 15 meters for longer deployments over a larger area. The HMM fit to historical animal movement data outperforms a generic velocity motion model, and both outperform a baseline random walk motion model.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-AUV system with compact hydrophones and a particle filter with HMM-based motion model to localize acoustic transmitters for tracking marine animals, achieving ~10m RMSE in real-world tests and ~15m in simulations, outperforming baseline motion models.
AI.motivation: Existing AUV-based tracking systems use large hydrophone arrays that increase drag and limit speed, making it difficult to track highly mobile aquatic animals. The authors aim to provide a low-drag alternative using multiple AUVs each carrying a single compact hydrophone.
AI.method: Multiple AUVs equipped with single compact hydrophones collect acoustic pulse detections. A particle filter algorithm with a hidden Markov model (HMM) behavioral motion model (fitted to historical animal movement data) fuses measurements across AUVs to estimate transmitter position.
AI.result: Real-world data shows ~10m RMSE for short-term deployments; simulated data over larger areas shows ~15m RMSE. The HMM motion model outperforms a generic velocity motion model, and both outperform a random walk baseline.
AI.conclusion: The multi-AUV single-hydrophone approach offers a viable, low-drag alternative for tracking acoustically tagged marine animals with competitive localization accuracy, and using behavior-informed motion models significantly improves tracking performance.

title: Holmes: Multimodal Agentic Diagnosis for Mixed-Language Mobile Crashes at Industrial Scale
summary: Diagnosing mobile crashes in ultra-large-scale industrial applications is a formidable challenge due to the sheer volume of code, the complexity of mixed-language environments, and the inability to reproduce failures locally. Traditional static analysis struggles with scalability, while existing LLM-based agents often rely on reproducible environments unavailable in post-mortem scenarios. We present Holmes, a multi-agent system that automates root cause analysis by synthesizing multimodal runtime signals--stack traces, logs, and thread states--to reconstruct failure contexts without reproduction. Holmes introduces a hierarchical Retrieve-Explore-Reason architecture that leverages low-level artifacts (e.g., registers, assembly) to bridge the semantic gap between open-source business logic and closed-source system frameworks. By dynamically compressing the search space using runtime clues, Holmes precisely navigates 70-million-line codebases to identify non-local defects. Evaluated on real-world crashes from WeChat, Holmes achieves 87.6% accuracy in function-level fault localization and reduces average investigation time by over 98% (to ~77 seconds), demonstrating its effectiveness in transforming labor-intensive debugging into an efficient verification workflow.

AI.tldr: Holmes is a multi-agent system that automates root cause analysis of mobile crashes in ultra-large-scale industrial applications (like WeChat with 70M+ lines of code) by synthesizing multimodal runtime signals (stack traces, logs, thread states, low-level artifacts) without requiring crash reproduction, achieving 87.6% function-level fault localization accuracy and reducing investigation time by over 98% to ~77 seconds.
AI.motivation: Diagnosing mobile crashes in ultra-large-scale industrial applications is extremely challenging due to massive code volume, mixed-language environments, and inability to reproduce failures locally. Traditional static analysis cannot scale, and existing LLM-based agents depend on reproducible environments unavailable in post-mortem scenarios.
AI.method: Holmes uses a multi-agent system with a hierarchical Retrieve-Explore-Reason architecture that synthesizes multimodal runtime signals (stack traces, logs, thread states, registers, assembly) to reconstruct failure contexts without reproduction. It dynamically compresses the search space using runtime clues to navigate 70-million-line codebases and bridges the semantic gap between open-source business logic and closed-source system frameworks via low-level artifacts.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-world crashes from WeChat, Holmes achieves 87.6% accuracy in function-level fault localization and reduces average investigation time by over 98% (to approximately 77 seconds).
AI.conclusion: Holmes effectively transforms labor-intensive debugging into an efficient verification workflow for ultra-large-scale industrial mobile applications, demonstrating that automated root cause analysis is feasible without crash reproduction by leveraging multimodal runtime signals and hierarchical reasoning.

title: Benchmarking Robot Memory Under Interference
summary: Robots deployed in realistic settings will accumulate experience across many sessions and tasks over their deployment. The robot's tasks may often require it to remember information from multiple sessions ago, making long-context robot memory important for real-world deployments. However, most robot-memory benchmarks today are based on single episodes or a short context. To measure how current robot memory systems perform on longer sessions with more distractions, we introduce RoboMME-Interference, a cross-session benchmark built on RoboMME. For each query episode, we construct a session history using the query's relevant prior demonstration followed by a controlled number of unrelated sessions, which we provide to the VLA as memory and measure accuracy. Running RoboMME's released memory-augmented $π_{0.5}$ variants unmodified through this benchmark, we find that while perceptual memory variants improve success when given the history without any distractors, they decay strongly and steadily as unrelated sessions accumulate. With this release, we emphasize the importance of long-context memory and robustness to interference and show that current systems largely fail on such capabilities. The project page, videos, code, and data are at https://robotmemorybench.com.

AI.tldr: RoboMME-Interference is a benchmark evaluating robot memory systems across long sessions with distractions. Tests on memory-augmented $π_{0.5}$ variants show performance decays as unrelated sessions increase, revealing current systems lack robustness to interference.
AI.motivation: Real-world robots operate across many sessions and need long-context memory, but existing benchmarks only test single-episode or short-context memory.
AI.method: Built cross-session benchmark on RoboMME; each query episode is paired with a relevant prior demonstration plus controlled numbers of unrelated sessions, fed to VLAs as memory to measure accuracy.
AI.result: Perceptual memory variants succeed without distractors but degrade strongly and steadily as unrelated sessions accumulate.
AI.conclusion: Long-context memory and robustness to interference are underevaluated; current systems largely fail on these capabilities.

title: REBA: A Revealed Belief Automaton Framework for Online Planning in Continuous POMDPs
summary: Online planning in continuous partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) using $ω$-regular specifications requires handling continuous belief dynamics within the finite symbolic memory in order to track temporal progress. Existing methods based on either direct search in belief space or predefined discrete abstractions suffer from drawbacks, e.g., lack of symbolic memory for long-horizon logical progress or difficult to certify from noisy online beliefs. As such, obtaining reliable symbolic states online from continuous observations remains a challenge. To address this issue, we introduce the Revealed Belief Automaton (REBA), an event-driven framework that advances the research from global belief-space discretization to a fundamental new way of thinking, namely online certification of revelation events. Specifically, we propose an online revelation method that, through information-theoretic gates, can dynamically analyse and establish belief abstraction from the continuous belief space by discovering reliable anchors among noisy beliefs. We then develop an incremental topology adaptation mechanism over the certified anchors to realise the online finite Belief Automaton. By combining with the $ω$-regular specification, REBA is able to support formal parity policy synthesis without a predefined discrete abstraction, which in turn can guide the Monte Carlo Tree Search process to perform online search beyond its local horizon. In addition, we design an error decomposition analysis which can assess the effectiveness and reliability of this discrete guidance for the underlying continuous POMDP. Empirical evaluations in patrolling and navigation scenarios show that REBA matches or exceeds all evaluated baselines, with primary metric gains of +17.0\% to +47.4\% over state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: REBA is an event-driven framework for online planning in continuous POMDPs with ω-regular specifications, using information-theoretic gates to reveal reliable belief anchors and incrementally build a finite Belief Automaton without predefined discrete abstractions, outperforming baselines by +17% to +47.4%.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for online planning in continuous POMDPs with ω-regular specifications suffer from either lack of symbolic memory for long-horizon logical progress or difficulty in certifying discrete abstractions from noisy online beliefs, motivating the need for a framework that can dynamically obtain reliable symbolic states online.
AI.method: REBA proposes an online revelation method using information-theoretic gates to dynamically analyze and establish belief abstraction from continuous belief space by discovering reliable anchors among noisy beliefs, then incrementally adapts topology over certified anchors to build a finite Belief Automaton, combined with ω-regular specification for formal parity policy synthesis guiding Monte Carlo Tree Search.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations in patrolling and navigation scenarios show REBA matches or exceeds all evaluated baselines, with primary metric gains of +17.0% to +47.4% over state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: REBA advances from global belief-space discretization to online certification of revelation events, enabling reliable discrete guidance for continuous POMDP planning without predefined abstractions, with an error decomposition analysis to assess effectiveness and reliability.

title: A Taxonomy of Conceptual Alignment in Human-Robot Dialogue
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. To be presented at RO-MAN 2026
summary: Successful conversations require speakers to align on the meaning of concepts, a challenging but crucial task for human-robot interaction. Understanding the process of establishing such alignment is hindered by competing interpretations of the term and isolated, unidirectional investigations of its design space. This paper argues for a design-centric understanding of conceptual alignment as a bidirectional and co-constructive process. We introduce a taxonomy that characterizes conceptual alignment dialogues along what triggers its initiation and what level(s) of conceptual understanding it concerns. We further present a dialogue act schema as an operational tool that captures the interactional moves through which alignment is achieved. Together, these contributions provide a structured foundation for analyzing, comparing, and designing conceptual alignment in human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a design-centric understanding of conceptual alignment in human-robot interaction as a bidirectional, co-constructive process, introducing a taxonomy and dialogue act schema to analyze and design such alignment.
AI.motivation: Successful human-robot conversation requires aligned conceptual understanding, but current research is hindered by competing definitions and isolated, unidirectional investigations of the design space.
AI.method: The authors propose a taxonomy characterizing conceptual alignment dialogues by initiation triggers and levels of conceptual understanding, along with a dialogue act schema operationalizing interactional moves for achieving alignment.
AI.result: A structured foundation including a taxonomy and dialogue act schema for analyzing, comparing, and designing conceptual alignment in human-robot interaction.
AI.conclusion: Conceptual alignment should be understood as bidirectional and co-constructive, and the proposed taxonomy and schema enable systematic analysis and design of this process.

title: Human vs Machine Mathematical Difficulty on Project Euler: An Experimental Analysis
summary: We study how the effort and success probability of frontier AI systems scale with human difficulty on problems from Project Euler, an online platform of computational mathematics problems. Our dataset, from the MathArena benchmark, consists of 3840 attempts across 50 problems and 26 model configurations, with problem difficulty measured by the site's public human solve times. Motivated by a proposal of Timothy Gowers, we test a power-law relation $t_{\text{machine}} = a \cdot t_{\text{human}}^b$ between generated-token cost per successful answer and human time, and find $b < 1$ for 20 of the 25 models with usable fits, including the strongest base models; this operationalization therefore does not support an earlier prediction that machines scale worse than humans with difficulty. We also investigate whether success probability on the tested problems can be modeled by a simple exponential decay $p_{\text{success}} = e^{c t_{\text{human}}}$, predicting a linear relation between $\log p_{\text{success}}$ and $t_{\text{human}}$. Using a binning approach for data aggregation we find moderate empirical support (median bin-level $R^2 = 0.92$ across the 22 best-covered configurations) for this model. Following METR, we also fit logistic success curves and extract 50\% task-length horizons $h_{50}$; the strongest configurations in our 20 April 2026 snapshot reach roughly $2.5$--$4.3$ hours on our fastest-five human baseline, with a log-linear fit through the state-of-the-art frontier giving a descriptive doubling time of about $75$~days for the SOTA $h_{50}$.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how frontier AI systems' effort and success probability scale with human difficulty on Project Euler problems. It finds that machine cost scales sublinearly with human time (b<1 for most models), contradicting earlier predictions of worse scaling. Success probability follows an exponential decay model with moderate support. The 50% task-length horizon for the strongest models reaches 2.5-4.3 hours, with the SOTA horizon doubling approximately every 75 days.
AI.motivation: To test whether machine performance on difficult reasoning tasks scales worse than human performance with problem difficulty, motivated by a proposal from Timothy Gowers that AI systems may require disproportionately more compute as tasks become harder.
AI.method: Analyzed 3840 attempts across 50 Project Euler problems and 26 model configurations from the MathArena benchmark. Used public human solve times as difficulty measure. Tested power-law relation between token cost and human time, exponential decay model for success probability, and logistic success curves for task-length horizons.
AI.result: Found b<1 for 20 of 25 usable model fits (sublinear scaling), contradicting the prediction that machines scale worse. Exponential decay model showed median bin-level R^2=0.92. Strongest models had h50 of 2.5-4.3 hours on fastest-five human baseline, with SOTA h50 doubling time of ~75 days.
AI.conclusion: Machine scaling with problem difficulty is more favorable than previously predicted, and frontier AI capabilities on reasoning tasks are improving rapidly with a doubling time of roughly 75 days for the 50% task-length horizon.

title: Do Rigid-Body Simulators Dream of Soft Robots? Learning Contact-Rich Manipulation for Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots
summary: Learning contact-rich, whole-body manipulation for soft continuum robots is held back by the lack of simulation infrastructure that has accelerated rigid-robot manipulation. Existing soft robot simulators are physically grounded but lack the contact handling, actuation support, or learning integration needed for contact-rich manipulation; rigid-body approximations offer these capabilities but sacrifice physical grounding. We bridge this gap for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) by deriving a continuum-mechanics-informed discretization that places the soft robot natively inside MuJoCo, unifying tendon forces, body contact, and dynamics in a single physics pipeline. We validate the simulator against a Cosserat rod reference (static and dynamic) and real TDCR hardware. We then train state-based imitation learning policies via teleoperation in simulation and deploy them zero-shot to a physical 3-segment TDCR on a 7-DoF Franka arm across two contact-rich manipulation tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich manipulation with continuum robots.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel simulation framework that places tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) natively inside MuJoCo using a continuum-mechanics-informed discretization, enabling sim-to-real transfer of contact-rich whole-body manipulation policies for the first time.
AI.motivation: Learning contact-rich manipulation for soft continuum robots is hindered by the lack of simulation infrastructure that has accelerated rigid-robot manipulation. Existing soft robot simulators lack contact handling, actuation support, or learning integration needed for contact-rich manipulation, while rigid-body approximations sacrifice physical grounding.
AI.method: The authors derive a continuum-mechanics-informed discretization that places the TDCR natively inside MuJoCo, unifying tendon forces, body contact, and dynamics in a single physics pipeline. The simulator is validated against a Cosserat rod reference and real TDCR hardware. State-based imitation learning policies are trained via teleoperation in simulation and deployed zero-shot to a physical 3-segment TDCR on a 7-DoF Franka arm.
AI.result: The simulator matches both static and dynamic Cosserat rod references and real hardware. Imitation learning policies trained entirely in simulation transfer zero-shot to the physical robot across two contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating the first sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich manipulation with continuum robots.
AI.conclusion: The MuJoCo-native TDCR simulator bridges the gap between physically grounded soft robot simulation and the contact handling/learning integration needed for contact-rich manipulation, enabling sim-to-real policy transfer for continuum robots.

title: IRumAI: Reinforcement Learning for Indian Rummy
summary: Despite its massive player base and complex hidden-information dynamics, Indian Rummy has received no reinforcement learning attention. Existing agents rely on combinatorial search, which is tactically strong but slow at inference. We present IRumAI, the first RL agent for the domain. IRumAI integrates Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), meld-aware observation encoding, deadwood-driven reward shaping, and a dual-branch convolutional architecture. IRumAI is RL-trained solely against weak heuristics, after a one-time behaviour-cloning warm-start on stronger demonstration data. It generalises to defeat the entire baseline hierarchy, including a 53.9% win rate against the strongest search-based opponent unseen during RL training. Bypassing explicit search, IRumAI requires just 0.33 ms per action, which is over 7,000x faster than the state-of-the-art heuristic. Ablations validate our architectural choices, and linear probing reveals that the network implicitly models the opponent's hidden hand from public interactions.

AI.tldr: IRumAI is the first RL agent for Indian Rummy, using PPO, meld-aware encoding, deadwood-driven rewards, and a dual-branch CNN. Trained only against weak heuristics (with a behaviour-cloning warm-start), it beats all baselines including a 53.9% win rate vs. the strongest search-based opponent, while being 7,000x faster (0.33 ms/action). Ablations confirm the architecture, and linear probing shows the network implicitly models opponent's hidden hand.
AI.motivation: Indian Rummy has a massive player base and complex hidden-information dynamics but has received no reinforcement learning attention; existing agents rely on slow combinatorial search.
AI.method: IRumAI integrates PPO, meld-aware observation encoding, deadwood-driven reward shaping, and a dual-branch convolutional architecture. It is RL-trained solely against weak heuristics after a one-time behaviour-cloning warm-start on stronger demonstration data.
AI.result: IRumAI defeats the entire baseline hierarchy, achieving a 53.9% win rate against the strongest search-based opponent unseen during RL training. It requires only 0.33 ms per action, over 7,000x faster than the state-of-the-art heuristic.
AI.conclusion: RL can produce a highly efficient and effective agent for Indian Rummy without explicit search; the network implicitly models the opponent's hidden hand from public interactions.

title: SPiralRoll: A Novel Adjustable-Stiffness Underactuated 3-DoF Joint with Torsion Springs for Rolling Robots
summary: Compliant mechanisms are important in robotics because they can improve adaptability, safety, and energy efficiency while reducing hardware complexity. This paper presents SPiralRoll, a novel torsion-spring-based underactuated compliant mechanism for rolling robots and compliant robotic actuation. The mechanism uses arc-distributed elastic members and two motor inputs to realize three physically observable output motions: rotational motion, radial expansion/contraction, and axial spin induced by nonlinear compliant deformation. Two configurations, namely full-arc and single-arc designs, are developed and experimentally evaluated. Beyond benchtop validation, the mechanism is integrated into a spherical rolling robot, where proof-of-concept experiments demonstrate forward rolling and turning. The results show that the full-arc design provides better structural support and smoother deformation, whereas the single-arc design yields larger deformation and stronger inertial excitation, making it more suitable for pendulum-driven rolling locomotion. Overall, SPiralRoll provides a low-cost, compact, and fully 3D-printable solution for underactuated compliant rolling robots and adaptive robotic joints.

AI.tldr: SPiralRoll is a novel torsion-spring-based underactuated compliant mechanism that uses arc-distributed elastic members and two motor inputs to produce three output motions (rotation, radial expansion/contraction, axial spin). Two configurations (full-arc and single-arc) are tested, with the mechanism integrated into a spherical rolling robot for forward rolling and turning. The full-arc design offers better structural support and smoother deformation, while the single-arc design provides larger deformation and stronger inertial excitation for pendulum-driven locomotion. The mechanism is low-cost, compact, and fully 3D-printable.
AI.motivation: Compliant mechanisms improve robot adaptability, safety, and energy efficiency while reducing hardware complexity, but existing solutions for rolling robots and compliant actuation face trade-offs between simplicity, controllability, and mechanical performance.
AI.method: SPiralRoll uses arc-distributed elastic members with two motor inputs to achieve three observable output motions (rotational, radial, axial) via nonlinear compliant deformation. Two designs—full-arc and single-arc—are implemented, benchtop-tested, and integrated into a spherical rolling robot for proof-of-concept locomotion experiments.
AI.result: Both designs successfully realize the three output motions. The full-arc design provides superior structural support and smoother deformation; the single-arc design achieves larger deformation and stronger inertial excitation, making it more suitable for pendulum-driven rolling. The spherical robot demonstrates forward rolling and turning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: SPiralRoll is an effective, low-cost, compact, fully 3D-printable underactuated compliant mechanism suitable for rolling robots and adaptive robotic joints, with design-specific trade-offs between structural stability and deformation capacity.

title: CFAgentBench: A Reproducible Environment and Benchmark for Autonomous Construction-Finance Agents
comment: 28 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables. Benchmark, environment spec, and app contract released. First open-weight three-model sweep (k=5) on a 40-task oracle-validated executable suite; frontier-model leaderboard committed in the roadmap
summary: We introduce CFAgentBench, a reproducible, self-hostable environment and benchmark for autonomous construction-finance agents: a CFO/controller-class agent operating across the real software stack a US construction finance team runs - ERP, project management, email, documents, pay applications, payroll, certified payroll, lien waivers, and bank/treasury portals. It contains 1,014 machine-gradeable task specifications across 8 domains and 77 families, every family grounded in a real source; a self-validated subset of 40 tasks (54 with a project-management extension) is compiled into oracle-validated executable evaluators, the runnable suite reported here. Following WebArena, the benchmark runs on an executable environment rather than static traces: 35 mock applications (31 reconciled to one company book, plus 4 PM platforms) over 9 archetypes, each implementing a uniform self-hostable app contract, so every task is graded by functional correctness - a state diff plus forbidden-side-effect checks plus required-output regexes - with an LLM judge used only for reply quality, never as reward. A distinguishing principle is a money-movement guard: 278 instances embed a payment, payroll, e-signature, or e-filing step where the correct behavior is to stop and stage for human approval, and executing even the correct transaction fails the task. The public split (n=711) is sized for a 95% Wilson half-width of +/-4.1%; a private, contamination-protected split (n=303) is reserved for remote scoring. In a first three-model open-weight sweep (k=5), the strongest agent reaches pass^1 = 0.67 but only pass^5 = 0.38 - losing 43% of its successes when required to repeat them under temperature-0 decoding. The within-model pass^1 to pass^5 collapse and sharp per-domain heterogeneity are clear evidence that single-attempt accuracy overstates deployable construction-finance competence.

AI.tldr: CFAgentBench is a reproducible benchmark for autonomous construction-finance agents with 1,014 tasks across 8 domains, 35 mock apps, and a money-movement guard. First tests show a strong agent achieves pass^1=0.67 but pass^5=0.38, revealing significant unreliability.
AI.motivation: Construction finance involves complex, multi-system workflows (ERP, PM, payroll, lien waivers, bank portals) where errors have direct financial consequences. Existing benchmarks lack domain-specific, executable environments for evaluating autonomous agents in this high-stakes setting.
AI.method: Built a self-hostable executable environment with 35 mock applications (31 unified under one company book + 4 PM platforms) across 9 archetypes. Contains 1,014 tasks (711 public, 303 private) from 8 domains and 77 families. Tasks graded by functional correctness via state diff, forbidden-side-effect checks, and output regexes. Includes a money-movement guard where executing any transaction (even correct) fails the task. Evaluated 3 open-weight models with k=5 runs.
AI.result: Best model achieves pass^1=0.67 but drops to pass^5=0.38 under temperature-0 decoding (a 43% loss). Clear within-model collapse and sharp per-domain heterogeneity, indicating single-attempt accuracy overstates real competence.
AI.conclusion: Current open-weight agents are not reliable enough for construction-finance tasks. The large drop from pass^1 to pass^5 shows that repeated success is far lower than single-attempt accuracy, demonstrating the need for more robust agents and highlighting that single-shot benchmarks overestimate deployable competence in high-stakes financial domains.

title: BLENDS: Bayesian Learning-Enhanced Deep Smoothing for GNSS-Denied Environments
summary: Maintaining accurate navigation during GNSS outages remains a significant challenge for autonomous systems relying on low-cost inertial sensors. While classical smoothing methods, such as the two-filter smoother and Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother, exploit measurements collected before and after an outage, their performance remains limited by the accuracy of conventional GNSS measurements. This paper presents Bayesian learning-enhanced navigation with deep smoothing (BLENDS), a transformer-based framework that augments Bayesian smoothing with learned covariance adaptation and state correction. The proposed method preserves the statistical foundations of Bayesian estimation while leveraging data-driven learning to improve navigation accuracy. Evaluations on the quadrotor dataset with GNSS outages demonstrate that BLENDS consistently outperforms both model-based smoothers, achieving up to 25.6% improvement in the position root mean square error while also reducing estimation uncertainty. Furthermore, BLENDS learns to compensate for the systematic bias between conventional GNSS positioning and RTK ground truth, enabling accuracy beyond that achievable with conventional GNSS measurements alone. The results demonstrate the potential of learning-enhanced Bayesian smoothing for resilient and high-accuracy navigation in GNSS-challenged environments.

AI.tldr: BLENDS is a transformer-based Bayesian smoothing framework that enhances navigation accuracy during GNSS outages by learning covariance adaptation and state correction, achieving up to 25.6% improvement in position RMSE and compensating for systematic GNSS biases.
AI.motivation: Maintaining accurate navigation during GNSS outages is a significant challenge for autonomous systems with low-cost inertial sensors. Classical smoothing methods are limited by the accuracy of conventional GNSS measurements.
AI.method: BLENDS augments Bayesian smoothing with a transformer-based framework that learns covariance adaptation and state correction, preserving Bayesian estimation foundations while incorporating data-driven learning.
AI.result: Up to 25.6% improvement in position root mean square error over model-based smoothers on a quadrotor dataset with GNSS outages, along with reduced estimation uncertainty and compensation for systematic bias between conventional GNSS and RTK ground truth.
AI.conclusion: Learning-enhanced Bayesian smoothing shows strong potential for resilient and high-accuracy navigation in GNSS-challenged environments, achieving accuracy beyond what conventional GNSS measurements alone can provide.

title: Nous: A Predictive World Model for Long-Term Agent Memory
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Preprint; ablations, LongMemEval evaluation, and a controlled comparison against concurrent work (BeliefMem) planned for a future revision
summary: We present Nous, a novel agent memory architecture grounded in the principle that knowledge is prediction, not storage. Rather than persisting facts as database records, vector embeddings, or knowledge-graph triples, Nous maintains a predictive world model: a collection of categorical probability distributions, called dimensions, one per entity-attribute pair observed in conversation. Each incoming observation is scored by its information-theoretic surprise S = -log2 P(obs | D), and the distribution is updated via a closed-form Bayesian posterior. The primary stored artifact is the delta, a record of the shift from prior to posterior belief, rather than the fact itself. Forgetting emerges naturally as entropy decay toward the uniform distribution, and identity resolution is handled through mutual information between entity dimension sets. Evaluated on the LoCoMo long-term conversational memory benchmark across ten conversations (1,540 questions) using GPT-4o-mini as backbone, Nous achieves F1 of 63.50 (single-hop), 55.32 (multi-hop), 58.57 (temporal), and 62.50 (open-domain). Against A-MEM's self-reported GPT-4o-mini numbers, Nous shows substantial gains in three of four categories, though we note that independent citations of A-MEM's results disagree with each other on category assignment, a reproducibility issue we discuss openly rather than resolve unilaterally. We additionally compare against BeliefMem, a concurrently developed system built on the same core premise of belief-based rather than deterministic memory; on the same benchmark and backbone, Nous's self-reported numbers exceed BeliefMem's self-reported numbers on all four categories, though we flag several uncontrolled differences between the two evaluation pipelines that prevent this from being a fully controlled comparison. Nous requires no external vector database or graph engine.

AI.tldr: Nous is a novel agent memory architecture that treats knowledge as prediction, using Bayesian-updated categorical distributions over entity-attribute pairs, storing belief shifts (deltas) rather than facts, with natural forgetting via entropy decay. It achieves strong results on the LoCoMo benchmark (e.g., 63.50 F1 single-hop) without external vector/graph databases, outperforming A-MEM and BeliefMem, though comparisons suffer from reproducibility issues.
AI.motivation: Existing memory architectures for LLM agents store facts as static database records, vector embeddings, or knowledge-graph triples, which fail to capture uncertainty, belief change, and forgetting naturally. The authors argue that knowledge should be prediction (probability distributions over states) rather than storage of fixed facts, enabling more flexible and cognitively plausible memory.
AI.method: Nous maintains a predictive world model as a collection of categorical probability distributions (dimensions), one per entity-attribute pair. Each observation is scored by information-theoretic surprise S = -log2 P(obs | D). Distributions are updated via closed-form Bayesian posterior. The stored artifact is the delta (shift from prior to posterior), not the fact itself. Forgetting emerges via entropy decay toward uniform. Identity resolution uses mutual information between entity dimension sets. No external vector database or graph engine is needed.
AI.result: On LoCoMo benchmark (10 conversations, 1,540 questions) with GPT-4o-mini, Nous achieves F1 of 63.50 (single-hop), 55.32 (multi-hop), 58.57 (temporal), and 62.50 (open-domain). Self-reported gains over A-MEM in 3/4 categories (though reproducibility issues noted in A-MEM's reported numbers). Self-reported numbers exceed BeliefMem on all four categories (though evaluation pipeline differences prevent fully controlled comparison).
AI.conclusion: Nous demonstrates that a predictive, Bayesian memory architecture (knowledge = prediction, not storage) is viable and competitive, achieving strong conversational memory performance without external infrastructure. The work highlights important reproducibility issues in benchmark comparisons and advocates for transparent reporting of such discrepancies rather than unilateral resolution.

title: Scalable Multi-Task Data Generation via Reinforcement Learning for Language-Conditioned Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
summary: A key bottleneck in training generalist policies for bimanual dexterous manipulation is the lack of large-scale, high-quality datasets. Synthetic data generation in simulation provides a scalable alternative to human video demonstrations by overcoming challenges such as morphology mismatch, missing physical interactions, and the generation of robot actions. However, existing approaches based on human teleoperation offer limited task diversity, as object-centric trajectory matching often neglects the feasibility of robot execution. Reinforcement learning (RL) enables broader scalability but is often constrained by handcrafted, task-specific rewards. In this work, we propose a systematic RL-based data generation pipeline that integrates generalizable reward design, effective domain randomization, and language-conditioned task annotations. This pipeline synthesizes diverse, high-quality datasets for dexterous bimanual manipulation and enables training of language-conditioned multi-task policies. Our experiments show that the generated data significantly improves generalization across three representative manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Proposes a systematic RL-based data generation pipeline for bimanual dexterous manipulation that uses generalizable reward design, domain randomization, and language-conditioned annotations to synthesize diverse, high-quality datasets, improving multi-task policy generalization.
AI.motivation: Lack of large-scale, high-quality datasets is a key bottleneck for training generalist bimanual dexterous manipulation policies. Existing methods (human teleoperation, object-centric trajectory matching, handcrafted RL rewards) suffer from limited task diversity, morphology mismatch, and scalability issues.
AI.method: A systematic RL-based data generation pipeline with three components: (1) generalizable reward design, (2) effective domain randomization, and (3) language-conditioned task annotations. The pipeline synthesizes diverse datasets for dexterous bimanual manipulation and trains language-conditioned multi-task policies.
AI.result: Generated data significantly improves generalization across three representative bimanual manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RL-based synthetic data generation approach effectively addresses the data scarcity problem in bimanual dexterous manipulation and enables better generalization for multi-task policies compared to existing alternatives.

title: Attractor Domain Theory: A Mathematical Framework for Cardiovascular Attractor Analysis with Wearable Photoplethysmography (PPG) Validation
summary: The cardiovascular system evolves along a bounded trajectory in physiological state space that converges to a compact geometric object: the cardiac attractor. A wearable photoplethysmograph (PPG) or electrocardiograph (ECG) observes a one-dimensional projection of this attractor; by Takens' embedding theorem, delay coordinates reconstruct its full geometry. Three decades of nonlinear cardiac dynamics have extracted Lyapunov exponents, recurrence statistics, and sample entropy from reconstructed attractors, yet no principled account exists of which attractor properties capture which cardiovascular quantities, or why, leaving feature selection as a search problem and negative results uninterpretable. We introduce Attractor Domain Theory (ADT), which proves that the reconstructed attractor's information partitions into three mutually non-redundant domains: the Geometry Domain G (delay embedding; native capability: artifact rejection), the Ergodic Domain S (asymptotic statistical invariants; native capability: stability estimation), and the Variational Domain V (finite-time Lyapunov exponent field; native capability: hemodynamic inference). We prove a Domain Sufficiency Theorem (the Parseval analog for attractor information) and establish that three domains are necessary and sufficient. Geometry Domain validation via the SCSI framework across 176,742 PPG segments from four datasets yields AUC = 0.757 [0.686-0.828] and NPV = 0.966 after correcting three systematic evaluation artifacts (+0.179 net inflation). Ablation confirms C_NL as the dominant Geometry Domain component (Delta AUC = -0.413) and intra-domain redundancy across five components.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Attractor Domain Theory (ADT), which proves that the reconstructed cardiac attractor's information partitions into three non-redundant domains: Geometry (artifact rejection), Ergodic (stability estimation), and Variational (hemodynamic inference). A Domain Sufficiency Theorem establishes these three domains as necessary and sufficient. Validation on 176,742 PPG segments shows AUC=0.757 and NPV=0.966 after correcting evaluation artifacts.
AI.motivation: Existing nonlinear cardiac dynamics methods (Lyapunov exponents, recurrence statistics, sample entropy) lack a principled framework for understanding which attractor properties capture which cardiovascular quantities, leaving feature selection as an uninterpretable search problem with no way to explain negative results.
AI.method: The authors prove a Domain Sufficiency Theorem (analogous to Parseval's theorem for attractor information) showing the attractor's information partitions into three mutually non-redundant domains: Geometry Domain G (delay embedding), Ergodic Domain S (asymptotic statistical invariants), and Variational Domain V (finite-time Lyapunov exponent field). Validation uses the SCSI framework across 176,742 PPG segments from four datasets with ablation studies.
AI.result: Geometry Domain validation yields AUC=0.757 [0.686-0.828] and NPV=0.966 after correcting three systematic evaluation artifacts that caused +0.179 net inflation. Ablation confirms C_NL as the dominant Geometry Domain component (Delta AUC=-0.413) and reveals intra-domain redundancy across five components.
AI.conclusion: The three-domain decomposition of attractor information (G, S, V) is theoretically necessary and sufficient for characterizing cardiovascular dynamics from reconstructed attractors, providing a principled alternative to heuristic feature selection.

title: ARP: Enhancing Quantized Skill Abstractions via Visual Alignment and Iterative Refinement for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Learning visuomotor policies for long-horizon manipulation remains a fundamental challenge. Recent skill-based imitation learning methods based on discrete quantization have shown promising results by representing complex behaviors as temporally extended skills. However, most existing approaches primarily encode action trajectories into latent skills, yielding weak visual-semantic grounding and limiting the ability to leverage visual observations for skill selection. Moreover, discrete tokenization inevitably incurs precision errors during continuous action generation. To alleviate these issues, we propose Aligned Refinement Policy (ARP), a discrete-skill framework that couples semantic grounding with execution-level refinement. Specifically, ARP introduces (i) a visual--action alignment objective that contrastively aligns visual embeddings with pre-quantized action representations in a shared latent space while preserving a state-independent skill decoder, and (ii) a lightweight Iterative Residual Head (IRH) that performs a two-step refinement to recover fine-grained control for precise execution. Extensive experiments show that ARP achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and Meta-World benchmarks. Moreover, real-robot experiments on the Kuavo 4 Pro humanoid platform further validate its effectiveness, yielding consistent performance gains over several baselines on two challenging manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: ARP introduces visual-action alignment and iterative residual refinement to improve discrete-skill imitation learning for long-horizon manipulation, achieving SOTA on LIBERO, Meta-World, and real-robot humanoid tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing discrete skill-based imitation learning methods lack visual-semantic grounding for skill selection and suffer from precision errors due to discrete tokenization of continuous actions.
AI.method: (i) Visual-action alignment objective that contrastively aligns visual embeddings with pre-quantized action representations in shared latent space while preserving a state-independent skill decoder; (ii) Iterative Residual Head (IRH) for two-step refinement to recover fine-grained control.
AI.result: State-of-the-art on LIBERO and Meta-World benchmarks; consistent performance gains over baselines on Kuavo 4 Pro humanoid real-robot platform for two challenging manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Coupling semantic grounding with execution-level refinement in a discrete-skill framework effectively addresses both skill selection ambiguity and precision loss in long-horizon visuomotor policy learning.

title: When Does a Video-Language Model Stop Watching? Reward Strength Controls the Formation and Reversal of Visual Shortcuts in Multimodal RLVR
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is increasingly applied to large vision-language models (LVLMs), yet outcome-only optimization can drive a model to stop attending to the video and instead exploit linguistic priors -- a failure we call a visual shortcut. While the existence of such perception bypass is by now documented, how it forms, whether it can be undone, and when intervention still helps remain open. We treat the strength of a grounding penalty, lambda, as a control knob and characterize the formation-reversal dynamics of visual shortcuts along the training time axis. On a held-out, out-of-distribution diagnostic set, we find: (i) a sharp onset -- shortcut reliance emerges abruptly over a narrow window of optimization steps and is robust across random seeds; (ii) a monotone dose-response -- increasing lambda progressively suppresses the shortcut, and at an intermediate dose the trajectory first forms and then reverses the shortcut, exposing a hysteresis-like asymmetry between acquiring and removing it; and (iii) a critical intervention window -- applying the penalty before onset arrests shortcut formation, whereas the same penalty applied after consolidation is markedly less effective. Together these results recast visual-shortcut collapse not as a binary defect but as a controllable, time-dependent, and asymmetric process, with direct implications for when and how strongly to regularize multimodal RLVR.

AI.tldr: This paper studies visual shortcut formation in RLVR for LVLMs, showing it emerges abruptly, follows a hysteresis-like asymmetry (harder to reverse than to prevent), and is controllable via a grounding penalty with a critical early intervention window.
AI.motivation: While visual shortcuts (models ignoring video and exploiting linguistic priors) in RLVR-trained LVLMs are known, how they form, whether they can be undone, and when intervention is effective remain open questions.
AI.method: The authors treat a grounding penalty strength λ as a control knob and characterize the formation-reversal dynamics of visual shortcuts over training time, using a held-out OOD diagnostic set to measure shortcut reliance.
AI.result: (i) Sharp onset: shortcut reliance emerges abruptly over a narrow optimization window, robust across seeds. (ii) Monotone dose-response: increasing λ progressively suppresses shortcuts; intermediate λ causes first formation then reversal, showing hysteresis-like asymmetry. (iii) Critical intervention window: early penalty application arrests formation, while the same penalty applied after consolidation is much less effective.
AI.conclusion: Visual-shortcut collapse is not a binary defect but a controllable, time-dependent, asymmetric process, with direct implications for when and how strongly to regularize multimodal RLVR.

title: PenduMorph: Development and Motion Analysis of Pendulum-Actuated Rolling Reconfigurable Spherical Robot with Magnetic-Coupling
summary: This paper presents "PenduMorph", a wireless reconfigurable rolling spherical robot designed as a modular platform for enclosed locomotion and inter-module interaction in challenging environments. The proposed robot extends our previous pendulum-actuated rolling disk concept to a fully enclosed spherical architecture integrating a 2-DoF internal pendulum, onboard control, battery-powered operation, and magnetic docking. The design aims to combine independent rolling mobility with protected hardware and reliable reconfigurability. We first present the robot design and an analytical study of the magnetic coupling mechanism to evaluate retention and interaction between coupled modules. We then experimentally investigate key motion behaviors at both the single-module and dual-module levels, including independent rolling, magnetic coupling, and coordinated coupled motion. The results show that the proposed platform enables stable wireless operation and a set of distinctive reconfigurable rolling behaviors, providing a useful foundation for future modular spherical robots operating in contact-rich and demanding environments.

AI.tldr: PenduMorph is a wireless, reconfigurable rolling spherical robot with a 2-DoF internal pendulum, magnetic docking, and enclosed design for locomotion and inter-module interaction in challenging environments. Experiments validate single and dual-module rolling, magnetic coupling, and coordinated motion.
AI.motivation: To extend a pendulum-actuated rolling disk concept to a fully enclosed spherical robot that combines independent rolling mobility, protected hardware, and reliable reconfigurability for operation in contact-rich and demanding environments.
AI.method: Design of a spherical robot with 2-DoF internal pendulum, onboard control, battery power, and magnetic docking; analytical study of magnetic coupling; experimental investigation of single and dual-module rolling, coupling, and coordinated motion.
AI.result: Stable wireless operation and a set of distinctive reconfigurable rolling behaviors at both single-module and dual-module levels, including independent rolling, magnetic coupling, and coordinated coupled motion.
AI.conclusion: The PenduMorph platform provides a useful foundation for future modular spherical robots operating in contact-rich and demanding environments.

title: Can Reasoning Models Detect Changes to their Chains of Thought?
summary: There are many reasons one may want to edit a model's chain of thought (CoT) -- e.g., to prefill it with reasoning from a stronger model or to remove steps that may yield unsafe outputs. The success of these interventions plausibly depends on a model's inability to notice them, as the model may alter its behavior if it suspects tampering. In this work, we study whether recent reasoning models are able to detect such interventions on their CoTs under a variety of conditions: both during reasoning and after it, and when prefilled both with their own CoTs and with those of other models. Broadly, we find that (i) models exhibit only very modest detection accuracy; (ii) models struggle to identify *how* their CoT was modified; and (iii) models are about as good at detecting changes to their own CoTs as to those of other models.

AI.tldr: Recent reasoning models show only modest ability to detect edits or interventions made to their chain-of-thought (CoT), including prefilling with other models' reasoning or removing unsafe steps, and struggle to identify how their CoT was modified.
